traditional_medicine.uses: Anti-inflammatory, emollient, diuretic; used for skin diseases (psoriasis, wounds, burns), mucous membrane inflammation (respiratory/digestive), intestinal disorders, diarrhea, rheumatism, urinary issues, aheadaches/convulsions(Acero et al., 2023).

scientific_data.experimental: Ethanol extract of A. mollis leaves (high benzoxazinoid and phenylpropanoid content) significantly inhibited LPS-induced NO production in RAW 264.7 macrophages in vitro; DIBOA and verbascoside identified as principal active compounds responsible for anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects respectively. Combination of DIBOA + verbascoside showed synergistic tyrosinase inhibition (IC50 lower for combination than either compound alone). ( Matos et al., 2018)Hexane extract of A. mollis rhizomes (GC-MS profiling: beta-sitosterol 70% of detected compounds, campesterol, stigmasterol, fatty acids): dose-dependent inhibition of LPS-induced NO production in RAW 264.7 macrophages; HepG2 cell pre-treatment with rhizome extract prevented ROS-induced oxidative stress both via direct ROS scavenging and upregulation of antioxidant enzymes (SOD, catalase, GPx). First reported rhizome phytochemical characterization and pharmacological study. ( Acero et al., 2023)A. mollis leaf ethanolic extract showed antifungal activity against C. albicans (MIC 8 mg/mL), A. niger (MIC 4 mg/mL), and T. mentagrophytes (MIC 2 mg/mL); DPPH radical scavenging IC50 = 18.4 microg/mL (leaf extract); total phenol content 58.6 mg GAE/g DW; anthraquinone content 1.8 mg/g DW. (Jara et al .,2017)First-ever development of A. mollis leaf topical formulations for transdermal drug delivery; three formulations compared (oil-in-water cream, Carbopol 940 hydrogel, Pluronic F-127 hydrogel) via Franz diffusion cell in vitro permeation testing (HPLC-PDA quantification); DIBOA showed Weibull release kinetics in Carbopol and Pluronic F-127 formulations; identified as a candidate active agent for topical anti-inflammatory and skin-depigmenting pharmaceutical applications. ( Matos et al.,2024)

safety_profile.toxicity: Acute toxicity testing of hydroethanolic extract showed no mortality at doses up to 1500 mg/kg and an LD₅₀ >2000 mg/kg in experimental animals(Boubertakh et al., 2025).

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antioxidant, antimicrobial (antibacterial against oral microorganisms, antifungal against phytopathogenic and clinical fungi), anti-psoriatic, antidiabetic (α-amylase inhibitory), insecticidal (against Culex quinquefasciatus and Musca domestica), photoprotective (SPF activity in UV-B spectrum), cytotoxic/antiproliferative and neurotrophic activities.Phytochemical profile: Essential oil composition is highly variable depending on geographic origin. The major constituents include linalool, artemisia ketone, 2,7-dimethyl-4,6-octadien-2-ol, santolina alcohol, borneol, sabinol, trans-sabinyl acetate, α-thujone, viridiflorol, and β-pinene. Polar fractions are dominated by guaianolide sesquiterpene lactones, mainly matricarin and desacetylmatricarin, together with a new epimeric sesquiterpene lactone. Flavonoids identified include santin, 6-hydroxykaempferol 3,6-dimethyl ether, luteolin, apigenin, apigenin 7-O-glucoside, and two novel 6-methoxyflavonols. Phenolic acids (20 in the EtOAc extract and 22 in the BuOH extract), as well as piperidine amides and additional guaianolides, have also been characterized.

scientific_data.experimental: EO from A. ligustica naturalized in central Italy (Camerino, Marche region) was characterized by GC-MS and its antibacterial activity against oral cariogenic bacteria evaluated; β-pinene (11.7%), viridiflorol (9.8%), terpinen-4-ol (8.0%) and linalool (7.7%) were the dominant components; the study concluded that A. ligustica EO is an ideal candidate for anti-cariogenic formulations in oral hygiene products due to its selective antimicrobial profile and favorable safety characteristics.(Maggi et al.,2009)EO from A. ligustica inflorescences (central Italy, linalool 24.8%, viridiflorol 9.6%, β-pinene 6.4%, 1,8-cineole 5.8%, terpinen-4-ol 5.3% as major constituents) was evaluated for antifungal activity by in vitro disc agar diffusion and agar vapor assay against 5 phytopathogenic fungi: Fusarium graminearum, F. semitectum, F. avenaceum, Pythium cryptogea and Alternaria alternata; the EO showed good antifungal activity against all five fungal strains, achieving 61.9–100% inhibition depending on the assay method and strain, being a valid candidate in the fight against plant pathogens that harm traditional Mediterranean crops.( Giamperi et al.,2018)A. ligustica EO was evaluated alongside seven commercially valuable EOs in acute and sub-lethal toxicity assays against two public health-relevant insects: Culex quinquefasciatus (4th instar larvae — a vector of filariasis, St. Louis encephalitis and West Nile virus) and Musca domestica adults (a housefly transmitter of more than 100 pathogens); A. ligustica EO showed insecticidal activity at LC50 = 89.5 µL/L against 4th instar C. quinquefasciatus larvae and LD50 = 121 µg/adult against M. domestica adults; sub-lethal exposure assays also evaluated effects on insect longevity, fertility and fecundity, establishing A. ligustica EO as a botanical insecticide candidate against these disease vectors.( Benelli et al.,2008)DPPH radical scavenging activity and α-amylase inhibitory activity (—the key enzyme of starch digestion and a primary antidiabetic drug target) were comparatively assessed across methanolic extract and sequential fractions (petroleum ether, chloroform, ethyl acetate, n-butanol, water) of A. ligustica aerial parts; this was the first pharmacological study demonstrating antidiabetic potential for this species and established the fractionation-dependent distribution of bioactivity, with polar fractions showing superior antidiabetic effect.(Conforti et al.,2005)

safety_profile.toxicity: Acute oral toxicity testing of aqueous leaf extract of Apium graveolens in mice showed no mortality up to 2000 mg/kg (LD₅₀ >2000 mg/kg). Sub-acute administration for 28 days suggested good tolerability at 200 mg/kg, whereas higher doses (400 mg/kg) produced biochemical changes; therefore, prolonged use requires caution(Kma et al., 2023).
safety_profile.plant_interactions: The essential oil of Apium graveolens exhibited significant antioxidant activity, particularly when combined with the essential oils of Thymus vulgaris and Coriandrum sativum. Using FRAP and ABTS assays, the study demonstrated a synergistic enhancement of antioxidant capacity, with the most effective mixture containing 66.7% T. vulgaris, 16.7% C. sativum, and 16.7% A. graveolens. Among the three oils, T. vulgaris contributed the most to the antioxidant effect, followed by A. graveolens and C. sativum, highlighting the potential of A. graveolens essential oil as a natural antioxidant in synergistic formulations for food preservation. (Crespo et al.,2019)

traditional_medicine.dosage: According to the British Herbal Pharmacopoeia, the recommended dose of dried fruits is 500 mg–2 g, administered three times daily(Tobyn et al., 2011).

scientific_data.clinical: Celery seed extract showed a possible blood pressure–lowering effect in hypertensive patients in randomized clinical trials(Shayani Rad et al., 2022). Some studies reported improvements in metabolic parameters (blood pressure, triglycerides, uric acid) (Escobedo-Gutiérrez et al., 2026).
scientific_data.experimental: EXPERIMENTAL DATA:Apium graveolens exhibited strong antioxidant activity in DPPH, ABTS, and reducing power in vitro assays, showing potent free-radical scavenging activity (din et al., 2015).Leaf extract of Apium graveolens significantly reduced inflammation in carrageenan-induced paw edema in rats (Mencherini et al., 2007).Apium graveolens extract inhibited α-amylase and α-glucosidase in vitro and improved glucose homeostasis, demonstrating antidiabetic potential (Assaggaf, 2025)Apium graveolens extract protected against acetaminophen-induced acute liver toxicity in rats by reducing oxidative stress and inflammation (Emad et al., 2020).Root flavonoid extract significantly reduced serum cholesterol and triglyceride levels in high-fat diet-induced hyperlipidemic rats (He et al., 2019).

safety_profile.toxicity: Adiantum capillus-veneris is generally considered safe based on available preclinical evidence, with no significant acute toxicity observed at oral doses up to 2,000 mg/kg. However, clinical safety data in humans are limited, and its long-term safety has not been established. Therefore, its use during pregnancy and lactation is not recommended due to insufficient safety evidence. .(Dehdari & Hajimehdipoor, 2018) Drug-Plant interactions.Antihyperlipidemic medications:Enhanced lipid-lowering effects (LDL, VLDL, cholesterol) may increase the danger of excessive lipid reduction.Antidiabetic medications:may raise the risk of hypoglycemia by increasing insulin secretion and its glucose-lowering impact.Levothyroxine:may raise the levels of thyroid hormones (T3, T4), which could intensify thyroid activity and raise the possibility of hyperthyroid consequences. (Humadi , 2026)Plant-Plant interactions:

pharmacology.activities: Pharmocological activities:Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, analgesic/antinociceptive, antidiabetic/hypoglycemic, antimicrobial (antibacterial and antifungal), wound healing, anti-urolithiatic/diuretic, antidiarrheal, antispasmodic, anti-asthmatic, hypocholesterolemic, anti-obesity, hair growth-promoting (anti-alopecia), anticonvulsant/neuroprotective, and nephroprotective/detoxifying effects.Phytochemical profile:The plant is rich in triterpenoids (adiantane, filicane, and hopane types, e.g., isoadiantone, 4-α-hydroxyfilican-3-one), flavonoids and glycosides (quercetin, rutin, kaempferol, astragalin, isoquercitrin), phenolic acids (chlorogenic, caffeic, ferulic, p-coumaric acids), along with tannins, saponins, carotenoids, phytosterols, mucilage, and essential oils (carvone, carvacrol, thymol as major components). It also contains minerals (high Ca and K) and trace elements. These compounds, especially flavonoids, triterpenoids, and phenolics, underpin its bioactivities.

Essential oil and flavonoid extracts show potent activity, sometimes comparable or superior to standards like BHT or ascorbic acid. ( Qadir et al.,2025)Ethyl acetate fractions and isolated triterpenoids inhibit NO, PGE2, TNF-α, IL-6; suppress NF-κB; effective in carrageenan paw edema, LPS-induced models, and writhing/hot plate/tail-flick tests. Supports traditional use for inflammatory conditions. ( Ibraheim et al .,2011)Aqueous/methanolic extracts lower fasting blood glucose in streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats, comparable to acarbose in some assays; may involve flavonoids/tannins and pancreatic effects. ( Dehdari &Hajimehdipoor ,2018)Improves angiogenesis, fibroblast protection (aqueous/butanol fractions); ointments with the plant show benefits in diabetic wound models. (Nilforoushzadeh et al.,2014)Ethanolic extracts increase follicular density and anagen/telogen ratio in testosterone-induced alopecia mouse models. ( Olimat , 2020 )Reduces calcium oxalate crystals, serum Ca/P/urea in rat models; inhibits crystallization; supports UTI treatment and Candida reduction in some studies. ( Olimat , 2020 )Crude extracts inhibit castor oil-induced diarrhea and K+-induced contractions in rabbit jejunum.Effective in histamine-induced asthma models in guinea pigs.( Dehdari &Hajimehdipoor ,2018) Hypocholesterolemic (lowers TC/LDL in high-cholesterol diet rats); anti-obesity (phospholipase inhibition); goitrogenic/anti-thyroidal effects; neuroprotective/anticonvulsant (PTZ/MES models),detoxifying/nephroprotective. scientific_data.experimental: Quantitative determinations of cardiac glycosides (herzglykoside) were performed on different organs (herb, leaves, stems, roots, flowers, fruits) and developmental stages of Adonis dentata (wild) and A. autumnalis (cultivated). In A. dentata, glycoside content across organs was relatively higher during the fruiting stage compared to A. autumnalis. The highest overall content in related studies (e.g., A. autumnalis) occurred in leaves at fruit ripening. This supports cardiotonic potential via cardiac glycosides, similar to digitalis-like effects. (Elkiey et al., 1967)Extracts and glycosides show positive inotropic effects, used traditionally for heart conditions, heart failure, and arrhythmias. Genus extracts (e.g., total glycosides) demonstrate cardiotonic activity in pharmacological studies. ( Shang et al.,2019)Other activities for adonis: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, antiangiogenic, diuretic, central nervous system effects, and acaricidal properties. These stem from glycosides, flavones, etc. ( Shang et al.,2019)

safety_profile.toxicity: Agrimonia eupatoria extract is considered practically non-toxic, with no mortality or morphological alterations of internal organs observed following intragastric administration at doses exceeding 5,000 mg/kg. Under the tested conditions, no LD₅₀ could be established. (Huzio et al., 2022)Drug-Plant innteractions:Plant-Plant interactions:

scientific_data.experimental: Experimantal data:Novel steroidal saponins from Allium porrum bulbs were tested in an acute inflammation model using carrageenan-induced mouse paw edema. The saponins significantly inhibited edema formation in both early (histamine/serotonin-mediated) and late (prostaglandin-mediated) phases, with potency comparable to dexamethasone. ( Monika & Sakthi Abiram ,2018)Ethanol extracts of leek stems and leaves (prepared by ultrasound-assisted extraction) were evaluated for total phenols/flavonoids and activity via DPPH, ORAC, and FRAP assays (compared to vitamin C and BHT). Stem extracts showed higher phenolic/flavonoid content and antioxidant capacity; green leaves outperformed white parts. Phenolics and ascorbic acid correlated strongly with activity. ( Monika & Sakthi Abiram ,2018)Oral administration of alcoholic extract of Allium porrum (250 and 500 mg/kg) in L-NAME-induced hypertensive rats significantly reduced elevated systolic blood pressure compared to controls, linked to nitric oxide pathways. . ( Monika & Sakthi Abiram ,2018)Extracts of Allium porrum (2.5 and 5.0 mg/ml) were incubated with everted rat intestinal sacs. They significantly inhibited D-glucose absorption and transport across the intestine (more potent than garlic at tested concentrations). ( Monika & Sakthi Abiram ,2018)Hydroalcoholic bulb extract (250, 500, and 1000 mg/kg) was given to rabbits on a hypercholesterolemic diet for 12 weeks. It dose-dependently reduced plasma total cholesterol and atherogenic index, with benefits increasing over the treatment period. ( Monika & Sakthi Abiram ,2018)Aqueous leaf extracts showed zones of inhibition (up to 31 mm) against Gram-positive bacteria (Bacillus subtilis, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae) and moderate activity (24–26 mm) against Gram-negatives (E. coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Proteus vulgaris). Leaf/stem extracts were also effective against Klebsiella pneumoniae and others. Organosulfur compounds contribute to this. ( Monika & Sakthi Abiram ,2018)New spirostanol saponins and dibenzofurans (porric acids A–C) from bulbs inhibited Fusarium culmorum. Leaf/stem extracts showed activity against Candida albicans and Aspergillus niger. ( Monika & Sakthi Abiram ,2018)Glucofructans from hot water extracts and steroidal saponins reduced acute lesions induced by acidified ethanol in models, showing cytoprotective effects interfering with ulcerogenic mechanisms.( Monika & Sakthi Abiram ,2018)Hydroalcoholic extract (200–400 mg/kg or in vitro) demonstrated significant iron chelation (comparable to deferoxamine) in iron-overload rat models, reducing serum iron/ferritin via flavonoid interactions.( Monika & Sakthi Abiram ,2018)Alcoholic extract (250–500 mg/kg) elevated bone mineral density in osteoporotic rats via antioxidant effects; flavonols like kaempferol/quercetin support osteoblastic activity.( Monika & Sakthi Abiram ,2018)

safety_profile.toxicity: Acute toxicity studies conducted according to OECD Guideline 423 showed that Allium sativum ethyl acetate extract caused no mortality or significant clinical, gross pathological, or histopathological changes in rodents following oral administration of 300, 2,000, and 5,000 mg/kg, indicating an oral LD₅₀ > 5,000 mg/kg. In addition, garlic extracts exhibited protective effects against lead nitrate and zearalenone-induced toxicity by reducing oxidative stress and tissue damage, supporting the favorable safety profile of A. sativum(Tudu et al., 2022).Contraindications: Allium sativum L. is contraindicated in individuals with known hypersensitivity to garlic or its constituents and in patients receiving saquinavir/ritonavir therapy due to the potential for clinically significant drug interactions. safety_profile.drug_interactions: Allium sativum (garlic) is associated with several clinically relevant herb–drug interactions. It may enhance the effects of anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs, particularly warfarin, increasing INR and the risk of bleeding. Garlic can also reduce the efficacy of isoniazid, oral contraceptives, and several antiretroviral drugs (e.g., saquinavir, nevirapine, delavirdine, and efavirenz), while potentially interacting with cyclosporine. In addition, garlic may alter the metabolism of drugs that are CYP2E1 and CYP3A4 substrates, thereby affecting their efficacy or toxicity. Because of the significant interaction with saquinavir, the FDA advises against the concomitant use of garlic supplements with this medication. European Medicines Agency. (2017). Assessment report on Allium sativum L., bulbus – Final. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/7686/2013.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Combining the extracts of Allium sativum, Allium cepa, Zingiber officinale, Garcinia kola exhibited favorable synergism, as they provided stronger antibacterial effects on several of the organisms.The combination of Allium sativum and Citrullus colocynthis reduces diabetes mellitus -induced reproductive damage compared to when taken separately. ( Nnamchi et al 2021)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities:antimicrobial effects , antioxidant , Cardiovascular benefits include lipid-lowering (reduction in total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides), mild antihypertensive, antiplatelet, and fibrinolytic properties. Other activities include anti-inflammatory , anticancer , antidiabetic and hepatoprotective effects.Phytochemical profile:organosulfur compounds, which are the primary bioactive constituents. The main precursor is alliin (S-allyl-L-cysteine sulfoxide), which is rapidly converted to allicin (diallyl thiosulfinate) upon crushing the cloves. Other important sulfur-containing compounds include diallyl disulfide (DADS), diallyl trisulfide (DATS), ajoene (E and Z isomers), vinyldithiins, and S-allyl cysteine. Additionally, it contains flavonoids (such as quercetin and kaempferol), phenolic acids, saponins, polysaccharides, and small amounts of vitamins and minerals.

scientific_data.clinical: Clinical studies have demonstrated the therapeutic potential of Allium sativum L. In patients with type 2 diabetes, garlic supplementation improved fasting blood glucose and lipid profile when used alongside conventional antidiabetic therapy. A combination of garlic and curcumin further reduced fasting glucose, HbA1c, LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, and body mass index, while increasing HDL cholesterol. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial involving women with rheumatoid arthritis, supplementation with 1,000 mg/day of garlic for 8 weeks significantly reduced C-reactive protein (CRP), TNF-α, pain severity, disease activity, and fatigue, demonstrating anti-inflammatory benefits. (Tudu et al., 2022)

distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering stage: The plant flowers from March to June, with peak flowering usually during April–May. Harvesting period: Roots: Harvested mainly in autumn (September–November), usually after the aerial parts have dried.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Roots(Elazzouzi et al., 2022).
traditional_medicine.uses: Toothache, salivary stimulant, aphrodisiac, rheumatism, paralysis, digestive issues, neuralgia, and as tonic/stimulant(Elazzouzi et al., 2022).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Root powder : around 0.5–3.5 g in traditional use(Fahim et al., 2025).

scientific_data.experimental: EXPERIMENTAL DATA:In vitro antioxidant and antimicrobial activities of the Anacyclus pyrethrum demonstrated that different plant parts had prominent antioxidant and antimicrobial properties. ( Elazzouzi et al.,2022)The anti-inflammatory effect was studied in vivo using aqueous and methanolic root extracts on xylene-induced rat ear edema and Freund's adjuvant (CFA)-induced paw edema models. The tested extracts significantly reduced both types of edema. Oral administration of 250 and 500 mg/kg reduced CFA-induced mechanical hypersensitivity .( Elazzouzi et al.,2022)Aqueous and methanolic root extracts (AEAPR and MEAPR) at high doses caused a significant decrease in the number of abdominal writhes induced by acetic acid injection (52.2% and 56.7%, respectively), a marked increase in paw withdrawal latency in the hot plate test, and significant inhibition of both phases of the formalin test. This antinociceptive effect was partially reversed by naloxone pretreatment, suggesting partial opioid-mediated mechanisms. (Elazzouzi et al.,2022)The antidepressant activity of root extract was assessed using the forced swim test, tail suspension test, locomotor activity, haloperidol-induced catalepsy, and reserpine/clonidine-induced hypothermia in Swiss male albino mice. The root extract reduced immobility, significantly affected the forced swim and tail suspension tests, increased ambulatory behavior, inhibited haloperidol-induced catalepsy, and reversed clonidine- and reserpine-induced hypothermia — supporting significant antidepressant activity.(Elazzouzi et al.,2022)Studies evaluated the anabolic, aphrodisiac, and reproductive activity of A. pyrethrum in male rats, as well as androgenic and spermatogenic activity of its alkylamide-rich ethanol extract. Additional studies examined the effects of aqueous root extracts on gonadotropins and testosterone serum levels in adult male rats.(Elazzouzi et al.,2022)

safety_profile.toxicity: An acute toxicity study of the total hydroalcoholic extract in mice showed no mortality or toxic signs after oral administration up to 2000 mg/kg, with LD₅₀ >2000 mg/kg, indicating low acute toxicity. Subacute administration showed no major toxic effects at tested doses, although higher prolonged doses produced some hematological and liver changes (Arbabi Bidgoli et al., 2012).

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities : antioxidant (radical scavenging), antimicrobial and antifungal (against bacteria like E. coli, S. aureus), gastroprotective/anti-ulcer (antisecretory), anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antispasmodic, hypolipidemic, diuretic, hepatoprotective, and carminative/digestive effects.Phytochemical profile :Essential oil: Major components include carvone (often 30–50%+), limonene, α-phellandrene, dillapiole, myrcene, and others. Composition varies by plant part, growth conditions, and extraction method.Other compounds: Flavonoids (e.g., kaempferol, rutin), phenolic acids (e.g., chlorogenic acid), coumarins, tannins, terpenoids, fatty acids, and steroids. Seeds and leaves are rich in these phenolics

traditional_medicine.dosage: Infants (1–6 months): 2.3 mg dill water (one teaspoonful of 5 ml preparation) during or after feeding. Infants (6–12 months): 2 teaspoonfuls of dill water during or after feeding (maximum 6 times/day). Adults: Dill oil 0.05–2 ml, 3 times daily or 0.1–0.3 g/day in divided doses. Children: Pure essential oil should not be used in infants and young children; use only appropriate pharmaceutical preparations under medical supervision. Extracts: Dose depends on extract type, age, and health condition. Other preparations: 3 g/day or equivalent. Egyptian Herbal Monograph(2022). Anethum graveolens,210-214.EDA, Egypt

scientific_data.clinical: In 91 hyperlipidemic patients, dill tablets used for 2 months decreased total cholesterol and triglyceride levels, with no significant adverse effects reported(Mirhosseini et al., 2014). In 24 patients with metabolic syndrome, dill extract for 12 weeks improved some lipid parameters, especially triglycerides(Mansouri et al., 2012). In 118 women after cesarean section, dill essential oil reduced intestinal gas, flatulence, and abdominal pain compared with placebo(Fazel et al., 2017).

Carvone and other terpenes contribute; effective in food preservation applications. ( Milenković et al.,2024)Seed extracts show antisecretory and protective effects against HCl/ethanol-induced ulcers in animal models. (et al.,Reduces inflammation and pain in various models. Artemisia absinthium L. preparations are contraindicated in patients with bile duct obstruction, cholangitis, or liver disease. Individuals with gallstones or other biliary disorders should seek medical advice before use, and persistent symptoms lasting more than two weeks require consultation with a healthcare professional. safety_profile.toxicity: Acute toxicity studies reported an intraperitoneal LD₅₀ of 1 g/kg for an Artemisia absinthium extract in rats, while the oral LD₅₀ of the essential oil was 0.96 g/kg in rats. In a 13-week repeated-dose toxicity study, rats receiving up to 2.06 g/kg/day of the extract showed no mortality, no significant changes in body weight, hematological parameters, or histopathology, indicating no toxicologically relevant effects. Toxicity is mainly attributed to thujone, whose repeated administration produced dose-dependent neurotoxicity (convulsions and increased mortality), with a NOEL of 12.5 mg/kg/day in male rats.Contraindications: Artemisia absinthium L. preparations are contraindicated in patients with bile duct obstruction, cholangitis, or liver disease. traditional_medicine.uses: Artemisia absinthium L. has traditionally been used to stimulate appetite, promote digestion, and relieve dyspepsia, hypoacidity, chronic gastritis, and other gastrointestinal complaints. In traditional medicine, it has also been used as a choleretic and for the management of liver disorders, hepatitis, jaundice, diabetes, skin diseases, allergies, scabies, and as a brain tonic.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Herbal tea (infusion): 1–1.5 g of comminuted dried herb infused in 150 mL of boiling water; 2–3 g/day. Expressed juice: 5 mL per dose; 10 mL/day. Tincture (1:5, ethanol 70% v/v): 1 g herbal substance equivalent per dose, taken 3 times daily (3 g/day). European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2020). European Union herbal monograph on Artemisia absinthium L., herba. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/751490/2016 Corr. 1.

scientific_data.clinical: Clinical studies suggest that Artemisia absinthium L. may be beneficial in Crohn’s disease. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, administration of 500 mg capsules three times daily for 10 weeks resulted in clinical remission in 65% of patients, reduced disease activity, improved quality of life, and decreased depressive symptoms. In another randomized trial, 750 mg of dried powdered herb three times daily for 6 weeks significantly improved Crohn’s disease symptoms and reduced TNF-α levels compared with placebo. Additionally, a clinical study in patients with amoebiasis showed that 6 g/day of powdered herb for 15 days relieved symptoms in approximately 85% of cases and eliminated Entamoeba histolytica from stool in 70% of patients. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2017). Assessment report on Artemisia absinthium L., herba. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/751484/2016.
scientific_data.experimental: Methanolic extracts and essential oils from different regions showed strong DPPH scavenging (lowest IC50 ~31 µg/mL) and inhibited Gram-positive/negative bacteria (e.g., up to 31 mm zone vs. E. coli), linked to camphor and chamazulene . (Ksibi et al., 2022)Extracts validated traditional use in in vitro and in vivo models, supporting tissue repair. (Boudjelal et al., 2020)Preclinical studies report hepatoprotective, anti-inflammatory, antiprotozoal, anthelmintic, neuroprotective, antidepressant, and cytotoxic effects, attributed to thujone, flavonoids, and lactones. (Batiha et al., 2020)

scientific_data.clinical: A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study in healthy adults showed that green oat extract improved working memory and multitasking performance after 4 weeks of use. It also reduced physiological stress responses and was well tolerated with no serious side effects reported(Kennedy et al., 2020). Another randomized controlled study showed that wild green oat extract reduced perceived stress and improved sleep quality after 8 weeks of treatment. It also improved overall quality-of-life scores compared with placebo and was considered safe and well tolerated.(Friling et al., 2024).
scientific_data.experimental: Avenanthramides showed potent antioxidant activity and inhibited pro-inflammatory cytokines in cell and animal models (Kim et al., 2021)Oat β-glucan improved glycemic control and insulin sensitivity in human and animal studies. scientific_data.experimental: Experimenta data:The essential oil of Anacyclus valentinus demonstrated potent in vitro antifungal activity against several toxigenic fungi. It was most effective against Fusarium graminearum, Aspergillus parasiticus, and Penicillium expansum (MFC = 1.25 μL/mL), while A. flavus and F. moniliforme were inhibited at 2.5 μL/mL. Higher concentrations (10 μL/mL) were required to achieve fungicidal activity against A. ochraceus and P. citrinum. These findings suggest that A. valentinus essential oil has potential as a natural biocontrol agent for protecting food crops against fungal pathogens. ( Houicher et al.,2018)the aqueous extract of the plant exerted a marked hypoglycemic effect in both normal and diabetic rats. In diabetic treated rats, blood glucose levels began to decrease from the first week of treatment, with reductions reaching 52% during the second week and 55% by the end of the experiment. These changes became statistically significant on days 21 and 28. In normal treated rats, a significant reduction in glycemia was also observed during the final week (p < 0.05). In comparison, treatment with glimepiride produced a smaller, non-significant decrease in blood glucose levels. ( Tadjeddine et al.,2013)Both the essential oil and the oxygenated fraction exhibited notable antioxidant properties. The oxygenated fraction demonstrated the strongest activity, with IC₅₀ values of 8.2 mL/L in the DPPH assay and 5.6 mL/L in the β-carotene bleaching test. In addition, the essential oil of A. valentinus showed strong anti-inflammatory effects, with an IC₅₀ value of 0.3 g/L, exceeding the activity of diclofenac (IC₅₀ = 0.53 g/L). (Ainseba et al.,2024)

safety_profile.toxicity: Atractylis gummifera is a highly toxic plant due to atractyloside and carboxyatractyloside, which block mitochondrial energy production (ATP), causing severe liver and kidney damage. Acute toxicity studies show an LD₅₀ around 115 ± 22 mg/kg in mice, indicating strong toxicity. Poisoning can rapidly lead to vomiting, abdominal pain, acute hepatic and renal failure, coma, and death, and there is no specific antidote, only supportive treatment(Belmahi et al., 2025).

traditional_medicine.uses: Traditionally, Brassica nigra leaves have been used as a sedative, wound-healing agent, digestive remedy, and for treating cough, nausea, vomiting, and nervousness. It has also been used as an antiparasitic remedy and as an insect repellent(Kumar & Kumari, 2021) .
traditional_medicine.dosage: Adults (including elderly): 1.5–5 g of dried drug per single dose, taken as a tea infusion or as an extract prepared with water or ethanol (max. 45% v/v). Children (3–12 years): Use only under medical supervision; preferably non-alcoholic preparations, with dose adjusted according to body weight. Pregnancy & lactation: Use is not recommended without medical advice due to lack of safety studies(Przerwa et al., 2020).

scientific_data.experimental: - An early study reported that the water extract of Ballota nigra subsp. anatolica exhibited antidepressant activity in the forced swimming test. Although its effect was less pronounced than those of amitriptyline and Passiflora extract, the plant extract significantly reduced immobility time compared with the control group, supporting its potential antidepressant properties.( Vural et al.,1996)- Phytochemicals isolated from Ballota nigra, including ballotinone and ballonigrin, have shown molecular docking affinity for the HPV E6 oncoprotein, suggesting a potential role in preventing cervical cancer by disrupting the E6–p53 interaction. Additionally, 7α-acetoxyroyleanone exhibited in vitro cytotoxic activity against pancreatic (MIA PaCa-2) and melanoma (MV-3) cancer cell lines, indicating the plant's potential anticancer properties.( Marimuthu et al.,2017, Fronza et al.,2011):The extract exhibited greater inhibition of BChE (71.58%) than AChE (44.71%), with BChE inhibition exceeding that of the reference drug galantamine, suggesting potential neuroprotective properties. ( Przerwa et al.,2020)Ballota nigra extract demonstrated hypoglycemic activity by reducing blood glucose levels in albino rats. The effect is thought to be mediated through a possible insulinotropic mechanism, although further studies are needed to confirm its mode of action.( Nusier et al.,2007)A 2014 study demonstrated that an extract of B. nigra subsp. curdica from Iran exhibited significant tyrosinase inhibitory activity.( Przerwa et al.,2020 )An ethanolic (EtOH) extract of B. nigra stems was found to reduce the production of δ-hemolysin, a key virulence factor of Staphylococcus aureus, indicating anti-quorum sensing activity. These findings suggest that B. nigra may have potential as an alternative or adjunct to conventional antibiotics. ( Quave et al.,2011)

traditional_medicine.uses: Traditionally, Borago officinalis is used as a food plant and herbal remedy. It is used for metabolic and hormonal regulation, relief of PMS and menopausal symptoms, and as an infusion for colds, flu, bronchitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and kidney inflammation. The seeds are a source of GLA, associated with anti-inflammatory effects. (Lozano-Baena et al., 2016)

scientific_data.clinical: Atopic eczema: A trial in 151 patients using borage oil (GLA source) for 12 weeks showed no significant benefit compared with placebo(Takwale et al., 2003) Rheumatoid arthritis: Borage seed oil studies showed possible improvement in symptoms, but evidence remains limited(Reed et al., 2014). Asthma: A randomized study evaluated borage extract (5 mL, 3 times/day for 1 month) and assessed asthma control and inflammation markers(Mirsadraee et al., 2016) .
scientific_data.experimental: - GLA metabolism/anti-inflammatory mechanism (in vitro/in vivo): Dietary GLA (from borage oil) is elongated to DGLA (dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid) via delta-5-desaturase; DGLA is converted by COX-1/2 to anti-inflammatory PGE1 and 15- HETE (15-hydroxyeicosatrienoic acid) rather than pro-inflammatory PGE2/LTB4 derived from arachidonic acid. Simultaneously, DGLA competitively inhibits delta-5-desaturase reducing AA levels. Borage oil supplementation (3 g/day GLA for 12 weeks) significantly increased DGLA in plasma phospholipids and reduced LTB4 production by stimulated neutrophils vs. sunflower oil control. (Calder, 2006)- Immune modulation (in vitro/animal): Borage seed oil supplementation (3 g GLA/day equivalent in rodents) significantly enhanced NK (natural killer) cell cytotoxic activity against target cells and increased lymphocyte proliferation response to phytohemagglutinin. ( Tasset-Cuevas et al.,2013)

safety_profile.toxicity: Acute toxicity study of the root extract showed dose-dependent toxicity. Oral administration in mice gave an LD₅₀ ≈ 500 mg/kg. Doses above 250 mg/kg caused toxic signs (reduced activity, abnormal movements, convulsions, and mortality). Repeated administration of 250 mg/kg for 28 days showed no major liver or kidney toxicity changes. Bryonia dioica has a narrow safety margin due to its toxic root compounds(Bourhia et al., 2019).

safety_profile.toxicity: Limited studies have investigated the potential adverse effects of Caper (Capparis spp.) (Taghavi et al., 2014; Kazemian et al., 2015). Overall, it is considered safe for consumption. Studies in rats showed that Caper fruits did not produce hepatic toxicity or signs of kidney damage (Heidari et al., 2010; Huseini et al., 2013). Acute toxicity evaluation of a polyphenolic extract from Caper leaves revealed no toxic effects at doses up to 100 mg/kg body weight (Ouadah Hamam et al., 2019). traditional_medicine.parts_used: The whole plant
traditional_medicine.uses: The caper plant is traditionally used in different countries for treating a wide range of conditions. It is used as a diuretic, tonic, analgesic, and depurative, and is employed against malaria, hemorrhoids, rheumatism, toothache, paralysis, cough, and intestinal worms. It is also used to treat digestive disorders such as stomachache, diarrhea, and infections, as well as anemia and dropsy. In addition, it is traditionally used for eye infections, diabetes, kidney stones, and skin problems, and its buds and leaves are also consumed as food and seasoning. (Annaz et al., 2022)
traditional_medicine.dosage: Root bark (decoction / infusion): 15 g per 1 liter of water; boiled for about 5 minutes, used as a diuretic, astringent, and tonic, especially for liver and spleen disorders. Root powder: prepared from dried root bark and used internally for conditions such as dropsy, chlorosis, cachexia, general weakness, and nervous depression. Cooked root bark (poultice): applied externally on ulcers. Flower buds (decoction): 30 g per 1 liter of water, used internally as a remedy for sciatica. Beloued, A. (2009). Plantes médicinales d’Algérie (5e éd.).

scientific_data.clinical: Several investigations on Caper (Capparis spp.) have demonstrated encouraging findings, leading to clinical evaluations to validate earlier in vitro and in vivo observations. Banerjee et al. (2011) studied Caper as a component of a polyherbal formulation to evaluate its antioxidant activity and safety in elderly patients. The treatment resulted in a significant improvement in antioxidant status compared with the control group. Additionally, a clinical trial assessed the antihyperglycemic potential of Caper fruit extract in patients with type 2 diabetes. Administration of 400 mg of the extract produced significant improvements without causing adverse effects on liver or kidney functions (Huseini et al., 2013).
scientific_data.experimental: Root extract in streptozotocin-diabetic rats: improved hyperglycemia , dyslipidemia and increased liver markers in an insulin-independent way. (Kazemian et al.,2015).P-Methoxy benzoic acid extracted from the methanolic soluble portion of the aqueous extract demonstrated hepatoprotective activity against CCl4 and Pcl-induced liver toxicity in rats (Gadgoli & Mishra, 1999).Aqueous extract (20 mg/kg) significantly reduced fasting blood glucose in STZ-diabetic mice (Eddouks et al.,2005)Confirming antimicrobial, antifungal , anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic, antioxidant ,cardioprotective,anti-cancer, immunomodulatory activities.(Alsharif & Boylan, 2025)

safety_profile.toxicity: Calycotome villosa showed low toxicity in experimental studies. Acute toxicity tests demonstrated that oral administration of the aqueous seed extract up to 12 g/kg did not cause mortality or severe toxic effects, indicating low oral toxicity. However, intraperitoneal administration produced dose-dependent toxic effects with an LD50 value of 4.06 ± 0.01 g/kg in mice.(Lyoussi et al., 2018)

scientific_data.clinical: A randomized clinical study conducted in 2018 investigated the efficacy of hydroalcoholic capsules prepared from Capsella bursa-pastoris in women suffering from heavy menstrual bleeding. Eighty-four participants were assigned to either treatment or placebo groups, and the extract demonstrated a significant reduction in menstrual blood loss compared with the control group. (Naafe et al., 2018)In a 2017 randomized clinical trial involving 100 postpartum women, researchers examined the effect of sublingual hydroalcoholic extract of Capsella bursa-pastoris administered alongside oxytocin after delivery. The treated group experienced a greater decrease in postpartum hemorrhage than the placebo group. (Ghalandari et al., 2017)A double-blind clinical trial published in 2019 evaluated the effect of Capsella bursa-pastoris extract on women with uterine leiomyoma-associated heavy bleeding. Although improvements in menstrual bleeding and quality of life were observed, the results were not statistically significant compared with placebo. (Danesh et al., 2019)A 2023 triple-blind randomized study assessed capsules containing 400 mg of hydroalcoholic extract of Capsella bursa-pastoris in patients with primary dysmenorrhea. The findings indicated a reduction in pain intensity and an improvement in menstrual-related symptoms. (Ahmadipoor et al., 2023)
scientific_data.experimental: Antibacterial activity: Inhibited the growth of several pathogenic bacteria, with greater activity observed against Gram-positive bacteria in some studies. scientific_data.clinical: Limited clinical evidence is available for Cichorium intybus. A phase I trial showed that chicory root extract was safe and well tolerated in patients with osteoarthritis. Another pilot study in 27 healthy volunteers found that daily consumption of chicory coffee reduced blood viscosity and inflammatory markers. Additionally, the polyherbal formulation Liv-52, which contains C. intybus, demonstrated hepatoprotective effects in patients with liver cirrhosis. (Street et al., 2013).
scientific_data.experimental: Chicory extracts demonstrate liver-protective properties. In rodent models with acetaminophen or carbon tetrachloride-induced liver damage, aqueous and methanolic seed/root extracts reduced mortality, lowered serum liver enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP), and improved histological outcomes. ( Riaz et al.,2024)Ethanol extracts (e.g., 125 mg/kg in streptozotocin-induced diabetic Sprague-Dawley rats) significantly lowered blood glucose in oral glucose tolerance tests, reduced serum triglycerides and cholesterol, and decreased hepatic glucose-6-phosphatase activity. ( Riaz et al.,2024)Extracts exhibit strong free radical scavenging (via DPPH, etc.) due to high phenolic and flavonoid content (higher in leaves). They reduce oxidative stress in models of aging myocardium and inflammation. (Al-Haliem et al .,2025)Sesquiterpene lactones and phenolics provide antibacterial, antifungal, and antiparasitic effects. (Duda et al.,2024)Leaf/root extracts promote wound healing in experimental models. (Kaçmaz et al.,2025)These include analgesic (in mouse models), immunomodulatory, cardioprotective (reducing oxidative damage in rat hearts), anti-ulcer, and potential anticancer properties. Chicory also acts as a prebiotic via inulin, supporting gut health.(Duda et al.,2024)

scientific_data.experimental: Cnicin and the essential oil showed broad-spectrum antibacterial activity in vitro against Bacillus subtilis, Brucella spp., Escherichia coli, Proteus spp., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus faecalis (Vanhaelen-Fastrè ,1972,1973,1976 reviewed in Southern Cross University monograph).Pharmacokinetic studies in rats showed the lignans arctiin and tracheloside are metabolized to arctigenin and trachelogenin, which inhibited cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase and histamine release from mast cells, supporting traditional anti-inflammatory use.(Nose et al ., (1993) reviewed in Southern Cross University monograph)An ethanolic leaf extract showed a measurable inhibitory zone against E. coli (8 mm at 50 mg/mL) and against Micrococcus species (11 mm at 25 mg/mL) in a disc-diffusion antibacterial assay (Yasin& Ibrahem 2017).Cnicus benedictus root extract promoted burn wound healing within 14 days in rats, reducing wound size and showing activity comparable to the commercial ointment Baneocin. (Chabane et al .,2013 ).Behavioral assessments demonstrated that both CBHE(Cnicus benedictus leaf methanolic extract) and cnicin( major constituent) possess antinociceptive properties. The pain-relieving activity of CBHE is likely associated with the modulation of several neural pathways, particularly the L-arginine–nitric oxide–cGMP pathway and the opioid system. (Ahmadimoghaddam et al ., 2020).

safety_profile.toxicity: To Coriandrum sativum L. is considered safe when consumed in normal dietary amounts and shows low toxicity. Adverse effects are uncommon, although allergic reactions may occur in sensitive individuals. Acute toxicity studies reported an LD₅₀ value above 5000 mg/kg body weight, indicating a high safety margin. (Patel et al., 2012)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Co-administration of Coriandrum sativum seed extract with glimepiride resulted in a significant herb–drug interaction, increasing glimepiride bioavailability and enhancing its hypoglycemic and lipid-lowering effects in diabetic rats compared with either treatment alone. ( Spandana et al ., 2021 )Coriandrum sativum may enhance the effects of antidiabetic medications, potentially leading to excessive reductions in blood glucose levels and requiring careful monitoring.Coriandrum sativum may potentiate the effects of antihypertensive medications, increasing the risk of excessive blood pressure reduction and requiring careful monitoring.Coriandrum sativum may enhance the effects of sedative medications, potentially leading to excessive drowsiness and respiratory depression when used concurrently.Coriandrum sativum may increase the photosensitizing effects of certain medications, potentially elevating the risk of sunburn, skin irritation, and rashes following sun exposure. ( Varpe et al.,2023)Coriandrum sativum essential oil demonstrated synergistic antibacterial interactions with chloramphenicol, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, and tetracycline against Acinetobacter baumannii, enhancing their antimicrobial activity and potentially restoring bacterial susceptibility to chloramphenicol. In contrast, its combination with piperacillin or cefoperazone produced only additive effects.( Duarte et al., 2012 )Plant-Plant interaction : The essential oil of Apium graveolens exhibited significant antioxidant activity, particularly when combined with the essential oils of Thymus vulgaris and Coriandrum sativum. Using FRAP and ABTS assays, the study demonstrated a synergistic enhancement of antioxidant capacity, with the most effective mixture containing 66.7% T. vulgaris, 16.7% C. sativum, and 16.7% A. graveolens. Among the three oils, T. vulgaris contributed the most to the antioxidant effect, followed by A. graveolens and C. sativum, highlighting the potential of A. graveolens essential oil as a natural antioxidant in synergistic formulations for food preservation. (Crespo et al.,2019)

scientific_data.experimental: An insulin-releasing and insulin-like activity was demonstrated for C. sativum extract in the traditional antidiabetic plant screening study by (Gray & Flatt , 1999).Coriander seed extract exhibited cytotoxic effects on neuroblastoma cells, inducing apoptosis via increased caspase-3, -8 and -9 activity and Bax/Bcl-2 modulation, with in silico docking supporting good pharmacokinetic properties of the isolated isocoumarins and flavonoids ( Marcucc et al ., 2022).Methanolic seed extract showed concentration-dependent radical scavenging activity across DPPH, hydroxyl, superoxide and nitric oxide assays, supporting antioxidant and hepatoprotective effects via reduced lipid peroxidation ( Ismail et al ., 2025).

safety_profile.drug_interactions: In a randomized crossover study involving healthy volunteers, coadministration of Crataegus special extract WS 1442 with digoxin for three weeks did not produce any significant changes in digoxin pharmacokinetic parameters, including systemic exposure (AUC), peak and trough plasma concentrations, or renal clearance. These findings indicate that hawthorn extract did not affect the absorption, distribution, or elimination of digoxin, suggesting that the two agents can be administered concomitantly without clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interactions. (Tankanow et al., 2003)Plant-Plant interaction : An in vivo study in rats with diet-induced atherosclerosis evaluated the combined effects of hawthorn tincture (Crataegus oxyacantha) and Mangifera indica stem bark extract. Oral co-administration of both extracts significantly reduced lipid levels in the serum, heart, liver, and aorta while improving hyperlipidemia. The combination also restored antioxidant defenses by increasing the activities of superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, and glutathione. These beneficial effects were attributed to the synergistic action of hawthorn flavonoids and mango polyphenols. (Akila&Devaraj , 2008)In a rat model of myocardial infarction, combined Crataegus oxyacantha and Rosmarinus officinalis extracts synergistically reduced oxidative stress, improved antioxidant status, restored the balance of vasoactive mediators, and enhanced cardiac function, demonstrating cardioprotective effects. traditional_medicine.parts_used: Leaves with flowers (folium cum flore); also fruits.
traditional_medicine.uses: Cardiac tonic for heart failure, hypertension, angina, and circulatory issues. Also for digestive complaints. (Wang et al., 2013)
traditional_medicine.dosage: Standardized extract (e.g., WS 1442 or LI 132): 160–900 mg/day (often 600–1800 mg in divided doses). Infusion from dried leaves/flowers. Duration typically 4–8 weeks or longer. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2016). Assessment report on Crataegus spp., folium cum flore. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/159076/2014.

scientific_data.clinical: Multiple randomized trials and meta-analyses support use as adjunct in mild to moderate heart failure (NYHA I–III): improved exercise tolerance, symptoms, and quality of life. (Dahmer & Scott, 2010)
scientific_data.experimental: The tincture of Crataegus (hawthorn) may exert cardioprotective effects by reducing lipid peroxidation and preventing elevations in cardiac marker enzymes. It also helps preserve the activity of endogenous antioxidant enzymes that are otherwise diminished by isoproterenol-induced cardiac stress. Furthermore, hawthorn enhances mitochondrial function by increasing ADP-stimulated oxygen consumption and improving the respiratory coupling ratio, thereby supporting cardiac energy metabolism and protecting the heart from oxidative damage.(Jayalakshmi & Devaraj , 2004 cited in Wang et al., 2013).An in vitro study investigating the hawthorn extract WS 1442 demonstrated a positive inotropic effect by increasing the contractile force of isolated human ventricular muscle tissue through a mechanism independent of cAMP. The extract appeared to inhibit the sarcolemmal Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, leading to enhanced intracellular calcium availability and increased myocardial contraction. Additionally, WS 1442 elevated peak intracellular Ca²⁺ levels in myocardial tissue obtained from patients with congestive heart failure, suggesting a potential mechanism underlying its cardiotonic activity. (Schwinger et al.,2000 cited in Wang et al., 2013).The anti-inflammatory activity of hawthorn fruit extracts appears to be mediated through suppression of key inflammatory mediators, including COX-2, TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6. Additionally, alcoholic extracts of Crataegus oxyacantha exert cardioprotective effects by reducing oxidative and nitrosative stress, inhibiting apoptosis, decreasing lipid peroxidation, and lowering the expression of inflammatory markers. These effects are further associated with reduced cytochrome c release and protection against DNA fragmentation, contributing to myocardial protection. (Vijayan et al., 2012 cited in Wang et al., 2013)Hawthorn treatment attenuated left ventricular remodeling and improved myocardial function in a model of pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy by reducing left ventricular chamber volume, increasing relative wall thickness, and preserving ventricular contractility.(Hwang et al ., 2008 cited in Wang et al., 2013 )At doses of 100–500 mg/kg, Crataegus extract exhibited significant antiplatelet activity by prolonging bleeding time, inhibiting platelet aggregation, and reducing serum thromboxane B₂ levels, indicating a potential antithrombotic effect. (Shatoor et al.,2012 cited in Wang et al., 2013)In both in vitro and in vivo studies, the standardized hawthorn extract WS 1442 promoted endothelium-dependent vasorelaxation by stimulating endothelial nitric oxide (NO) production through phosphorylation and activation of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) at serine 1177. (Brixius et al.,2006 cited in Wang et al., 2013)The standardized hawthorn extract WS 1442 protected endothelial barrier integrity by reducing endothelial permeability through inhibition of the calcium/PKC/RhoA signaling pathway and activation of the cAMP/Epac1/Rap1 pathway, thereby stabilizing endothelial cell junctions and the cytoskeleton. (Bubik et al., 2012 cited in Wang et al., 2013)Hawthorn has demonstrated cardioprotective potential by inhibiting vascular smooth muscle cell migration and proliferation, suggesting a possible role in reducing restenosis following balloon angioplasty.( Landau et al ., 1994 cited in Wang et al., 2013) Crataegus extract demonstrated antiarrhythmic activity by reducing the incidence of reperfusion-induced malignant arrhythmias, including ventricular fibrillation, ventricular flutter, and ventricular tachycardia.( Al Makdessi et al ., 1999 cited in Wang et al., 2013)Crataegus extract exhibited antiarrhythmic effects by prolonging cardiac action potential duration and delaying recovery of the maximum depolarization velocity (Vmax), although the underlying mechanism remains unclear.( Müller et al., 1996 cited in Wang et al., 2013)In an atherosclerotic mouse model fed an atherogenic diet, hawthorn fruit compounds demonstrated lipid-lowering effects by significantly reducing the LDL-C/TC ratio and decreasing triglyceride levels, indicating a potential protective role against the development of atherosclerosis.( Xu et al 2009 cited in Wang et al., 2013)In a rat model, Crataegus extract, particularly its hyperoside-rich fraction, prevented L-NAME-induced hypertension and exerted protective effects on the cardiovascular system, suggesting potential antihypertensive and cardioprotective properties.( Koçyõldõz et al ., 2006 cited in Wang et al., 2013)

scientific_data.experimental: Flower essential oil and ethanolic extract were tested for vasodilatory activity on noradrenaline-precontracted rat aortic rings; the flower extract and its main phenolic constituent chlorogenic acid produced stronger vasodilation than the essential oil and limonene, while essential oils showed greater cholinesterase-inhibitory activity than the extracts ( Generalić Mekinić et al., 2016)Crithmum maritimum aqueous extracts exhibited significant antioxidant activity despite their relatively low total phenolic content, demonstrating strong ABTS•+ radical scavenging activity (IC₅₀ = 3.83 μg/mL) and high ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP). In addition, the extracts showed promising hypoglycemic potential by inhibiting pancreatic lipase and key carbohydrate-hydrolyzing enzymes. These findings indicate that C. maritimum possesses noteworthy antioxidant and antihyperglycemic activities, supporting its potential application in the prevention and management of oxidative stress- and hyperglycemia-related disorders.( Nartea et al ., 2023)Studies have shown that sea fennel possesses antimicrobial activity against diverse microbial species, including several Gram-positive bacteria associated with human infections.( Ashim et al.,2024)Sea fennel extracts showed considerable anticancer potential in experimental studies.( Gnocchi et al ., 2020 cited in Karkanis et al., 2021 )Crithmum maritimum essential oil demonstrated potent antifungal activity against dermatophytes, with dillapiole identified as the major active constituent, while sabinene and β-phellandrene may also contribute to its antifungal efficacy. ( Ma et al.,2021 cited in Karkanis et al., 2021)

traditional_medicine.uses: Cupressus sempervirens leaves and cones are traditionally used for cough, cold, bronchitis, hemorrhoids, varicose veins, venous circulation disorders, and urinary problems. The essential oil is used as an antispasmodic and antiseptic (Rawat et al., 2010; Mahmood et al., 2013; Al-Snafi, 2018).

scientific_data.experimental: GC-MS analysis of hydrodistilled essential oil identified α-pinene (48.6%), δ-3-carene (22.1%), limonene (4.6%) and α-terpinolene (4.5%) as the principal components; the methanol extract strongly inhibited growth of tested bacteria (except yeasts), while the essential oil showed moderate antibacterial but no anti-Candida activity (Selim et al ., 2014).Ethanolic and ethyl acetate extracts demonstrated differential antibacterial action, with the ethanolic extract active against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and the ethyl acetate extract more active against E. coli and Salmonella typhimurium (Zhang et al., 2012, as reviewed in Batiha et al., 2022).Ethanolic extract showed acaricidal activity against the cattle tick Rhipicephalus annulatus, with the lowest LC50 (12.2%) and LC95 (17%) among tested extract types after 14 days; GC-MS identified eicosapentaenoic acid, docosadiynedioic acid and palmitic acid as major bioactive components (Taha & Ali, 2025).The essential oil's antibacterial multitarget mechanisms were evaluated alongside a chemcomputational toxicity prediction and an in vivo zebrafish embryo safety assessment, supporting a favorable safety profile at tested concentrations ( Akermi et al.,2022).

safety_profile.toxicity: Generally considered safe with long history of food and traditional use. No major toxicity reported in reviewed studies.(Cvetkovska & Bauer, 2018)

scientific_data.experimental: Aqueous fruit extract (80, 160 and 240 mg/kg, 28 days) produced a significant, dose-dependent reduction in fasting blood glucose in streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats; the active fraction was identified as containing 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (5-HMF) as a key contributor to the antihyperglycemic effect (Mohebbi et al., 2019).Ethanolic seed extract showed in vitro α-glucosidase and α-amylase inhibitory activity alongside DPPH and hydroxyl radical scavenging, supporting antidiabetic and antioxidant potential ( Khalil et al .,2022).Fruit extract demonstrated antioxidant, antidiabetic and immunomodulatory activity in vitro, with DPPH and ABTS IC50 values of 249.26 ± 3.75 µg/mL and 117.34 ± 1.41 µg/mL respectively (Sakhri et al .,2021).Fruit extract improved behavioral and neurological parameters in a chronic immobilization stress rat model, suggesting an adaptogenic/neuroprotective effect (Sakhri et al., 2020).A comprehensive 2025 review compiled preclinical evidence for neuroprotective, anti-hyperglycemic, anti-hyperlipidemic, anti-inflammatory and wound-healing activities across formal preclinical and early clinical investigations ( Tuba et al., 2025).Clinical studies:

safety_profile.drug_interactions: A case report described a patient who developed severe muscle pain, anemia, cholestatic liver abnormalities, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and marked inflammation after consuming large amounts of Cynara cardunculus infusion while receiving multiple medications, including colchicine. Extensive investigations excluded other causes, and the patient's complete recovery after discontinuation suggested a probable herb–drug interaction, potentially due to inhibition of CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 by artichoke constituents, which may have increased colchicine toxicity.( Campos et al.,2018)

scientific_data.experimental: Cynara cardunculus extract conferred protection in a diet-induced non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) model, with mechanistic involvement of OCTN1/OCTN2 organic cation transporters implicated in the hepatoprotective and lipid-lowering effect (Oppedisano et al., 2020).The Cynara scolymus extract with the highest phenolic content showed the strongest choleretic, hepatoprotective, and antioxidant activities in rats. In contrast, chlorogenic acid alone, at equivalent doses, did not produce significant protective or choleretic effects, suggesting that the therapeutic activity results from the combined action of multiple phenolic compounds rather than a single constituent. (Speroni et al., 2003).

safety_profile.toxicity: Cratageus monogyna (hawthorn) is generally considered safe, especially at therapeutic doses, with adverse effects being rare and mostly mild to moderate. Reported effects include sweating, headache, mild skin rash, palpitations, drowsiness, agitation, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Clinical studies have not shown significant safety concerns. Acute toxicity studies reported LD₅₀ values of 18.5 mL/kg in mice and 33.8 mL/kg in rats for hydroalcoholic leaf and fruit extracts.(Nabavi et al., 2015)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Available evidence suggests that hawthorn may cause adverse effects such as nausea, palpitations, and dizziness, which could be related to its cardiovascular activity. Although clinically significant herb–drug interactions have not been consistently demonstrated, hawthorn should be used cautiously with conventional cardiovascular medications, particularly digoxin and vasodilators, because of its potential pharmacological interactions. If combined therapy is considered, it should be undertaken only under medical supervision following an appropriate risk–benefit assessment. ( Woerdenbag et al.,2014)

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Leaves, flowers, fruits.
traditional_medicine.uses: Crataegus monogyna has traditionally been used to support cardiovascular health, including the management of heart disorders, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atherosclerosis, angina, arrhythmias, and circulatory problems. It has also been used to improve blood circulation and reduce blood stasis. Additionally, hawthorn has been employed for digestive disorders, including indigestion, epigastric distension, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, as well as to stimulate digestion and stomach function. Traditional uses also include its application as an antispasmodic, cardiotonic, astringent, and diuretic agent. (Nabavi et al., 2015)

scientific_data.clinical: Clinical studies have shown that hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna) extracts may improve symptoms of chronic heart failure, particularly fatigue, dyspnea, and exercise tolerance. Hawthorn has also been investigated for hypertension and cardiovascular health, with mixed results regarding blood pressure reduction. Recent randomized controlled trials further suggest potential benefits in improving lipid profiles and reducing body fat in overweight individuals. Overall, clinical evidence supports its use mainly as an adjunctive therapy for cardiovascular conditions. (Kępińska-Pacelik & Biel, 2026
scientific_data.experimental: Algerian C. monogyna butanolic fraction: identified 23 phenolic compounds; major compounds epicatechin (99.9 mg/g), isoquercetrin (53.3 mg/g), chlorogenic acid (47.5 mg/g). AChE inhibition IC50 = 43.65 ± 2.10 µg/mL; alpha-amylase inhibition IC50 = 91.19 ± 0.10 µg/mL; urease inhibition IC50 = 26.36 ± 0.05 µg/mL. Strong antioxidant (DPPH, ABTS, CUPRAC). (Goudjil et al., 2024)C. monogyna hydroethanolic extract (leaves/stems): in vivo anti-inflammatory effect — 1000 mg/kg dose inhibited carrageenan-induced paw edema by 99.10% at 6 h in rats; hepatoprotective against acetaminophen-induced toxicity; in vitro cytotoxicity against K-562 and HL-60 leukemia cell lines (MTT assay); molecular docking showed catechin most active against tyrosine kinase (-9.037 kcal/mol). (Martinelli et al., 2024)Procyanidins from C. monogyna/oxyacantha extract caused endothelium-dependent vasorelaxation in isolated rat aorta via NO/cGMP pathway (inhibited by N(G)-nitro-L-arginine, methylene blue). (Schussler et al., 1995)

safety_profile.toxicity: clinical and experimental studies suggest that lemon juice supplementation may increase urinary citrate excretion, which helps reduce the risk of calcium oxalate kidney stone formation. Some human studies have also reported potential benefits on lipid metabolism, blood pressure regulation, and glycemic control, although most clinical evidence remains limited and based on small-scale or short-duration trials. Overall, while lemon shows promising therapeutic potential, further well-designed clinical trials are still needed to confirm its efficacy and establish standardized medical use. (Ruggenenti et al., 2021)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: In an open-label, three-way crossover study involving healthy male volunteers, pretreatment with lemon juice for three consecutive days did not significantly alter the pharmacokinetics of a single 50 mg oral dose of sildenafil. No treatment-related adverse effects were observed, indicating that lemon juice is unlikely to produce a clinically significant interaction with sildenafil. ( Abdelkawy et al., 2016).

traditional_medicine.uses: A side from being rich in vitamin C, which assists in warding off infections, the juice is traditionally used to treat scurvy, sore throats, fevers, rheumatism, high blood pressure, and chest pain. In Trinidad, a mixture of lemon juice with alcohol or coconut oil has been used to treat fever, coughs in the common cold, and high blood pressure; moreover, the juice or grated skin mixed with molasses has been used as a diuretic, and the juice mixed with olive oil has been administered for womb infection and kidney stones. (Klimek-Szczykutowicz et al., 2020)

scientific_data.experimental: A comparative phytochemical review of C. sinensis and C. limon confirmed antioxidant, antibacterial, antifungal and anticancer potentials linked to their flavonoid and limonoid content ( Zahr et al.,2023).Hesperidin and hesperetin exhibited potent antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities by enhancing cellular antioxidant defenses through the ERK/Nrf2 pathway and suppressing inflammatory mediators such as NF-κB, iNOS, and COX-2. These findings suggest their potential in protecting against oxidative stress and inflammation-related diseases. ( Parhiz et al ., 2014)The methanol:water (80:20) extract of lemon seeds exhibited the strongest antioxidant activity, showing high free radical scavenging capacity in both DPPH and ABTS assays. It also significantly inhibited the proliferation of MCF-7 breast cancer cells by inducing apoptosis through DNA fragmentation, PARP cleavage, increased Bax and cytochrome c levels, and reduced Bcl-2 expression. These findings suggest that lemon seed flavonoids and limonoids possess antioxidant and potential chemopreventive properties against breast cancer.( Kim et al ., 2012 )The ethanol extract of Citrus limon fruits exhibited significant hepatoprotective activity against carbon tetrachloride-induced liver injury. It restored liver function markers, reduced lipid peroxidation, enhanced antioxidant defenses by increasing SOD, catalase, and glutathione levels, and improved liver histology in a dose-dependent manner, with the highest dose showing effects comparable to silymarin. In HepG2 cells, the ethyl acetate fraction also dose-dependently improved cell viability following CCl₄-induced toxicity, supporting its hepatoprotective potential. ( Bhavsar et al.,2007)Both in vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated that Citrus limon possesses significant anticoagulant activity. It prolonged thrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and bleeding time, reduced fibrinogen levels, and increased protein C and thrombin–antithrombin complex levels, indicating inhibition of thrombin activity and platelet aggregation. The strongest anticoagulant effect was observed at 0.4 mL/kg, suggesting a potential cardioprotective role in the prevention of thrombosis. ( Riaz et al., 2014)

safety_profile.toxicity: Capsaicin shows moderate acute toxicity with oral LD₅₀ values of 97.4–118.8 mg/kg in mice and 148.1–161.2 mg/kg in rats, indicating dose-dependent toxic effects at high exposure levels. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2015). Assessment report on Capsicum annuum L. var. minimum (Miller) Heiser and small fruited varieties of Capsicum frutescens L., fructus. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/674138/2013.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: In an in vivo study, the combination of metformin (100 mg/kg) and Capsicum annuum (500 mg/kg) produced the greatest hypoglycemic effect and significantly reduced serum cholesterol and urea levels. Additionally, combining metformin (50 mg/kg) with Capsicum annuum enhanced the hypoglycemic response compared with either metformin (50 mg/kg) or Capsicum annuum alone. (saritharani et al., 2024)

scientific_data.clinical: Study on 28 women (12 weeks): fermented red pepper paste improved cholesterol levels compared to placebo. Randomized clinical trial in hyperlipidemic patients (12 weeks): reduced total cholesterol and LDL-C. Crossover study (36 subjects): chili diet improved post-meal glucose control and reduced insulin needs. Clinical trial in gestational diabetes (44 women, 4 weeks): capsaicin improved glucose control and reduced insulin levels. 12-week study (capsaicinoids): reduced abdominal fat and improved body composition. (Sanati et al., 2018)
scientific_data.experimental: An acute dermal toxicity study in Wistar rats following OECD guideline 402 evaluated a 5% capsaicinoid gel at 200, 1000 and 2000 mg/kg, alongside its analgesic efficacy in a formalin-induced paw-licking pain model ( Mwandah et .,2026).In an in vitro study using androgen-independent PC-3 and DU-145 prostate cancer cell lines, along with an in vivo mouse model of prostate tumors, capsaicin induced cell cycle arrest and apoptosis through ROS generation, ceramide accumulation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, and caspase-3 activation. It also significantly inhibited prostate tumor growth in mice, demonstrating its potential antitumor activity. (Díaz-Laviada , 2010)Algerian C. annuum (capsaicinoid and carotenoid reported for the first time; carotenoid fraction showed superior antioxidant activity, anticancer activity 90% inhibition of U937 celland and antiùicrobial against pathogen bacteria.( Mokhtar et al., 2025)

safety_profile.toxicity: Carum carvi (caraway) is considered a plant with low toxicity at therapeutic doses. Acute toxicity studies show that its essential oil has an oral LD50 in rats ranging from 3.5 to 7.4 mL/kg, while the dermal LD50 in rabbits is about 1.78–1.8 mL/kg. The main active compound, d-carvone, shows an oral LD50 of 1640 mg/kg in rats and 766 mg/kg in guinea pigs, with additional values of 1500 mg/kg (intravenous) and 482.2 mg/kg (intraperitoneal) reported in mice. In humans, studies indicate good tolerance, with no significant toxic or irritating effects observed at normal therapeutic doses. Overall, caraway is considered safe when used properly, and toxicity is mainly associated with excessive intake of the essential oil. (Mahboubi, 2018)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: the combination of carvone with itraconazole or caspofungin(anti-fungals) had synergistic/additive effects, suggesting potential therapeutic efficacy for the treatment of A. fumigatus-related infections.( Saremi et al ., 2024)

distribution.habitat_description: Eastern and Central Regions: These are the areas where caraway grows most naturally. It is found growing wild in forests, meadows and on mountains. High Plateaus: The plant adapts very well to the northern plateaus. The West: The plant is much rarer, or even absent, in the western regions.
distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering stage: The plant flowers from May to July, with peak flowering usually during June. Harvesting period: Fruits/seeds: Harvested after flowering, usually from July to August, when fruits are fully mature and dry.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Fruits.
traditional_medicine.uses: Digestive disorders, flatulence, bloating, spasms, galactagogue.(Mahboubi, 2018)
traditional_medicine.dosage: Fruits (seeds): 1.5–6 g/day, used as infusion (herbal tea). Essential oil (oral): 0.15–0.3 mL/day, divided into 3 doses. Essential oil (topical): 2% semisolid preparation, applied as a thin layer on the abdominal area. (Mahboubi, 2018)

scientific_data.clinical: Functional dyspepsia: In clinical trials including 100–118 patients, caraway oil (± peppermint/menthol) significantly improved dyspepsia symptoms such as abdominal pain and bloating compared to placebo, with good safety and no serious adverse effects. Obesity: In randomized controlled studies in overweight and obese women (BMI 25–39.9 kg/m²), caraway water/extract significantly reduced body weight, BMI, waist circumference, body fat, and appetite after several weeks/months of treatment. Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS): In a crossover trial involving 48 patients with diarrhea-predominant IBS, caraway oil poultice improved symptom severity, stool pattern, and quality of life compared with olive oil, with higher response rates. Thyroid/metabolic effects: In clinical observations in patients treated with caraway, changes in TSH, T3, and T4 levels were reported, suggesting a possible effect on metabolism and body weight regulation.(Mahboubi, 2018)
scientific_data.experimental: Caraway extract and essential oil reduced TNBS-induced colitis severity in rats, supporting anti-inflammatory, spasmolytic, antimicrobial, antioxidant and immunomodulatory properties relevant to inflammatory bowel disease (Keshavarz et al., 2013)A study found Menthacarin (peppermint and caraway oil combination) altered cultured human fecal microbiota composition, increasing short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, offering a possible mechanism for its established clinical efficacy in functional dyspepsia and IBS. ( Lehner et al.,2025)

safety_profile.toxicity: Flower extracts may negatively affect embryonic development in mice, suggesting caution during pregnancy. Prolonged administration of aqueous extract (40 mg/kg for 25 days) was associated with adverse effects on testicular function in mice.(Delshad et al., 2018)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: In a rat thrombosis model, aqueous safflower extract enhanced the antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel by significantly prolonging bleeding time, although it did not affect bleeding time when administered alone. However, safflower alone prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and thrombin time (TT), indicating anticoagulant activity.( Lim et al ., 2018)Plant-Plant interaction :In an Aβ25–35-induced mouse model of Alzheimer's disease, combined treatment with Carthamus tinctorius seed and Taraxacum coreanum produced greater improvements in spatial learning, memory, and object recognition than either treatment alone. The combination also attenuated amyloidogenesis by modulating amyloid-β metabolism, demonstrating synergistic neuroprotective effects.(He et al ., 2020)

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Flowers (dried petals/stigmas – primary medicinal part); seeds (for oil). (Delshad et al., 2018)
traditional_medicine.uses: Dysmenorrhea, amenorrhea, postpartum abdominal pain, postpartum abdominal mass, trauma, joint pain, promotion of blood circulation, removal of blood stasis, and pain relief in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM).(Zhou et al., 2014)
traditional_medicine.dosage: the recommended amounts are up to 3 g/day for flowers and 20–40 g/day for seeds. (Delshad et al., 2018)

scientific_data.clinical: A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial in 67 patients with metabolic syndrome showed that safflower seed oil (8 g/day for 12 weeks) improved abdominal obesity, blood pressure, fasting glucose and insulin resistance, although lipid profile changes were not significant. (Ruyvaran et al., 2022)
scientific_data.experimental: In a mouse model of myocardial ischemia–reperfusion injury, safflower extract (62.5–250 mg/kg) administered before reperfusion significantly reduced infarct size, improved cardiac function, lowered LDH levels, and increased SOD activity. These cardioprotective effects were associated with suppression of inflammatory cytokines, inhibition of apoptosis, and activation of the PI3K/AKT, HIF-1α, MAPK, TNF, and NF-κB signaling pathways.( Zhao et al., 2023).A network pharmacology study found that safflower ameliorated ox-LDL-induced apoptosis and mitochondrial membrane dysfunction in vitro, decreasing Bax expression while increasing Bcl-2 and SIRT1 expression, supporting anti-apoptotic mechanisms relevant to coronary heart disease treatment ( Meng et al ., 2022).Safflower polysaccharides were shown to regulate hepatic lipid homeostasis through dual modulation of antioxidant and anti-inflammatory pathways (Hu et al., 2025).A comprehensive review covering ethnomedicine, phytochemistry and pharmacology from 1978–2025 confirmed antioxidant, hepatoprotective, anti-inflammatory and anticancer bioactivities for safflower extracts and metabolites, with flavonoids (notably hydroxysafflor yellow A) identified as the predominant active compound class (Bai et al., 2025).

safety_profile.toxicity: Ceratonia siliqua is practically non-toxic, with high LD₅₀ values (>1.5–5 g/kg depending on extract), no observed organ toxicity, and strong safety in both acute and repeated exposure studies, supporting its safe traditional and dietary use. (Dahmani et al., 2023)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: study investigated the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects of a combination of rosmarinic acid-rich extract from Ocimum basilicum and aqueous extract of Ceratonia siliqua. In carrageenan-induced paw edema and vascular permeability models, the combination (200 mg/kg) significantly reduced inflammation, with effects comparable to indomethacin (50 mg/kg). It also inhibited plasma lipoprotein oxidation and demonstrated strong free radical scavenging activity against lipoperoxyl and DPPH radicals, suggesting potential benefits in managing inflammation and oxidative stress-related disorders. ( Touiss et al ., 2024)
