scientific_data.experimental: Methanolic leaf extracts obtained by maceration and ultrasound-assisted extraction from the Oued Souf region (Algeria) showed DPPH radical scavenging of 41% and 60.67% respectively, and measurable antibacterial inhibition zones against Escherichia coli (up to 12 mm) and Staphylococcus aureus (up to 13 mm) ( Chouikh et al., 2020).Isolation and characterization of a novel steroid derivative from Cleome arabica identified it as a powerful antioxidant during screening of the in vitro antioxidant capacity of 18 Algerian medicinal plants (Djeridane et al., 2010).Cleome arabica leaf extract treated with naringinase affected human neutrophil chemotaxis in vitro, suggesting an immunomodulatory mechanism (Bouriche & Arnhold, 2010).A 2023 study found that Cleome arabica fruit extract significantly ameliorated formalin-induced chronic inflammation in female Wistar rats, improving histological skin integrity and reducing inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α), C-reactive protein and oxidative stress markers (TBARS −49%, AOPP −42%), while in silico docking showed fruit extract compounds binding more strongly to COX-2 than the reference drug indomethacin ( Allagui et al ., 2022).Extracts of Cleome arabica leaves and stems demonstrated insecticidal activity against larvae of the cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis, affecting feeding and survival ( Ladhari et al ., 2013).

safety_profile.toxicity: Acute toxicity studies indicate that saffron has low toxicity at therapeutic doses. The oral LD50 of saffron aqueous extract in mice is about 4120 ± 556 mg/kg (≈ 4.1 g/kg), while stigma and petal extracts show LD50 values of 1.6 g/kg (IP) and 6 g/kg (IP) respectively. These relatively high LD50 values confirm a wide safety margin, and saffron is generally considered safe when used at traditional and therapeutic doses, with adverse effects mainly observed only at very high or excessive intake levels. (Bostan et al., 2017)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Saffron and its active constituents, crocin and safranal, can inhibit several cytochrome P450 enzymes, particularly CYP3A4, CYP1A1/2, and CYP2E1, potentially leading to herb–drug interactions by altering the metabolism of certain medications. Further clinical studies are needed to clarify the significance of these interactions and identify safe dosage levels. ( Bathaei et al .,2025)

Harvesting period: Flowers: Collected during full flowering (October–November). traditional_medicine.parts_used: saffron stigma
traditional_medicine.uses: include the treatment of abdominal pain, fever, and stimulation of menstrual flow. It has also been traditionally used for managing haematoma, melancholia, convulsions, sedation, postpartum “blood stasis,” and skin eruptions associated with infectious diseases. (Barnes, 2022)

scientific_data.clinical: Depression (mild–moderate): 40 patients received saffron stigma extract 30 mg/day for 6 weeks; saffron improved depressive symptoms compared with placebo. (Hausenblas et al., 2015) Systematic review: 12 randomized clinical trials showed potential benefits of saffron in depression, PMS symptoms, sexual dysfunction, and appetite-related disorders. (Akhondzadeh et al., 2005)
scientific_data.experimental: The aqueous extract of saffron exhibited cytotoxic activity against A549 lung cancer cells, with an IC₅₀ value of 390 μg/mL in the MTT assay. Microscopic examination revealed marked inhibition of cell growth accompanied by cell shrinkage, while flow cytometric analysis demonstrated a significant increase in both early and late apoptotic cell populations, indicating that the extract suppressed cell proliferation by inducing apoptosis.( Samarghandian et al., 2013).The petroleum ether and methanolic extracts of Crocus sativus exhibited notable antimicrobial activity in the agar well diffusion assay. The petroleum ether extract was effective against Proteus vulgaris, Bacillus subtilis, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, while the methanolic extract inhibited the growth of Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli.( Muzaffar et al ., 2016). The antioxidant activity of ethyl acetate, methanol, and water extracts of Crocus chrysanthus was evaluated using DPPH radical scavenging, reducing power, metal chelating, andphosphomolybdenum assays. Among the tested extracts, the water extract exhibited the strongest antioxidant activity across the evaluated assays. ( Zengin et al., 2019).The antidiabetic potential of ethyl acetate, methanolic, and aqueous extracts of Crocus chrysanthus was evaluated through α-glucosidase and α-amylase inhibition assays. The extracts exhibited α-glucosidase inhibitory activity ranging from 1.89 to 14.8 mmol acarbose equivalents/g and α-amylase inhibitory activity ranging from 0.15 to 0.8 mmol acarbose equivalents/g, depending on the extract tested.( Zengin et al., 2019)

safety_profile.toxicity: The safety evaluation of Cucurbita pepo leaf extract indicates a high safety margin, as no deaths or clear toxic symptoms were observed in acute studies even at an oral dose of up to 5 g/kg in rats. In subacute administration (200–800 mg/kg for 14 days), the extract did not produce significant adverse effects on liver and kidney function, blood parameters, or antioxidant systems. Overall, the results suggest that Cucurbita pepo exhibits a good safety profile and is well tolerated in experimental models at the tested doses. (Akubugwo et al., 2022)

traditional_medicine.parts_used: the fruits and seeds,leaves
traditional_medicine.uses: Cucurbita pepo is traditionally used in several countries for the management of various diseases, including anti-inflammatory, antiviral, analgesic, anti-ulcer, antidiabetic, antioxidant, and urinary disorders. The plant is also used for wound healing, tumour growth inhibition, hypoglycaemic effects, and immunomodulatory activity. The seeds are traditionally employed as a vermifuge, and for treating urinary tract disorders, hypertension, prevention of kidney stone formation, prostate diseases, and skin infections such as erysipelas. (Perez Gutierrez, 2016)
traditional_medicine.dosage: The herbal substance (seeds) is used at a dose of 10–20 g/day, taken as a single dose or divided into 2–3 doses. The soft extract is administered at 1000 mg/day (2 doses), the dry extract at 300–320 mg/day (2–3 doses), and the fatty oil at 1–4 g/day in several divided doses, all taken orally for urinary and prostate disorders. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2011). Community herbal monograph on Cucurbita pepo L., semen. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/136024/2010.

scientific_data.clinical: A randomized clinical trial showed that pumpkin seed oil improved BPH symptoms (IPSS) and quality of life, but was less effective than tamsulosin, with good tolerability and no serious side effects(Zerafatjou et al., 2021). In addition, a 24-month noninterventional study using pumpkin seed soft extract reported a significant reduction in IPSS scores and improvement in urinary symptoms, while maintaining sexual function and showing a good safety profile. (Theil et al., 2022)
scientific_data.experimental: Pumpkin seed extract inhibited growth of hyperplastic and cancer cells in vitro independent of steroid hormone receptor activity, suggesting a non-hormonal mechanism for its traditional prostate use (Medjakovic et al.,2016).

safety_profile.toxicity: Avoid during pregnancy; wild carrot seeds have traditional emmenagogue and fertility-control uses, with reported uterine-stimulating and anti-fertility effects in traditional and preclinical studies. (Ismail et al., 2024)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Wild carrot may exhibit diuretic-like effects, potentially reducing lithium clearance and increasing the risk of lithium toxicity. It may also exert weak estrogenic activity, which could reduce the effectiveness of estrogen-containing medications. Additionally, concurrent use with photosensitizing drugs may increase the risk of sunburn, blistering, and skin rashes following sun exposure. ( Cummings et al., 1978 , Wisker et al., 1994 cited in Bahrami et al ., 2018)Clinical studies have also indicated that carrot consumption may prolong gastrointestinal transit time.according to a clinical study in lactating women, ingestion of grated carrots may increase serum levels of vitamin A, iron, and ferritin. ( Ncube et al., 2001 cited in Bahrami et al ., 2018)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Papaya and carrot root extracts possess anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties attributed to bioactive compounds such as β-carotene, polyphenols, flavonoids, vitamins, and papain. These compounds reduce oxidative stress, suppress pro-inflammatory cytokines, regulate inflammatory signaling pathways, and enhance immune function. Their combination may exert synergistic effects, although further standardized clinical studies are needed to confirm their therapeutic potential. ( Arshad et al.,2025)

scientific_data.experimental: Antidiabetic (in vivo, HFD-induced T2DM model): Hydro-alcoholic extract of C. erythraea aerial parts at 2 g/kg body weight in C57BL/6J HFD mice: significantly inhibited elevated blood glucose, triglycerides, serum insulin, and insulin resistance. Mechanism attributed to stimulation of hepatic glycogen synthesis and reduction of gluconeogenesis; secoiridoids and xanthones identified as main responsible compounds. (Hamza et al., 2010 — cited in Hamza et al., 2015)Antidiabetic (STZ-induced diabetic rats): Oral CE aqueous extract at 50 mg/kg significantly reduced blood glucose in STZ-induced diabetic rats; alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase inhibition compared favourably with glibenclamide .( Ouadni et al.,2024)Anti-inflammatory / analgesic / antipyretic (in vivo): Aqueous extract of C. erythraea (Erythraea centaurium) produced significant anti-inflammatory (carrageenan-induced paw edema), analgesic (acetic acid writhing), and antipyretic (yeast-induced pyrexia) effects in rats; comparable to standard anti-inflammatory/analgesic drugs. (Valentao et al., 2001)Cytotoxic (in vitro): Erythraeaxanthone I, erythraeaxanthone II, centauroside A (novel undescribed compounds) isolated from aerial parts and tested by XTT assay against MCF-7, MDA-MB-453 (breast cancer), and 3T3-L1 (mouse fibroblast) cell lines — erythraeaxanthone II showed most potent cytotoxic activity. Topical use (liquid form): a small amount (a few drops) is applied to the chest and back, 2–3 times daily. Topical use (semi-solid form, 10% oil): a thin layer is applied on the chest and back, 2–3 times daily. Inhalation or bath use: administered according to the specific product instructions.European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2024). Assessment report on Eucalyptus globulus Labill.; Eucalyptus polybractea R.T. Baker; Eucalyptus smithii R.T. Baker, aetheroleum. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/320282/2023.

scientific_data.clinical: Systematic review of RCTs showed that eucalyptus preparations (mainly cineole-containing products) may improve cough frequency and severity in respiratory infections. However, evidence is limited due to heterogeneity and risk of bias. Overall, eucalyptus products appear to provide modest symptomatic relief with generally good tolerability, but high-quality clinical evidence is still insufficient. (Her et al., 2022)
scientific_data.experimental: E. globulus essential oil showed antiviral / antibacterial activity against H. influenzae, parainfluenzae, S. maltophilia and S. pneumoniae.in cell culture. (Cermelli et al., 2008).Crude EO or 1,8-cineole alone and in combination with chlorhexidine exhibited antimicrobial efficacy against planktonic and biofilm cultures of multiple pathogens. (Henry et al., 2009)1,8-cineole suppressed NF- κB, TREM-1, and NLRP3 in lung macrophages; reduced TNF-α and IL-6 in COPD macrophages.(Yadav & Chandra, 2017).

safety_profile.toxicity: In a single oral administration toxicity test conducted on NMRI mice at a dose of 25 mL/kg, Eupatorium cannabinum L. extract did not produce any deaths or visible signs of toxicity during a 14-day observation period, suggesting that the maximum tolerated dose is relatively high; nevertheless, its long-term safety has not yet been confirmed. (Ionita et al., 2013)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antibacterial, immunomodulatory, cytostatic/antiproliferative, anti-inflammatory, fungicidal, hepatoprotective and antioxidant activities reported; notable toxicological concern due to pyrrolizidine alkaloid content.Phytochemical profile: Sesquiterpene lactones (including eupatoriopicrin), pyrrolizidine alkaloids (including echinatine and supinine), flavones (eupatorin, eupatilin), phenolic acids (caffeic acid), flavonoids (quercetin, rutin), polysaccharides and essential oil terpenoids (including germacrene).

scientific_data.experimental: Chloroform and aqueous extracts of E. cannabinum aerial parts were tested against four human cancer cell lines (BT-20, HepG2, Caco-2, Jurkat); Jurkat cells were most sensitive (IC50 7.35 µg/mL for chloroform extract, 13.77 µg/mL for aqueous extract), with HPLC analysis identifying eupatorin, eupatilin and quercetin in the chloroform extract and caffeic acid and rutin in the aqueous extract (Grigore et al., 2018).Essential oil samples from 11 wild Lithuanian populations were evaluated for antioxidant activity using cyclic and square-wave voltammetry techniques, alongside toxicity assessment, finding variability across populations (Judzentiene et al., 2016).A 2025 nanocarrier encapsulation study of wild-grown Romanian E. cannabinum confirmed antioxidant, antimicrobial and cytotoxicity profiles for metabolite-rich extracts, supporting further pharmaceutical development interest ( Vlase et al.,2025).

safety_profile.toxicity: All parts of the plant are toxic, particularly the fruit; documented serious adverse events include life-threatening uvular angioedema, severe nasal mucosal necrosis, and at least one case of fatal cardiac and renal failure following use of the fruit juice (Vlachos et al., 1994, J Toxicol Clin Toxicol).Intranasal use for sinusitis (a traditional Mediterranean practice) carries documented serious and life-threatening risk including airway edema and anaphylactoid-type reactions; multiple case reports describe emergency department presentations requiring oxygen, corticosteroids, antihistamines and epinephrine.Ocular exposure can cause conjunctivitis, corneal edema and erosion; dermal exposure has generally been better tolerated but should still be avoided.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Anti-inflammatory and solid-tumor-inhibiting properties have been attributed to the plant, with antibacterial, antioxidant and cytotoxic activities confirmed in extracts of leaves and fruits; many traditional indications (especially for sinusitis) have been at least partly confirmed in vitro and, in some cases, in vivo.Phytochemical profile: Numerous cucurbitacins (tetracyclic triterpenes — the primary bioactive and toxic principle class), with at least ten cucurbitacins identified in E. elaterium to date.

scientific_data.experimental: An aqueous extract of E. elaterium was evaluated in a rabbit model of rhinosinusitis, assessing antibacterial, antioxidant and cytotoxic activity of leaf and fruit extracts alongside total flavonoid and phenolic content ( Uslu et al .,2006).Ethyl acetate extract showed a cytotoxic effect (IC50 19.12 µg/mL) and significant antioxidant effect (SC50 >8.4 µg/mL) compared with vitamin C in laboratory evaluation ( Raikhlin-Eisenkraft & Bentur ,2000 ).A comprehensive chemical and pharmacological profile update confirmed traditional use for rheumatism, jaundice, sinusitis, fever, liver disorders and constipation specifically in Tunisia, Algeria and Turkey, with cucurbitacins identified as the primary bioactive component class ( Anzano et al., 2024).

safety_profile.toxicity: Equisetum arvense L. shows low acute toxicity with LD50 values higher than 5 g/kg in animal studies. Repeated-dose toxicity studies in rats demonstrated no significant toxic effects, with NOAEL values exceeding 1.79–1.85 g/kg/day. Histological and biochemical analyses also showed no hepatotoxicity, indicating a wide safety margin under experimental conditions. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2016). Assessment report on Equisetum arvense L., herba. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/278089/2015.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Although evidence is limited, these case reports raise concern that Equisetum arvense may interfere with the efficacy of efavirenz-containing antiretroviral regimens, potentially resulting in virological breakthrough. Healthcare providers should exercise caution and discourage the concurrent use of horsetail with these medications until further pharmacokinetic and clinical studies clarify the interaction.( Cordova et al .,2017).

scientific_data.clinical: Carneiro et al. (2014) conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial in 36 healthy male volunteers using Equisetum arvense dry extract (300 mg three times daily). The results showed a significant diuretic effect, with a negative fluid balance (−321.81 ± 481.02 mL, p < 0.001), without significant electrolyte changes or signs of toxicity, and only minor adverse effects such as headache were reported. scientific_data.experimental: An anabolic therapy study combining E. arvense with bone-mineralizing nutrients in an ovariectomized rat model of osteoporosis demonstrated supportive effects on bone parameters (Kotwal & Badole, 2016).A review of herbal medicines as diuretics found supportive scientific evidence for the traditional diuretic classification of E. arvense among other botanicals (Wright et al., 2007).

safety_profile.toxicity: No signs of toxicity in acute/subacute rodent studies (LD50 >2000 mg/kg). Safe at tested doses. (Benrahou et al., 2022)

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Aerial parts, flowers, leaves.(Amari et al., 2023)
traditional_medicine.uses: Anti-inflammatory, urolithiatic, antibacterial, analgesic; traditional Mediterranean uses for urinary/inflammatory conditions. (Amroun et al., 2021)

scientific_data.experimental: An ethnopharmacological study among 171 informants in Algeria's Bejaia region found 28.04% of respondents used E. arborea in traditional folk medicine; hydromethanolic extracts of leaves and flowers showed anti-urolithiatic activity (inhibiting in vitro crystal nucleation and aggregation), antibacterial activity, in vivo anti-inflammatory activity (xylene- and croton oil-induced ear edema models in mice) and analgesic activity (acetic acid-induced abdominal constriction test), with acute toxicity assessed per OECD guidelines ( Amari et al.,2023).HPLC-MS phytochemical profiling of Algerian E. arborea leaf and flower hydromethanolic extracts identified epicatechin, kaempferol-3-O-glucoside and palmitic acid as major compounds, supporting the anti-inflammatory mechanism via likely modulation of MAPK/NF-κB pathways ( Amari et al.,2023).E. arborea flower extract from Algeria showed significant leishmanicidal activity with a reliable selectivity index, most effective against Leishmania major ( Jabal et al., 2025).A review of phenolic compounds, antioxidant and antibacterial activities of three Ericaceae species from Algeria (including E. arborea) found measurable total phenolic and flavonoid content correlating with antioxidant (hydrogen-donating) activity ( Guendouze-Bouchefa et al.,2015).

safety_profile.toxicity: No significant anti-inflammatory or antinociceptive activity was detected in ethanolic and aqueous extracts in dedicated pharmacological testing, an important negative finding distinguishing this species from related Eryngium species with confirmed such activity; specific human toxicity data are otherwise limited.No documented traditional use among the Algerian population despite extensive phytochemical characterization of Algerian-sourced material, suggesting limited historical safety data specific to local use patterns.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antibacterial, antifungal, antileishmanial, antimalarial, antitumor, antioxidant, cytotoxic and anti-Alzheimer activities, with antinociceptive and antipyretic properties also reported for the broader Eryngium genus; notably, no significant anti-inflammatory or antinociceptive activity was detected specifically in ethanolic and aqueous extracts of E. campestre in dedicated testing.Phytochemical profile: Essential oil from Algerian populations dominated by Germacrene D and the novel marker compound Campestrolide (not previously detected in Eryngium essential oils); aerial parts also contain flavonoids (rutin, kaempferol, isoquercetin, luteolin, apigenin) and phenolic acids (caffeic, rosmarinic, chlorogenic, ferulic).
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Essential oil from Algerian populations dominated by Germacrene D and the novel marker compound Campestrolide (not previously detected in Eryngium essential oils); aerial parts also contain flavonoids (rutin, kaempferol, isoquercetin, luteolin, apigenin) and phenolic acids (caffeic, rosmarinic, chlorogenic, ferulic).

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Aerial parts, roots.Dosage & Preparation: Essential oil obtained by hydrodistillation of aerial parts; aqueous/ethanolic extracts used in research.
traditional_medicine.uses: Used in Turkish folk medicine as an antitussive, stimulant, aphrodisiac and diuretic agent, and as a folk remedy for anti-inflammatory disorders, an emetic, gastrointestinal infusion, antidote for poisons, hypoglycemic agent and remedy for diarrhea; notably, no traditional uses for this specific species have been documented among the Algerian population despite its local presence and naming.

scientific_data.experimental: Chemical composition of essential oils from 37 localities across Western Algeria was characterized by GC-FID/GC-MS, identifying 52 components (70.1–86.8% of total composition), with Germacrene D and the novel compound Campestrolide as distinguishing markers for Algerian E. campestre compared to other Mediterranean-origin oils ( Medbouhi et al., 2019).Campestrolide was identified as a key compound responsible for cytotoxic and antileishmanial activity of the Algerian essential oil, while myrcene and/or trans-β-farnesene showed more selective antitrypanosomal activity ( Medbouhi et al., 2019).A comparative metabolomic UPLC-MS/MS profiling study annotated 79 metabolites (flavonoids, phenolic acids, terpenoids, cinnamate esters, fatty acids) from root and aerial fractions of E. campestre, combined with antibacterial activity characterization ( H. Zaki et al ., 2025).A review of the genus Eryngium found that essential oils from E. campestre and related species (E. creticum, E. thorifolium) showed antibacterial activity against nine clinical strains of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) using disc diffusion methods ( Erdem et al.,2015).

safety_profile.toxicity: Limited dedicated human toxicological data are available in the literature, consistent with the broader observation that little information exists on this species despite long traditional use in Algeria.The demonstrated hepatoprotective effect against propiconazole-induced toxicity suggests a generally favorable safety profile for the extract in the tested experimental model, though this does not substitute for dedicated acute/chronic toxicity studies.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antioxidant, antimicrobial, hepatoprotective and multi-target bioactivities (supported by molecular docking) reported, with strong free-radical scavenging consistently demonstrated across multiple solvent fractions.Phytochemical profile: Phenolic compounds including shikimic acid, gallic acid, luteolin, isoquercitrin, hesperidin and quercetin 3-xyloside; high total phenolic (up to 332.76 µg GAE/mg in ethyl acetate fraction) and flavonoid content.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Phenolic compounds including shikimic acid, gallic acid, luteolin, isoquercitrin, hesperidin and quercetin 3-xyloside; high total phenolic (up to 332.76 µg GAE/mg in ethyl acetate fraction) and flavonoid content.

scientific_data.experimental: LC-MS/MS analysis of the hydroethanolic extract from northeastern Algeria identified 16 phenolic compounds (shikimic acid, gallic acid, luteolin and isoquercitrin as main components), with strong antioxidant activity (IC50 3.88 µg/mL DPPH, 6.33 µg/mL ABTS, A0.5 10.11 µg/mL FRAP) and multi-target bioactivity supported by molecular docking insights ( Ounissi et al., 2026).A separate Algerian study found the ethyl acetate fraction of E. guttatum aerial parts exhibited the highest phenolic and flavonoid content among tested fractions, with superior antioxidant activity (IC50 2.37 µg/mL DPPH, 1.49 µg/mL ABTS) compared to other solvent fractions (Ounissi et al., 2024).A hepatoprotective study found E. guttatum extract exerted protective and pregnane X receptor (PXR)-modulating effects in a propiconazole-induced toxicity model, supporting traditional gastrointestinal/hepatic use (Ounissi et al., 2025).

safety_profile.plant_interactions: The study investigated the antimicrobial properties of water extracts, tinctures, and essential oils from Foeniculum vulgare, Thymus vulgaris, and Salvia officinalis. Among the tested plants, Thymus vulgaris showed the strongest antimicrobial activity, while Bacillus subtilis was the most sensitive microorganism and Escherichia coli was the most resistant. Additionally, combining essential oils enhanced antimicrobial efficacy, with the Salvia officinalis–Foeniculum vulgare combination exhibiting the greatest synergistic effect, highlighting the potential of these plant-derived essential oils as natural antimicrobial agents.( György ,2010)

scientific_data.experimental: Botanical and phytochemical standardization of F. vaillantii whole plant established pharmacognostic identification markers via microscopy and confirmed the presence of protopine and rutin in methanol extract at defined concentrations, supporting quality control standards for this traditional crude drug ( Rajopadhye & Upadhye , 2011).A broader review of Fumaria genus alkaloids and biological activities confirmed that hepatoprotective, antiviral, anti-inflammatory, antinociceptive, antimicrobial, antioxidant and antitumor effects across Fumaria species (including F. vaillantii) are mainly attributable to isoquinoline alkaloids, with phthalideisoquinolines, protoberberines and spirobenzylisoquinolines identified as the major alkaloid classes (Zhang et al., 2020).Fumaria vaillantii extract was found to enhance wound healing in a dedicated experimental study cited in a broader review of Fumaria officinalis active compounds and biological activities (Aguiar, 2023).

scientific_data.experimental: Ferulenol and ferprenin, the prenylated coumarins responsible for the toxic chemotype's hemorrhagic activity, were shown to inhibit mammalian liver microsomal vitamin K epoxide reductase complex 1 (VKORC1) activity — the same molecular target as warfarin — providing the definitive mechanistic explanation for the plant's anticoagulant toxicity (Louvet et al., 2015).A comprehensive review of traditional uses, phytochemistry, pharmacology and toxicology confirmed that only plants containing prenylated coumarins (ferulenol/ferprenin derivatives) elicit the toxic symptoms of "ferulosis," whereas chemotypes containing daucane esters instead are not toxic, explaining historical confusion about the plant's safety ( Akaberi et al., 2015).Antimycobacterial coumarins were isolated and characterized from the Sardinian giant fennel chemotype (Appendino et al., 2004).Documented cases of Ferula communis intoxication in livestock (goats) in Tunisia illustrate the real-world toxicological significance of the toxic chemotype in Mediterranean grazing regions directly relevant to North Africa ( Lahmar et al., 2018).

scientific_data.experimental: Oral administration of G. robertianum leaf decoctions to Goto-Kakizaki model mice with type 2 diabetes produced a decrease in blood glucose levels, an improvement in liver mitochondrial respiratory parameters, and an increase in the efficiency of oxidative phosphorylation, directly validating the traditional Algerian and Portuguese antidiabetic use (Haj ali et al 2025).Hexane and ethyl acetate extracts of G. robertianum showed significant anticancer activity (selectivity index 2.02–4.39) and inhibited the development of HHV-1 (herpes simplex virus type 1)-induced cytopathic effect in virus-infected cells, decreasing viral load by 0.52 and 1.42 log respectively ( Świątek et al ., 2023).Phytochemical profiling confirmed the presence of organic and phenolic acids, hydrolysable tannins (gallo- and ellagitannins) and flavonoids in extracts from aerial parts, supporting the broad pharmacological activity profile ( Świątek et al ., 2023).A comprehensive up-to-date review of G. robertianum's biological activity confirmed antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic, neuroprotective, anticancer and diuretic properties, while noting that knowledge of this plant remains relatively limited and requires more detailed mechanistic study ( Haj ali et al.,2025).

safety_profile.toxicity: Licorice (Glycyrrhiza glabra) has relatively low acute toxicity, with an oral LD₅₀ in animal studies generally higher than 5 g/kg, indicating low risk from a single high dose. However, its main safety concern is chronic use rather than acute toxicity. Prolonged or excessive intake of glycyrrhizin can cause pseudo-hyperaldosteronism, leading to hypertension, hypokalemia, sodium and water retention, and metabolic alkalosis. These effects are dose- and time-dependent and are usually reversible after stopping use. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2011). Assessment report on Glycyrrhiza glabra L. and/or Glycyrrhiza inflata Bat. and/or Glycyrrhiza uralensis Fisch., radix. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/571122/2010.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: The flavonoid-rich fractions of Glycyrrhiza glabra roots and Sophora japonica leaves exhibited potent antioxidant activity and significantly enhanced wound healing in vivo. Topical treatment reduced oxidative stress by decreasing malondialdehyde (MDA) levels while increasing glutathione (GSH) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activities. These antioxidant effects, supported by histopathological and molecular docking analyses, contributed to accelerated wound repair and demonstrated the therapeutic potential of both plants, individually and in combination, as natural antioxidant and wound-healing agents. ( Aly et al ., 2023)

scientific_data.clinical: In a randomized clinical trial (96 patients with gastric ulcer), treatment with deglycyrrhizinated liquorice for 4 weeks showed no significant difference compared to placebo in ulcer healing or symptom improvement. scientific_data.experimental: • Hepatoprotective (in vitro/in vivo): Glycyrrhizin, 18β-glycyrrhetinic acid, glabridin, liquiritigenin, isoliquiritigenin, and magnesium isoglycyrrhizinate demonstrated hepatoprotective effects: Nrf2 activation (antioxidant), NF-κB suppression (anti-inflammatory), modulation of Bax/Bcl-2 and caspase signaling (anti-apoptotic), inhibition of CYP2E1-related toxic bioactivation, and partial attenuation of TGF-β1-associated fibrogenesis in both in vitro hepatocyte models and in vivo CCl4/paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity models. (Pastorino et al.,2018) • Immunomodulation: Aqueous root extract of G. glabra (glycyrrhizin) stimulated lymphocyte and macrophage production from human granulocytes in vitro. safety_profile.toxicity: Hedera helix L. folium preparations are generally safe and well tolerated at recommended doses. Reported adverse effects are mainly gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea) and allergic reactions (skin rash, urticaria, dyspnoea, rarely anaphylaxis). Safety during pregnancy and lactation is not established, and use is not recommended due to insufficient data. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2017). Assessment report on Hedera helix L., folium. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/325715/2017.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: The study evaluated the potential herb–drug interactions of Hedera helix L. extract by assessing its inhibitory effects on cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes involved in drug metabolism. The extract demonstrated concentration-dependent inhibition of CYP2C8, CYP2C19, and CYP2D6, with the strongest effects observed against CYP2C8 and CYP2C19. It also exhibited time-dependent inhibition of CYP2C8 and CYP2C19, suggesting a higher likelihood of clinically relevant interactions with drugs metabolized by these enzymes. These findings indicate that H. helix extract may alter the metabolism of co-administered medicationet highlighting the need for caution when it is used alongside conventional drugs. (Rehman et al ., 2017)

scientific_data.clinical: Clinical studies evaluated ivy leaf preparations mainly in patients with productive cough and acute bronchitis. Studies in adults showed that ivy leaf extract improved cough severity and respiratory symptoms compared with placebo. In children with acute bronchitis, ivy leaf preparations showed improvement of symptoms and were comparable to acetylcysteine. The EMA concluded that the evidence supports the well-established use of ivy leaf as an expectorant for productive cough, based on clinical and bibliographic data demonstrating efficacy and safety. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2017). Assessment report on Hedera helix L., folium. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/325715/2017.
scientific_data.experimental: • Gastroprotective (in vivo, mouse model): α-Hederin and Hederacoside C tested as a possible safe Omeprazole phyto-alternative in ethanol-induced gastric ulcer mice — demonstrated significant gastroprotective effect with reduced ulcer index and oxidative stress markers, comparable to omeprazole, via molecular dockingand in vivo assessment.( Shokry et al.,2025)Acute lung injury (in vivo, mouse model): Bioactive phenolics fraction of standardized H. helix leaf extract significantly ameliorated LPS-induced acute lung injury via inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) and reduction of oxidative stress markers in lung tissue.( Shokry et al ., 2022) Ocular/antibacterial keratitis (in vivo/in vitro): H. helix saponins (targeting PI3K/Akt and OPRL pathways) demonstrated therapeutic potential against Pseudomonas aeruginosa-induced bacterial keratitis.( Hamdy et al.,2025)

safety_profile.toxicity: According to the EMA report, Herniaria glabra L. showed low toxicity in animal studies, because adverse effects only appeared at very high doses far above traditional human use. In acute toxicity tests, the extract had an LD₅₀ of about 8.5 g/kg BW and a NOAEL of 5 g/kg BW, with signs such as reduced activity, anorexia, and ataxia occurring only at high doses. In a 90-day repeated-dose study in rats, doses of 1–4 g/kg/day caused decreased body weight gain and, at the highest dose, liver and kidney changes (including increased liver enzymes and histological damage). European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2020). Assessment report on Herniaria glabra L., Herniaria hirsuta L., Herniaria incana Lam., herba. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/554033/2018.

scientific_data.experimental: An animal study evaluating the diuretic effect of crude ethanol and saponin-rich extracts of H. glabra found that saponin-rich fractions were responsible for the herb's diuretic activity (Hakimet al., 2021).Phytochemical reinvestigation of H. glabra saponins identified twelve previously undescribed triterpenoid pentacyclic glycosides (medicagenic acid and zanhic acid derivatives) and characterized their structure via spectroscopic methods, providing the chemical basis for the genus's traditional diuretic, antispasmodic and hypotensive uses ( Kozachok et al ., 2020).A comparative phytochemical and anti-inflammatory study of three wild-growing Herniaria species found saponin fractions from H. glabra demonstrated anti- inflammatory activity and favorable hemocompatibility in vitro, with H. glabra showing the highest total herniariasaponin content (465.68 ± 3.24 mg/g) among the three species tested.( Kolodziejczyk-Czepas et al ., 2026).A review of the pharmacological importance of Herniaria glabra and H. hirsuta confirmed hypotensive, diuretic, antiurolithiasis, antimicrobial, insecticidal and antioxidant effects for H. glabra specifically, based on phytochemical analysis identifying herniaria saponins I-VII, flavonoids and hydroxycoumarins (umbelliferone, herniarin) as the active constituent classes (Al-Snafi, 2018).

scientific_data.clinical: Barley grass (Hordeum vulgare) has been investigated in a few small human clinical studies as a dietary supplement. In one study using approximately 1.2 g/day for 8 weeks, supplementation was associated with improvements in metabolic markers, including a decrease in fasting blood glucose, HbA1c, total cholesterol, and LDL cholesterol, along with an increase in HDL cholesterol. (Zeng et al., 2018)
scientific_data.experimental: An animal study found dietary hull-less barley β-glucan reduced plasma LDL cholesterol in hypercholesterolemic hamsters by promoting fecal lipid excretion and regulating HMG-CoA reductase and CYP7A1 activity, and barley bran supplementation (5–10%) ameliorated fatty heart and liver changes in a rat model of diet-induced hypercholesterolemia over 8 weeks ( Abulnaja & El Rabey , 2015).• Anti-inflammatory/cardiovascular mechanism (in vitro): Crude extract and fractions of H. vulgare significantly inhibited platelet aggregation and modulated cyclooxygenase (COX) and lipoxygenase (LOX) pathways of arachidonic acid metabolism, with effects on antioxidant enzyme activity; methanolic extract of aerial parts inhibited LPS-induced inflammation both in vitro and in vivo. ( Gul et al.,2014)Lipid metabolism/hepatoprotective (in vivo, ICR mice): Modified highland barley supplementation regulated lipid metabolism and reduced liver injury in mice fed a high-fat/high-cholesterol diet; attributed to high β-glucan, low-fat, low-sugar composition. ( Zhou & Wu , 2022)Antioxidant (in vitro): β-glucan/ferulic acid and β-glucan/quercetin phenol–polysaccharide complexes from highland barley showed greater DPPH (71.74%), ABTS (54.56%), and hydroxyl radical scavenging activity than individual phenolic acids or β-glucan alone or their physical mixtures — demonstrating synergistic antioxidant complexation. ( Ren et al., 2025)Anti-urolithiatic / antihyperuricemic (in vivo, cited reviews): Barley seed extracts inhibited growth of urinary stones and reduced mild hyperuricemia in animal models, supporting traditional Ayurvedic use for urinary calculi.(Gul et al.,2014)

safety_profile.toxicity: Hypericum perforatum has low toxicity, with LD₅₀ ≥ 5000 mg/kg and only mild, reversible effects at very high doses, while excessive exposure to hypericin may cause photosensitivity. However, it is contraindicated or not recommended in children and in patients taking drugs such as oral contraceptives, anticoagulants, immunosuppressants, antiretrovirals, and antidepressants, due to strong CYP450-mediated interactions that can reduce drug effectiveness. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2009). Assessment report on Hypericum perforatum L., herba. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/101303/2008.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: St. John's wort has been reported to cause clinically important interactions with several conventional medications, including Warfarin, Phenprocoumon, Cyclosporine, HIV protease inhibitors, Theophylline, Digoxin, and oral contraceptives, often reducing their therapeutic effectiveness. These interactions are primarily attributed to the induction of drug-metabolizing enzymes (CYP3A4, CYP2C9, and CYP1A2) and the drug transporter P-glycoprotein, although the extent of this effect varies because of differences in the composition of SJW products. Additionally, SJW may produce pharmacodynamic interactions with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and triptans, increasing the risk of serotonin-related adverse effects. ( Henderson et al.,2002)

scientific_data.clinical: Clinical studies show that Hypericum perforatum extracts are effective in mild to moderate depression, with significant improvement vs placebo and similar efficacy to some standard antidepressants after 2–4 weeks of treatment. Adverse effects are usually mild (gastrointestinal discomfort, dizziness, fatigue, rare photosensitivity), but the main limitation is strong drug interactions via CYP450 enzyme induction, which can reduce the effect of many medicines (e.g., oral contraceptives, anticoagulants). European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2009). Assessment report on Hypericum perforatum L., herba. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/101303/2008.
scientific_data.experimental: Mechanism of antidepressant action: Hyperforin inhibits synaptosomal reuptake of serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, GABA, and L-glutamate, attributed to its unique protonophore properties activating non-selective cation channels (e.g., TRPC6) and elevating intracellular Na+/Ca2+, distinct from classical synthetic antidepressant mechanisms (e.g., SSRIs). (Sell et al., 2014)Antiviral (in vitro, anti-HBV): H. perforatum extract demonstrated inhibitory effect on hepatitis B virus (HBV) replication in vitro, supporting traditional antiviral use. (Pang et al., 2010)Genotoxicity/safety (Allium cepa + rat bone marrow models): H. perforatum showed no cytotoxic or mutagenic potential in vegetal (Allium cepa meristematic cells) or animal (rat bone marrow, acute and subchronic gavage) test systems; demonstrated significant antimutagenic activity against cyclophosphamide-induced clastogenic damage — 76% reduction (pre-treatment), 95% (simultaneous), and 97% (post-treatment). (Peron et al.,2013)

traditional_medicine.uses: I. pseudacorus is traditionally used as an antimicrobial, expectorant, diuretic, and hemostatic agent, and has been reported in experimental antitumor herbal preparations. (Tikhomirova et al., 2020)

scientific_data.experimental: Comparative UPLC-ESI-MS/MS metabolic profiling of Egyptian and Japanese I. pseudacorus cultivars identified 43 compounds (33 flavonoids, 3 xanthones, 3 phenolic acids and others); all extracts showed significant lipase inhibitory activity (IC50 values 0.42–4.81 µg/mL, more potent than the reference drug cetilistat at 7.47 µg/mL), with in silico docking identifying quercetin, galloyl glucose and irilin D as top-binding metabolites at the α-glucosidase and lipase active sites (Yehia et al.,2023)A study correlating secondary metabolites with antiprotozoal activity found the non-polar fraction of I. pseudacorus was the most potent fraction tested against Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense (IC50 8.17 µg/mL, selectivity index 3.67), with specific triterpenoid iridals and lipid metabolites identified as the most strongly correlated active compounds (Abdel-Baki et al.,2023).Osteogenic activity research found I. pseudacorus extract modulated differentiation of osteoblasts and osteoclasts in an experimental bone-cell model . (Kim et al.,2012)

safety_profile.toxicity: The study on Juglans regia leaf extracts indicates a low acute toxicity in mice, with LD50 values of approximately 5.5 g/kg for the aqueous extract and 3.3 g/kg for the ethanolic extract. No severe toxic effects were observed at lower experimental doses, and pharmacological effects such as anti-inflammatory and analgesic activity occurred at doses far below toxic levels. Overall, the results suggest that Juglans regia leaf extracts have relatively low acute toxicity in animal models, although their long-term safety and human toxicity have not been fully established. (Hosseinzadeh et al., 2011)

It is found in Tlemcen, Médéa, Blida, Bouira, Tizi Ouzou, Béjaïa, Jijel, Skikda, Mila, Constantine, Guelma, Sétif, Batna, Khenchela, Souk Ahras, and El Tarf. It grows in mountain valleys, orchards, forest margins, and along streams, preferring deep, fertile, well-drained soils at elevations of approximately 400–1,800 m.-
distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering stage:March–May, depending on altitude and local climatic conditions.Harvesting stage:Leaves: May–July, collected when fully expanded and healthy.Green husks: June–August, depending on the intended medicinal use.Fruits (nuts): September–October, when the green husk splits naturally and the nuts are fully mature.Plant material is generally shade-dried (leaves and husks), while mature nuts are air-dried before storage.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Leaves, bark, green husks. (Sharma et al., 2022)
traditional_medicine.uses: traditionally used for the treatment of skin disorders (eczema, wounds), gastrointestinal diseases (diarrhea, intestinal parasites), diabetes, inflammatory conditions, respiratory ailments, and oral infections (Sharma et al., 2022)
traditional_medicine.dosage: Adults and elderly: cutaneous use only Preparation: 4–6 g dried leaf in 200 mL boiling water (decoction) Indications: impregnated dressing applied 2–4 times daily or up to 30 minutes twice daily on affected skin areas Duration: short-term use (maximum 1 week); not recommended in <18 years. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2013). Community herbal monograph on Juglans regia L., folium. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/346737/2011.

scientific_data.clinical: Juglans regia L. leaf preparations show clinical and experimental evidence of antidiabetic effects, improving fasting blood glucose and HbA1c. Additional studies indicate beneficial effects on lipid profile (reduction of total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL) and potential antihypertensive activity. The extract is generally well tolerated, with only mild gastrointestinal side effects reported. (Delaviz et al., 2017)
scientific_data.experimental: Topical administration of J. regia leaf extract ointment (2% and 5%) significantly accelerated diabetic wound healing in a controlled rat model, with the 5% concentration outperforming a phenytoin reference drug across wound closure rate, collagen deposition, fibroblast/blood vessel density and TGF-β/VEGF gene expression measures over a 21-day study period (Nasiry et al.,2022)A hydroalcoholic extract of walnut leaves (100, 200 and 400 mg/kg) demonstrated a protective effect against gentamicin-induced nephrotoxicity in male Wistar rats, improving biochemical kidney markers and histopathology.( Meraati et al.,2025)

In rats, oral administration of an ethyl acetate leaf extract at a dose of 2000 mg/kg body weight for 14 days caused no mortality, no significant physiological changes, and no observable toxic effects. (Gonçalves et al., 2022)

distribution.habitat_description: the most widely distributed conifers in the world. It occurs throughout Europe, North Africa (including the Atlas Mountains of Algeria and Morocco), Asia, and North America. It grows from sea level to mountainous regions, commonly inhabiting heathlands, rocky slopes, open woodlands, coniferous forests, and calcareous or sandy soils. In Algeria, it is mainly found in the Tell Atlas and Saharan Atlas mountain ranges, particularly in high-altitude forests.-
distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageApril–June (depending on altitude and climate).Harvesting StageBerries (galbuli): Harvested from September to November of the second or third year, when they have ripened to a dark blue-black color.Leaves and young twigs: Usually harvested from late spring to early summer (May–July) for medicinal and essential oil production.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Berries/leaves
traditional_medicine.uses: diuretic, antiseptic, for urinary tract issues, dyspepsia, rheumatism, respiratory complaints.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Herbal tea: 2–2.5 g in 150 ml boiling water, 2–3 times daily. Liquid extract (25% ethanol): 2–4 ml, 3 times daily. Tincture (45% ethanol): 1–2 ml, 3 times daily. Traditional use (berries): 5–15 berries daily, short-term use only (max ~21 days). European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2023). Assessment report on Juniperus communis L., galbulus (pseudo-fructus). Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/241319/2021.

scientific_data.experimental: Methanolic extract of J. communis (100 and 200 mg/kg) produced a significant reduction in blood glucose and an increase in HDL levels in streptozotocin-nicotinamide-induced diabetic rats over 21 days, with effects compared against the standard drug glibenclamide. ( Bais et al .,2014)A patented herbal antidiabetic preparation (Antidiabetis) containing J. communis berries among nine other herbs significantly decreased blood glucose in both acute and subacute alloxan-induced diabetic mouse models. ( Petlevski et al.,2001)Comparative α-glucosidase and α-amylase inhibition assays of two Juniperus species leaf and berry extracts found potent α-amylase inhibitory effects (51.7–53.6% at 3 mg/mL) alongside excellent radical scavenging activity (97.8–99.5% at 3 mg/mL) in the leaf extracts. ( Gök et al.,2021).

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity/safety:Juniperus phoenicea showed no mortality up to 2000 mg/kg in acute toxicity tests, with no significant liver enzyme changes, but increases in urea and creatinine suggest possible mild kidney stress, especially at higher doses. (Lafraxo et al., 2024)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: The essential oils of Juniperus phoenicea and Salvia officinalis showed antibacterial, antifungal, and moderate antioxidant activities. Salvia officinalis oil exhibited stronger antifungal effects than J. phoenicea, while Staphylococcus aureus was the most susceptible bacterium. However, combining the two oils produced an antagonistic effect, reducing their overall activity. ( Ait-Mimoun et al.,2023)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antioxidant, antimicrobial, gastroprotective and hepatoprotective activities have been directly demonstrated for Algerian J. phoenicea essential oil in recent in vitro and in vivo/in silico studies; cytotoxic effects against breast and colon cancer cells have also been reported.Phytochemical profile: Essential oil composition varies notably by region: Algerian Aïn El Orak material dominated by α-terpinolene (21.29%), limonene (14.68%), terpinen-4-ol (12.04%) and β-myrcene (9.93%); eastern Algeria material dominated instead by α-pinene (36.3–55.9%) with terpinolene and Δ³-carene as secondary components, illustrating significant chemotype variability within the species.

distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageJuniperus phoenicea flowers mainly from February to AprilHarvesting stage :The young leaves and twigs are generally harvested from April to June for medicinal and essential oil production, while the ripe berry-like cones (galbuli) are collected from September to November, when they are fully mature and have developed their characteristic reddish-brown color.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Leaves/berries. (Zouari Bouassida et al., 2018)
traditional_medicine.uses: for diabetes, menstrual regulation, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, rheumatism, wounds. (Zouari Bouassida et al., 2018)

scientific_data.experimental: A 2026 study characterizing J. phoenicea essential oil from Aïn El Orak, Algeria found DPPH radical-scavenging IC50 of approximately 0.23 mg/mL, and in vivo/in silico testing demonstrated gastroprotective and hepatoprotective effects, with serum ALT and AST levels normalized (especially at 300 mg/kg) and liver histoarchitecture nearly fully restored; molecular docking identified strong interactions of major essential oil compounds with H+/K+-ATPase, Helicobacter pylori urease, xanthine oxidoreductase and PPAR-α. (Medjekane et al ., 2016)A study of essential oils from five eastern Algeria localities found α-pinene (36.3–55.9%) as the dominant compound, with terpinolene, Δ³-carene and β-phellandrene present at variable concentrations, and confirmed antimicrobial activity of the oils. ( Ramdani et al.,2013).Comparative radical-scavenging and ferric-reducing studies evaluated J. phoenicea alongside J. thurifera, J. oxycedrus and Tetraclinis articulata, contributing to a broader understanding of antioxidant variability across Mediterranean conifer species. ( El Jemli et al.,2016).

safety_profile.toxicity: Can cause toxicity (e.g., blurred vision, dizziness, nausea, vomiting) especially in excess or fresh material (Besharat et al., 2009 case series of 8 patients). Generally considered mild but avoid high doses.at higher doses. (Lafraxo et al., 2024)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Sedative, analgesic, antitussive, mild hypnotic and acetylcholinesterase-inhibitory activities attributed to sesquiterpene lactones; anti-inflammatory activity also reported in combination studies; notably, rigorous human clinical trial evidence is explicitly absent from the literature despite long traditional use.Phytochemical profile: Sesquiterpene lactones (lactucin, lactucopicrin, 11β,13-dihydrolactucin — characteristic bitter guaianolides also found in Cichorium intybus).

distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageLactuca virosa flowers from May to August, with the peak flowering period occurring in June and July.Harvesting StageThe aerial parts (leaves and flowering stems) are generally harvested from May to July, preferably at the beginning of flowering when the latex (lactucarium) content is highest. traditional_medicine.parts_used: The milky latex,Leaves, Whole plant. (Besharat et al., 2009)
traditional_medicine.uses: Lactuca virosa has been traditionally used as a sedative, analgesic, antitussive, and antispasmodic agent. (Besharat et al., 2009)

scientific_data.experimental: Lactucin and its derivatives lactucopicrin and 11β,13-dihydrolactucin were evaluated for analgesic and sedative properties in mice; compounds showed analgesic effects at 15 and 30 mg/kg in the hot-plate test comparable to ibuprofen at 30 mg/kg, with lactucopicrin appearing most potent in analgesic outcomes, and lactucin and lactucopicrin (but not 11β,13-dihydrolactucin) also showing positive sedative properties (Wesolowska et al., 2006)A combined in vivo/in vitro study of aqueous extracts of Lactuca virosa and Euphorbia hirta found significant reduction of paw inflammation in albumin- and histamine-induced inflammatory tests in mice across multiple extract combination ratios (Uwaya, Okakwu & Omozuwa, 2021).

safety_profile.toxicity: Bay leaf (Laurus nobilis) showed no significant adverse effects in short-term human clinical studies (10–30 days) at dietary or low supplemental doses. However, the available data are limited, and only minor allergic reactions have been occasionally reported, so its long-term safety remains not fully established. (Singletary, 2021)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: The study demonstrated that combinations of Laurus nobilis, Lavandula stoechas, and Mentha pulegium essential oils exhibited strong synergistic antioxidant and anticholinesterase activities, with L. stoechas showing the highest enzyme inhibitory effect. These synergistic combinations enhanced efficacy while potentially reducing the required doses, highlighting their promise for food and pharmaceutical applications. ( Yakoubi et al.,2020)

distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageLaurus nobilis flowers from March to May, depending on local climatic conditions and altitude.Harvesting StageThe leaves are generally harvested from late spring to early autumn (May–September), when they are fully developed and rich in essential oil. The fruits (berries) are collected from October to December, once they have ripened and turned dark purple to black.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Leaves (primarily), fruits. (Awada et al., 2023)
traditional_medicine.uses: Used for gastrointestinal disorders (dyspepsia, flatulence), respiratory issues (colds, bronchitis), diabetes, inflammation, and as a diuretic/stimulant. (Singletary, 2021)

scientific_data.clinical: Human clinical studies on Laurus nobilis (bay leaf) are limited and show mixed results. Some small trials in patients with type 2 diabetes reported improvements in blood glucose and lipid profiles after short-term use (1–3 g/day), while studies in healthy subjects showed minimal or no significant effects. Overall, the clinical evidence remains limited and inconsistent. (Singletary, 2021)
scientific_data.experimental: Aqueous and methanol-acetone leaf extracts of Lebanese L. nobilis supplemented for 4 weeks improved plasma glucose and significantly decreased serum triglycerides, abdominal fat and body weight gain in a high-fat-diet rat model of type 2 diabetes, with 1,8-cineole identified as the major constituent of the methanol-acetone extract . ( Daher et al .,2021)The leaf essential oil demonstrated a significant analgesic effect in tail-flick and formalin tests, a dose-dependent anti-inflammatory effect in formalin-induced edema, and a moderate sedative effect at anti-inflammatory doses, with potency comparable to the reference drugs morphine and piroxicam. ( Sayyah et al., 2003)

safety_profile.toxicity: Lavandula angustifolia subsp. angustifolia shows low acute toxicity. In animal studies, the LD₅₀ of lavender essential oil was reported to be higher than 2000 mg/kg body weight, indicating a relatively low toxicity profile. Adverse effects are mainly associated with excessive exposure or ingestion of concentrated essential oil . (Manzoor et al., 2025)

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Flowers, aerial parts, essential oil. (Batiha et al., 2023)

scientific_data.clinical: Clinical studies on Lavandula angustifolia have reported potential benefits in reducing anxiety, improving sleep quality, and alleviating pain. Trials using lavender essential oil or oral preparations showed positive effects, but current evidence remains limited and further well-designed clinical studies are needed to confirm its therapeutic efficacy. (Manzoor et al., 2025)
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Lavender essential oil and its main components (linalool, linalyl acetate) show strong antibacterial activity against pathogens including S. aureus, E. coli, P. aeruginosa, MRSA, and oral bacteria .( Stamova et al.,2025, Moon et al., 2006)Antiviral potential against HSV-1 and other viruses (EOs reduced infectivity significantly). ( Abou Baker et al .,2021)Anti-inflammatory: Reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6), NF-κB, COX-2 in models like ear oedema and pleurisy; linalool is key. (Pandur et al.,2021)

safety_profile.toxicity: Lavandula stoechas essential oil is toxic at high doses due to its high camphor content. It can cause convulsions and neurotoxic effects, and poisoning cases (especially in children) have been reported after inhalation or misuse. In animal studies, it showed a very low LD₅₀ (1.88 mg/kg), confirming strong toxicity, and it was found to be pro-convulsant. (Şahinler et al., 2022)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: The study demonstrated that combinations of Laurus nobilis, Lavandula stoechas, and Mentha pulegium essential oils exhibited strong synergistic antioxidant and anticholinesterase activities, with L. stoechas showing the highest enzyme inhibitory effect. These synergistic combinations enhanced efficacy while potentially reducing the required doses, highlighting their promisefor food and pharmaceutical applications. ( Yakoubi et al.,2020).

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antimicrobial (antibacterial, antifungal, antibiofilm), antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, insecticidal/repellent and adaptogenic activities reported for essential oil and extracts; fenchone/camphor chemotype is the predominant constituent class across most studied populations.Phytochemical profile: Essential oil dominated by fenchone, camphor and 1,8-cineole; non-volatile phenolic compounds include rosmarinic acid, caffeic acid and salvianolic acid B as major phenolic acids, with luteolin and eriodictyol-O-glucuronide as main flavonoids.

distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageLavandula stoechas flowers from March to June, with peak flowering generally occurring between April and May.Harvesting StageThe flowering tops are harvested from April to June, preferably at the beginning of full bloom when the essential oil content is highest. scientific_data.experimental: A study of essential oils from wild Algerian L. stoechas populations characterized chemical composition, chemical variability and in vitro biological properties, contributing foundational data on the species' phytochemistry from its native Algerian range. (Benabdelkader et al., 2011)A 2025 Algerian study (Annaba, El-Tarf province) evaluating L. stoechas essential oil alongside Artemisia absinthium found very good antibacterial activity against Gram-positive bacteria (inhibition zones >15 mm) and average activity against Gram-negative bacteria (8–14 mm), with substantial reduction (61–80%) of Aspergillus niger mycelial growth at 1–3 mg/mL concentrations.( Bouzeraa et al.,2025)Adaptogenic activity of essential oils from L. stoechas, alongside Cinnamomum camphora, Eucalyptus globulus and Rosmarinus officinalis, used in North African folk medicine was specifically evaluated in a dedicated study (Boumendjel et al., 2021)

safety_profile.toxicity: Generally safe; mucilage can cause bloating/flatulence. Grind seeds fresh to avoid cyanide concerns (low risk at food doses). Safe in pregnancy at dietary levels. (Noreen et al., 2023)Drug-Plant interaction:Plant-Plant interaction:Dietary supplementation with flaxseed (Linum usitatissimum) and fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) seed meals improved growth performance, digestive function, intestinal and liver health, and immune responses in Labeo rohita fingerlings over a 30-day feeding trial. Fenugreek supplementation (3 g; G-2) produced the best growth performance, with the highest final body weight, specific growth rate, and amylase activity, while flaxseed (G-1) enhanced immune parameters by increasing white blood cell and lymphocyte counts. Histological examination showed normal liver architecture and elongated intestinal villi in supplemented groups, indicating improved gut health. Overall, flaxseed and fenugreek seed meals represent promising natural feed additives for enhancing fish health and productivity, offering a sustainable alternative to synthetic growth promoters in aquaculture. ( Areej et al.,2025)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Hypolipidemic, antidiabetic/glycemic-control-supporting, anti-inflammatory, phytoestrogenic (via lignans), antioxidant and anticancer (particularly breast cancer-related) activities, predominantly attributed to lignans (notably secoisolariciresinol diglucoside, SDG) and α-linolenic acid.Phytochemical profile: Lignans (secoisolariciresinol diglucoside as the predominant compound, ~95% of total lignans; also matairesinol, secoisolariciresinol, lariciresinol diglucoside), α-linolenic acid (omega-3 fatty acid), soluble and insoluble dietary fiber, mucilage, vitamin E (tocopherols).

scientific_data.clinical: Strong evidence for laxative effects and lipid-lowering (omega-3s); supports benefits in diabetes, inflammation, and menopausal symptoms in human studies. (Basch et al., 2007)

safety_profile.toxicity: Lythrum salicaria is generally safe, with no significant adverse effects reported. Acute toxicity studies showed an intravenous LD₅₀ of 0.1674–0.3289 g/kg bw. pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antidiarrheal, antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antinociceptive and antidiabetic activities have found experimental support; notably, a documented mutagenic/genotoxic finding for a high-tannin extract introduces an important safety caveat that should be weighed against the plant's pharmacopoeial status.Phytochemical profile: C-glucosidic ellagitannins (castalagin, vescalagin, salicarinins A and B — dominant compound class), C-glycosidic flavonoids (vitexin, isovitexin, orientin, isoorientin), anthocyanins, heteropolysaccharides, hydrolysable tannins.

scientific_data.experimental: L. salicaria herb extract and its dominant ellagitannins (castalagin, vescalagin, salicarinins A and B) inhibited enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) growth and adhesion to intestinal epithelial cell monolayers in a concentration-dependent manner, with inhibitory activity confirmed ex vivo in distal colon samples of postweaning piglets, and the same compounds stimulated intestinal monolayer formation by enhancing claudin 4 production, supporting the plant's traditional antidiarrheal reputation through a defined mechanism. ( Granica et al.,2020)A controlled feeding study in weaned rabbits supplemented with 0.2% and 0.4% ground L. salicaria herb found no significant adverse effects on performance, blood parameters, nutrient digestibility or gut microbiota composition, supporting a favorable safety profile at these dietary inclusion levels.( Granica et al.,2020)Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antinociceptive activities of sequential solvent extracts (petroleum ether, ethyl acetate, methanol, aqueous methanol, and reflux water extract) were evaluated using DPPH radical scavenging, iron(III) reductive activity, lipid peroxidation inhibition and the p-benzoquinone-induced abdominal constriction antinociceptive testA comprehensive review of L. (Tunalier et al.,2007)A comprehensive review of L. salicaria as an underestimated European traditional medicinal plant confirmed antidiarrheal, antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antidiabetic activities for extracts and isolated compounds, while noting the plant's status as a pharmacopoeial material despite declining contemporary use.(Piwowarski et al.,2015)A dedicated mussel micronucleus genotoxicity study (using Unio pictorum) found that an L. salicaria extract with high hydrolysable tannin content produced a significant mutagenic effect, leading the authors to recommend evaluating the plant's genotoxic potential both in aquatic ecosystems and with regard to its safe use as a medicinal herb.(Eck-Varanka et al .,2015)

scientific_data.experimental: A hydroalcoholic lentil extract reduced plasma cholesterol by 16.8% and increased fecal bile acid excretion after 71 days in a diet-induced hypercholesterolemic rat model, with an accompanying in vitro fermentation experiment supporting a prebiotic effect via short-chain fatty acid production (Micioni Di Bonaventura et al., 2017)Phenolic extract of beluga (black) lentil protected AML12 mouse hepatocytes against H2O2-induced oxidative cytotoxicity in a dose-dependent manner (up to ~50% viability preservation at 100 µg/mL) and reduced intracellular reactive oxygen species, with in vivo hepatoprotective effects confirmed in a CCl4-induced acute liver failure mouse model. safety_profile.toxicity: Lawsonia inermis shows low acute toxicity in animal studies (safe up to 2 g/kg in mice), with no mortality or major poisoning signs. However, some studies report possible delayed toxicity, reproductive effects, and teratogenic changes at high doses, and a rare case of acute kidney injury in a susceptible (G6PD-deficient) patient after ingestion. Overall, it is considered relatively safe at normal use, but caution is needed in pregnancy and high-dose exposure. (Batiha et al., 2023)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Aqueous extracts of Lawsonia inermis and Peganum harmala exhibited significant in vitro antileishmanial activity against Leishmania tropica promastigotes at low and moderate concentrations. Their combination showed enhanced inhibitory effects, indicating a synergistic interaction that outperformed the individual extracts. ( Al-Ogaili , 2016)An herbal mixture composed of Aloe vera, henna, Adiantum capillus-veneris and myrrh improved wound healing in streptozotocin-induced diabetic rats in a controlled experimental study. ( Galehdari et al.,2016)

A randomized clinical trial on oral lichen planus found that henna mouthwash improved oral symptoms and inflammation compared with standard treatment (chlorhexidine) in some patients. (Kakoei et al., 2022)
scientific_data.experimental: A comprehensive 2025 phytochemistry and pharmacology review compiled evidence for antioxidant, antidiabetic, antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activities, alongside immunomodulatory and wound-healing effects established in more recent investigations. safety_profile.plant_interactions: An in silico study investigated the antiviral potential of Salvia officinalis and Malva sylvestris against COVID-19. The results suggested that tiliroside from M. sylvestris, when combined with S. officinalis, showed greater predicted antiviral activity than when used alone. Additionally, 4-hydroxybenzoic acid and 9,12,13-trihydroxyoctadeca-10,15-dienoic acid were identified as promising synergistic compounds. These plant-derived metabolites were predicted to inhibit a key enzyme required for SARS-CoV-2 replication, highlighting their potential as accessible and cost-effective antiviral candidates. However, further laboratory and clinical studies are needed to confirm these findings. (Saraçoğlu et al .,2024)

safety_profile.toxicity: An aqueous leaf extract of Melissa officinalis showed no genotoxic effects in Ames and micronucleus tests. In a 90-day oral toxicity study in rats, no treatment-related adverse effects were observed in clinical signs, blood parameters, biochemical markers, or organ histology. The NOAEL was the highest tested dose, reaching 3046 mg/kg body weight/day in males and 3721 mg/kg body weight/day in females, indicating a high safety margin. (Lobach et al., 2024)Drug-Plat interactions:A study investigated the synergistic antibacterial effects of water, ethanol, and ethyl acetate extracts of Melissa officinalis combined with five commonly used antibiotics against antibiotic-susceptible and antibiotic-resistant pathogenic bacteria. All extracts exhibited synergistic interactions with at least one antibiotic, enhancing antibacterial activity, particularly against resistant strains. Ethanol and ethyl acetate extracts showed greater synergistic potential than the water extract, despite the latter having the highest total phenolic content, while the ethyl acetate extract contained the highest flavonoid levels. ( Stefanovic & Comic , 2012)Plant-Plant interactions:A preclinical study evaluated the antidepressant and antioxidant effects of aqueous extracts of Nepeta menthoides and Melissa officinalis, administered individually and in combination, in reserpine-induced depressed mice. The combined treatment produced synergistic antidepressant-like effects and significantly increased brain catalase activity, indicating enhanced antioxidant defense. These findings suggest that the combination may exert its antidepressant effects through synergistic antioxidant mechanisms, likely supported by their phenolic and flavonoid constituents. ( Talebi et al.,2022)The combination of Melissa officinalis and Nepeta menthoides demonstrated synergistic antidepressant and antioxidant effects in a preclinical mouse model, likely through enhanced antioxidant activity. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial, the same herbal combination significantly reduced insomnia severity as well as symptoms of anxiety and depression after four weeks of treatment, supporting its potential as a complementary therapy for sleep and mood disorders.( Ranjbar et al.,2018)

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Leaves (primarily), aerial parts.(Shakeri et al., 2016)
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditionally used for anxiety, insomnia, stress, digestive disorders (colic, dyspepsia), headaches, cold sores, and as a sedative/antispasmodic. (Shakeri et al., 2016)
traditional_medicine.dosage: Herbal tea (infusion): 1.5–4.5 g of dried herbal substance in 150 mL of boiling water, 1–3 times daily. Powdered herbal substance: 0.19–0.55 g, 2–3 times daily. Liquid extract: 2–4 mL, 1–3 times daily. Tincture: 2–6 mL, 1–3 times daily. Dried aqueous or hydroalcoholic extracts (45–53% V/V): doses equivalent to the herbal tea, liquid extract, or tincture depending on the preparation. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2013). Community herbal monograph on Melissa officinalis L., folium. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMA/HMPC/196745/2012.

scientific_data.clinical: Anxiety & stress: Clinical trials and meta-analyses show that Melissa officinalis extract significantly reduces anxiety and stress symptoms compared with placebo, especially in acute use, with mild sedative effects and good tolerability(Ghazizadeh et al., 2021) . Cognitive / mood effects: Some controlled studies show short-term improvements in attention, calmness, and cognitive performance at moderate doses (while higher doses may cause mild sedation), but overall evidence remains mixed and still limited. (Oliveira et al., 2025)
scientific_data.experimental: Bioassay-guided fractionation of the methanol extract against rat brain GABA transaminase (GABA-T) identified RA as responsible for 40% inhibition at 100 µg/mL (approximately 1.5% of dry leaf mass), with ursolic acid (UA) and oleanolic acid (OA) as additional active principles; this established the first mechanistic basis for the anxiolytic activity of M. officinalis, directly linking the major phytochemical to a validated neurological drug target used in treatment of anxiety and epilepsy. ( Awad et al., 2009)M. officinalis ethanolic extract produced anxiolytic-like effects in the elevated plus-maze (EPM) and forced swim test in male and female rats; effects in females were stronger in a model-dependent manner; anxiolytic potency was described as comparable to diazepam (DZP) across multiple animal anxiety models, and the results were attributed to GABA-T inhibition-mediated elevation of brain GABA levels. ( Taiwo et al., 2012)

safety_profile.toxicity: The acute oral toxicity of Mentha piperita L. essential oil is low, with reported LD₅₀ values of 2426–4441 mg/kg in rats, indicating a wide safety margin in experimental models.(Eickholt & Box, 1965)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: A study investigated the potential herb–drug interactions of seven edible herbs by evaluating their effects on CYP3A4 gene expression in rifampicin-treated HepG2 cells. Mentha piperita (peppermint) showed the strongest inhibitory activity, with pheophorbide a identified as the active compound responsible for suppressing CYP3A4 expression in a dose-dependent manner. These findings suggest that peppermint may influence the metabolism of drugs processed by CYP3A4, although the effective concentration of pheophorbide a was low, indicating a favorable safety margin. ( Kobayashi et al.,2019)This study evaluated the synergistic antimicrobial effects of Mentha piperita essential oil in combination with commonly used antibacterial and antifungal drugs against a broad range of bacterial and yeast strains. The essential oil exhibited strong synergistic activity with gentamicin, significantly enhancing antibacterial efficacy against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Synergistic effects with antifungal agents were also observed but were less pronounced, suggesting that M. piperita essential oil may serve as a useful adjuvant to improve antimicrobial therapy, particularly against multidrug-resistant bacteria. ( Rosato et al.,2018)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: This study evaluated the antimicrobial activity of Mentha piperita, Mentha longifolia, and Ocimum basilicum leaf extracts individually and in combination using the microbroth dilution method and fractional inhibitory concentration analysis. M. piperita exhibited the strongest individual antibacterial activity, while combinations of the three extracts generally produced enhanced antimicrobial effects, demonstrating synergism against most tested bacterial strains. The combination of M. longifolia and O. basilicum showed antagonistic activity against Staphylococcus aureus. Overall, combining these Lamiaceae species improved antibacterial efficacy compared with using the extracts individually.( Adham , 2015)

traditional_medicine.parts_used: the dried leaves
traditional_medicine.uses: Mentha piperita L. leaf preparations are traditionally used for the symptomatic relief of digestive disorders, especially dyspepsia (indigestion) and flatulence (bloating/gas).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Herbal tea: Children 4–11 years: 1–2 g in 100–150 mL boiling water, 3 times/day; adults and elderly: 1.5–3 g in 100–150 mL boiling water, 3 times/day. Tincture: 2–3 mL, 3 times/day. Not recommended for children <4 years. European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2007). Community herbal monograph on Mentha × piperita L., folium. scientific_data.clinical: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS): Clinical trials with peppermint oil (derived from Mentha piperita) showed improvement in IBS symptoms, including abdominal pain, bloating, and overall symptom severity compared with placebo. (Nee et al., 2021) Digestive disorders (functional dyspepsia and gastrointestinal discomfort): Studies suggest peppermint preparations have antispasmodic effects and may reduce gastrointestinal cramps and discomfort by relaxing intestinal smooth muscle. (Chumpitazi et al., 2018)
scientific_data.experimental: Strong antispasmodic effect on gastrointestinal smooth muscle (Ca²⁺ channel antagonism), antimicrobial against bacteria (e.g., S. aureus, E. coli) and fungi, antioxidant (radical scavenging), anti-inflammatory, cytotoxic/apoptotic effects in some cancer cell lines. ( Hudz et al.,2023)

safety_profile.toxicity: Mentha pulegium L. is potentially toxic due to its essential oil rich in pulegone, which can cause liver damage. Low doses of traditional preparations may be tolerated, but the essential oil is highly toxic and unsafe for internal use. (Amtaghri et al., 2024)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: This study used a mixture design approach and microdilution assays to evaluate the antimicrobial interactions among essential oils from Mentha piperita, Mentha pulegium, and Ormenis mixta against Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Candida tropicalis. The results demonstrated a synergistic interaction between M. piperita and M. pulegium essential oils, with optimized mixtures showing enhanced antimicrobial activity against all three microorganisms. These findings suggest that combining these essential oils may provide an effective natural strategy to combat antimicrobial resistance and serve as natural food preservatives. (Chraibi et al .,2021)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antibacterial and antioxidant activities have been demonstrated for the essential oil in vitro; however, the plant's pharmacological profile is dominated by severe, well-characterized hepatotoxicity and abortifacient/reproductive toxicity that substantially outweighs any therapeutic application.Phytochemical profile: Essential oil consisting of 62–97% R-(+)-pulegone (the principal toxic constituent), with menthofuran as a toxic downstream metabolite; pulegone is metabolized by cytochrome P450 to menthofuran, which depletes hepatic glutathione and directly damages hepatocytes.
