scientific_data.clinical: A randomized clinical trial showed that Myrtus communis berry extract (1000 mg/day for 6 weeks) improved gastroesophageal reflux and dyspeptic symptoms compared with control. (Zohalinezhad et al., 2016) A clinical study using myrtle leaf extract oral paste showed improvement in recurrent aphthous stomatitis symptoms (pain, ulcer size, and inflammation). (Tahrali, 2026) A randomized trial of hydroalcoholic myrtle extract (500 mg capsules) in Alzheimer’s patients reported improvement in cognitive function scores after treatment. (Kamali et al., 2026)
scientific_data.experimental: A study of Salvia verbenaca, Ferula vesceritensis and Myrtus communis (all used in Algerian traditional medicine) found infusion extracts of M. communis at 100 and 500 mg/kg produced antidiabetic effects across hypoglycemic testing in normal mice, oral glucose tolerance tests, and streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice, with general agreement (though not direct quantitative correlation) between in vivo and in vitro (α-amylase inhibition) antidiabetic effects. ( Harchaoui et al.,2026)Algerian M. communis essential oil demonstrated remarkable concentration-dependent free radical scavenging activity (DPPH IC50 15.317 µg/mL) and significant in vitro and in vivo anti-inflammatory activity, limiting carrageenan-induced paw thickness development in an animal model; in silico molecular docking identified 9 of 60 GC-MS-characterized compounds with higher COX-2 binding energy than the reference drug diclofenac. ( Belahcene et al ., 2023)Essential oil from Algerian M. communis demonstrated potent antifungal activity (notable inhibition zones against Fusarium oxysporum, Aspergillus fumigatus and Penicillium sp.) and strong insecticidal/repellent activity against Tribolium castaneum (contact toxicity LC50 0.029 µL/insect; 99.44% repellency at 0.23 mg/cm² after 24h), with density functional theory calculations supporting the mechanistic basis of bioactivity. ( Barboucha et al.,2025)A review of antioxidant activity comparing M. communis and the Saharan myrtle M. nivellei (both used in Algerian folk medicine) characterized galloyl derivatives, flavonol derivatives, anthocyanins and myrtucommulone as key bioactive compound classes underlying anti-inflammatory activity. (Hennia et al.,2018)

safety_profile.toxicity: The LD₅₀ of Morus alba leaf extract in mice was reported as 2 g/kg body weight after oral administration, indicating a relatively low acute toxicity and a wide safety margin.(Batiha et al., 2023)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: This in vitro study evaluated the potential herb–drug interactions of Morus alba extract and its major constituents, cyanidin 3-glucoside and rutin, in combination with acetaminophen, aspirin, simvastatin, and caffeine. While cyanidin 3-glucoside and rutin had no significant effects, M. alba extract altered the expression of several drug-metabolizing enzymes and transporters. The findings indicate that M. alba may interact with these drugs and therefore is recommended to be consumed at a low dosage when used concomitantly with acetaminophen, aspirin, simvastatin, or caffeine. ( Udomsak et al.,2022)

traditional_medicine.uses: Morus nigra L. has been traditionally used to treat metabolic, gastrointestinal, respiratory, and cardiovascular disorders, including diabetes, hypertension, diarrhea, cough, fever, and anemia. (Özgür et al., 2025)

scientific_data.clinical: Morus nigra shows moderate but promising clinical effects on menopausal symptoms and lipid profile, with potential anti-inflammatory and cardioprotective properties. However, the evidence remains limited (small clinical trials and short duration studies) and requires further confirmation. (Costa et al., 2020), (Keshtkar Aghababaee et al., 2015)
scientific_data.experimental: Brazilian Morus nigra attenuated hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia and prooxidant status in alloxan-induced diabetic rats, supporting traditional antidiabetic use. ( Junior et al.,2017).A phytochemical and lipid-lowering study found M. nigra leaf infusion had higher phenolic/flavonoid content and antioxidant activity than decoction or hydromethanolic extracts, and demonstrated hypolipidemic effects when compared against the reference drug fenofibrate.( Zeni et al.,2017)A comprehensive antioxidant and hepatoprotective study found black mulberry leaf, bark and seed oil ethanol extracts significantly lowered hepatosomatic index, potentiated superoxide dismutase and catalase enzyme activity, reduced lipid peroxidation and reduced P450 enzyme positivity in streptozotocin-induced oxidative stress mouse models . ( Vukmirović et al.,2023)Black mulberry leaf extract and pulp demonstrated anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties in an LPS-induced sepsis mouse model over a 21-day treatment period. ( de Pádua Lúcio et al.,2018)

safety_profile.toxicity: The study shows that the fixed oil of Nigella sativa has an oral LD₅₀ in mice ranging from 28.8 mL/kg to about 3,371 mg/kg, while the intraperitoneal LD₅₀ is around 2.06 mL/kg. In addition, very high doses of seed extracts (up to 21 g/kg) did not cause mortality, indicating a wide safety margin and low acute toxicity for most seed preparations, whereas concentrated oil can show mild toxicity at higher doses. (Mashayekhi-Sardoo et al., 2020)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Nigella sativa may interact with warfarin through its major bioactive constituent, thymoquinone, which competitively inhibits CYP2C9, the primary enzyme responsible for warfarin metabolism (Ki = 3.50 μM; IC₅₀ = 11.35 μM). This inhibition may reduce warfarin metabolism, alter its pharmacokinetics, and increase the risk of herb–drug interactions. Risk prediction suggests that coadministration of thymoquinone (>18 mg/day) or N. sativa supplements (>1 g/day of seeds or oil) may significantly affect warfarin-treated patients, warranting caution and clinical monitoring.(Wang et al.,2022)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Nigella sativa seed extract combined with honey exhibited enhanced antimicrobial activity against Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, and Salmonella spp. compared with the individual treatments. The combination (1:1, v/w) produced larger inhibition zones, reaching 14 mm at 100% concentration, comparable to the activity of ciprofloxacin against Salmonella spp. The petroleum ether extract showed a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 12 mg/mL, indicating that the combination has synergistic potential as a natural antimicrobial agent for enteric infections. ( Aziz et al.,2019)Nigella sativa essential oil combined with Zingiber officinale essential oil demonstrated significant synergistic antibacterial activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) isolated from burn patients. While Z. officinale oil alone showed little or no antibacterial activity, its combination with N. sativa oil produced inhibition zones of up to 52 mm, exceeding those of standard antibiotics. Furthermore, the combined oils exhibited synergistic effects when used alongside antibiotics, suggesting their potential as adjuvant antimicrobial agents against multidrug-resistant MRSA. ( Wada et al.,2020)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antidiabetic, antihypertensive, hypolipidemic, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and broad antimicrobial (antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral, antiparasitic) activities, predominantly attributed to thymoquinone, the most abundant and pharmacologically active volatile oil constituent.Phytochemical profile: Thymoquinone (principal bioactive compound), alkaloids (nigellicine, nigellidine), saponins (alpha-hederin), flavonoids, proteins, fatty acids.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Thymoquinone (principal bioactive compound), alkaloids (nigellicine, nigellidine), saponins (alpha-hederin), flavonoids, proteins, fatty acids.

distribution.habitat_description: widely cultivated in northern Algeria for its medicinal and culinary uses. It is grown mainly in the Tell Atlas and the High Plateaus, particularly in Sétif, Constantine, Guelma, Batna, Tlemcen, Médéa, Mascara, and Aïn Defla, where it thrives in well-drained, calcareous, and fertile soils under Mediterranean climatic conditions. It is only occasionally found as an escape from cultivation.-
distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageNigella sativa flowers from April to June, depending on the sowing date, altitude, and local climatic conditions.Harvesting StageThe aerial parts are harvested during the flowering period (April–June) for medicinal use, while the mature seeds are collected from June to July, when the seed capsules have dried and turned brown, ensuring maximum seed quality and oil content.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Seeds. (Ahmad et al., 2013)
traditional_medicine.uses: It is traditionally used for respiratory, digestive, kidney, liver, cardiovascular, and immune problems. It is also used for asthma, bronchitis, inflammation, indigestion, diarrhea, skin diseases, and general weakness. (Ahmad et al., 2013)

scientific_data.clinical: Nigella sativa shows potential clinical benefits in humans, especially in type 2 diabetes, where it helps reduce blood glucose and HbA1c. Some clinical trials also report improvements in lipid profile (cholesterol and triglycerides) and inflammatory markers. (Tavakkoli et al., 2017)
scientific_data.experimental: Thymoquinone shows potent antioxidant, anti-inflammatory (NF-κB inhibition), antimicrobial (broad-spectrum), and anticancer (apoptosis induction) activities in numerous in vitro/in vivo models. Hepatoprotective, antidiabetic, and immunomodulatory effects well-documented.( Ahmad et al.,2013)

safety_profile.toxicity: Nerium oleander is highly toxic due to cardiac glycosides, especially oleandrin. Ingestion of any part of the plant can cause severe poisoning affecting the heart, stomach, and nervous system, and may lead to death. It has no safe internal dosage because of its very narrow therapeutic index. Contact with the plant may also irritate the skin. It is contraindicated for all uses, especially in children, pregnant women, and people with heart disease, and poisoning requires urgent medical treatment. (Zhai et al., 2022)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: A hydroethanolic leaf extract of Nerium oleander demonstrated broad-spectrum antibacterial activity against Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and multidrug-resistant bacteria, with greater effectiveness against Gram-positive strains. The extract exhibited strong inhibition of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, and showed a synergistic interaction with ceftriaxone against MRSA, indicating its potential to enhance antibiotic efficacy and serve as an adjunct antibacterial agent. ( Bekhit , 2025)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Potent cardiac glycoside activity (Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition, digoxin-like mechanism) producing positive inotropic and negative chronotropic cardiac effects; this same mechanism underlies both the plant's severe, well-documented toxicity and an active but still unproven research interest in oleandrin as an investigational anticancer agent.Phytochemical profile: More than 30 different cardiac glycosides identified across the plant, including oleandrin (principal toxic/bioactive compound), oleandrigenin, neriine, digitoxigenin, folinerin and rosagenin; red-flowered plants in the flowering stage produce more cardiac glycosides than white-flowered shrubs.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: More than 30 different cardiac glycosides identified across the plant, including oleandrin (principal toxic/bioactive compound), oleandrigenin, neriine, digitoxigenin, folinerin and rosagenin; red-flowered plants in the flowering stage produce more cardiac glycosides than white-flowered shrubs.

distribution.habitat_description: widely distributed in northern Algeria, particularly throughout the Tell Atlas, the Mediterranean coastal region, and extending into parts of the Saharan Atlas. It is commonly found in Kabylie, Tlemcen, Blida, Chlef, Jijel, Skikda, Annaba, Constantine, and the Aurès Mountains, where it grows naturally along riverbanks, wadis, stream margins, rocky valleys, and dry watercourses, from sea level to approximately 1,500 m above sea level. It is also widely cultivated as an ornamental shrub.-
distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageNerium oleander flowers from May to September, with peak flowering occurring during June and July.Harvesting StageThe leaves and flowers are generally harvested from May to August, preferably during the flowering period. Because all parts of the plant are highly toxic due to their content of cardiac glycosides, harvesting should be carried out with appropriate protective measures.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Leaves, flowers (all highly toxic). (Zhai et al., 2022)
traditional_medicine.uses: Historically for heart conditions, asthma, skin issues, but extremely dangerous. (Zhai et al., 2022)

scientific_data.experimental: Oleandrin and related cardiac glycosides from N. oleander inhibit the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, increasing intracellular calcium and enhancing cardiac contractility in isolated heart preparations (comparable to digoxin but with a narrower therapeutic index). In vitro studies demonstrate cytotoxic effects against various cancer cell lines (e.g., prostate, pancreatic, leukemia) through apoptosis induction, ROS generation, and inhibition of NF-κB signaling. Antimicrobial activity has been reported against certain bacteria and fungi in disc diffusion assays. Animal models show hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and neurotoxicity at higher doses. (Newman et al.,2006, Yamamoto et al.,1981, Hussain& Gorsi,2004)

safety_profile.toxicity: The acute toxicity study of Opuntia ficus-indica fixed seed oil in mice showed dose-dependent toxic effects at very high doses, including behavioral disturbances, diarrhea, sedation, and death, with post-mortem findings of congested lungs and cardiac arrest; the LD₅₀ values were about 43 ± 0.8 mL/kg (oral) and 2.72 ± 0.1 mL/kg (intraperitoneal), indicating low acute toxicity and a relatively wide safety margin under experimental conditions. (Boukeloua et al., 2012)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Opuntia ficus indica extract and its flavonoid constituents were found to modulate hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes by inducing the expression of CYP2B, CYP3A, and UGT enzymes, while hydrolyzed extracts and certain flavonols inhibited CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 activity. These findings suggest that OFI-containing products may alter the metabolism of co-administered drugs, indicating a potential for herb–drug interactions. ( Jeong et al.,2018)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Hypoglycemic (via high pectin/dietary fiber content reducing carbohydrate absorption), hypolipidemic, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial (antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral), antiulcerogenic, diuretic and platelet-function-modulating activities documented across an extensive clinical trial literature.Phytochemical profile: Pectin and dietary fiber (key mechanism for glycemic effect), betalains and flavonoids (antioxidant pigments), polyphenols, vitamin C.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Pectin and dietary fiber (key mechanism for glycemic effect), betalains and flavonoids (antioxidant pigments), polyphenols, vitamin C.

distribution.habitat_description: widely cultivated and naturalized throughout Algeria, particularly in the Tell Atlas, the High Plateaus, and the Saharan Atlas. It is abundant in Tlemcen, Mascara, Sidi Bel Abbès, Chlef, Médéa, Bouira, Tizi Ouzou, Béjaïa, Jijel, Batna, Biskra, and Ghardaïa, where it grows in arid and semi-arid regions, on rocky slopes, degraded lands, field margins, and well-drained soils, from sea level to approximately 1,800 m above sea level.-
distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageOpuntia ficus-indica flowers from April to June, with peak flowering generally occurring during May.Harvesting StageThe cladodes (pads) are harvested throughout the growing season, preferably from April to July, while the fruits are collected from July to September, when they have reached full maturity and developed their characteristic color, depending on the cultivar.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: the fruits and cladodes (stems/pads). (Osuna-Martínez et al., 2014)
traditional_medicine.uses: Opuntia ficus-indica has been traditionally used in folk medicine for the treatment of diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, asthma, gastric disorders, rheumatic pain, wounds, and fatigue. (Osuna-Martínez et al., 2014)

scientific_data.clinical: Randomized clinical trials (5 studies, 382 participants) evaluated O. ficus-indica supplementation at doses of 400 mg–15 g/day for 6 weeks to 2 years. Results showed no significant effect on body weight, but a reduction in BMI, body fat percentage, blood pressure, and total cholesterol was observed. Reported adverse effects were mainly mild gastrointestinal intolerance and flu-like symptoms. (Onakpoya et al., 2015)
scientific_data.experimental: Algerian O. ficus-indica (Souk-Ahras study): Phytochemical characterization of peels, flowers, and seeds; flowers richest in total polyphenols; peel showed highest betalain content and strongest FRAP/TAC; seeds and flowers showed highest DPPH radical scavenging. ( Bousbia et al.,2022 cited in Cited in Martins et al., 2023 )Algerian O. ficus-indica:Alkaloids extracted from Algerian inermis (spineless) nopal showed significant antioxidant and cytotoxic activities.( Moussaoui et al., 2021)Anticancer/apoptosis: Betanin purified from O. ficus-indica fruits induced apoptosis in human chronic myeloid leukemia K-562 cells via caspase-3 activation and Bcl-2 downregulation at IC50 = 75 microg/mL. ( Sreekanth et al., 2007)Antidiabetic : OFI cladode polysaccharides significantly reduced blood glucose in alloxan-diabetic rabbits and in type 2 diabetic patients via reduction of intestinal glucose absorption. Aqueous cladode extract (6 mg/kg oral, normal mice) reduced blood glucose and increased plasma insulin, with direct effect on pancreatic beta-cells.( Alarcon-Aguilar et al.,2003 cited in Martins et al., 2023 )Indicaxanthin neuroprotection (in vivo, C. elegans model): Indicaxanthin (10-100 micromol/L) dose-dependently prevented juglone-induced oxidative stress and increased lifespan in TJ375 (hsp-16.2:GFP) C. elegans strain; linked to Nrf2/ARE antioxidant response pathway activation.( Attanzio et al.,2022)antimicrobial/antiviral OFI seed oil demonstrated antibacterial activity against S. aureus (MIC 25 mg/mL), E. coli (MIC 50 mg/mL),antifungal against C. albicans, A. flavus, antiviral activity against HSV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 . ( Alqurashi et al.,2022)Diabetic complications prevention: OFI red fruit extract (101 metabolites identified: polyphenolics, betalains, alkaloids, vitamins) demonstrated significant antidiabetic and antioxidant activity in STZ-diabetic rat model; histopathological improvement in liver and kidney; betanin-rich fraction identified as key active for diabetic complication prevention. ( Mohammed et al.,2025)

safety_profile.toxicity: Origanum majorana L. showed low acute toxicity in animal studies, with no mortality observed up to 2000 mg/kg body weight (oral LD₅₀ > 2000 mg/kg), indicating a relatively safe profile. No clear toxic signs or organ damage were reported at this dose range. However, very high concentrations of extracts may still present potential risks in experimental settings. (Beceren et al., 2025)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: This study evaluated the antibacterial effects of combining essential oils from Origanum majorana with Lavandula dentata and Thymus serpyllum. The major compounds identified in marjoram oil were terpinen-4-ol and trans-4-thujanol. The essential oil combinations showed additive and partial synergistic antibacterial effects, particularly against Staphylococcus aureus, while the marjoram–thyme combination was also effective against Escherichia coli. These results suggest that combining essential oils at lower concentrations can enhance antibacterial activity while minimizing their impact on the taste and aroma of foods, making them promising natural food preservatives. (Ouedrhiri et al .,2017)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Insulin-sensitizing, antiandrogenic (reduces adrenal androgens), antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and bronchodilatory activities; mechanistically linked to activation of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), which enhance insulin sensitivity and reduce metabolic dysfunction.Phytochemical profile: Flavonoids (including apigenin), phenolic compounds, oleic acid, essential oil terpenes.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Flavonoids (including apigenin), phenolic compounds, oleic acid, essential oil terpenes.

It is grown in the Tell Atlas, particularly in Blida, Médéa, Tizi Ouzou, Béjaïa, Tlemcen, Jijel, Skikda, Constantine, and Annaba, where it thrives in well-drained, calcareous soils, gardens, cultivated fields, and herb farms under Mediterranean climatic conditions. It is only occasionally found naturalized near cultivation sites.-
distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageOriganum majorana flowers from June to September, with peak flowering generally occurring during July and August.Harvesting StageThe flowering aerial parts are harvested from June to August, preferably at the beginning of full bloom when the essential oil content is highest.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Aerial parts.(Wang et al., 2021)
traditional_medicine.uses: Used for digestive issues (spasms, flatulence, indigestion), respiratory problems (cough, colds), anxiety, menstrual pain, hypertension, diabetes, and as sedative/antispasmodic.(Wang et al., 2021)

scientific_data.experimental: A DHEA-induced PCOS rat model study combining serum metabolomics, network pharmacology and molecular docking found marjoram increased estradiol levels, decreased insulin and glucose concentrations, addressed hormonal imbalances, and demonstrated ovulation-inducing effects, with apigenin and oleic acid identified as key bioactive compounds modulating metabolic and hormonal pathways ( Elfiky et al.,2025).A letrozole-induced PCOS rat model study found marjoram extract (20, 40 or 60 mg/kg) showed beneficial effects on hormonal profile, oxidative stress and inflammation, with mechanism of action involving Nrf2 activation and NF-κB suppression in ovarian tissue, compared against metformin as an active comparator. ( Al-Harbi et al.,2025)

safety_profile.toxicity: Origanum vulgare L. is considered safe at culinary doses. However, concentrated essential oil containing carvacrol and thymol should be used with caution because high doses may cause irritation and toxic effects. (Soltani et al., 2021)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: This case report describes a 77-year-old patient receiving the anticoagulant Acenocoumarol whose INR increased from the therapeutic range to 6.42 after consuming daily infusions of Origanum vulgare and occasionally Verbena. The INR returned to normal after discontinuing the herbal teas and adjusting the anticoagulant dose. The interaction is likely due to the inhibition of CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 enzymes by oregano and verbena polyphenols, along with oregano’s intrinsic anticoagulant effects from carvacrol and thymol, which enhance the effect of acenocoumarol and increase the risk of bleeding. The authors conclude that oregano can significantly interact with vitamin K antagonists and emphasize the need for healthcare professionals to monitor such herb–drug interactions and promote phytovigilance, especially in populations with widespread medicinal plant use. (Beghriche et al .,2025)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: This study investigated the antioxidant and antibacterial effects of combining essential oils from Origanum vulgare, Salvia officinalis, and Cuminum cyminum. GC–MS analysis identified carvacrol and γ-terpinene as the major compounds in oregano oil. The optimal mixture (74.0% oregano, 15.1% cumin, and 10.9% sage) showed enhanced antioxidant activity and strong antibacterial activity against Salmonella enterica, Escherichia coli, and Staphylococcus aureus. The results demonstrate a synergistic effect among the essential oils, suggesting that their combination could serve as an effective natural preservative for food and industrial applications. (Gheisary et al.,2025)This study evaluated the synergistic antibacterial activity of hydroalcoholic extracts from Origanum vulgare and Hypericum perforatum, as well as their active compounds carvacrol and hypericin, against Staphylococcus aureus. Using the checkerboard method, both combinations showed synergistic antibacterial effects, with fractional inhibitory concentration (FIC) indices of 0.50 for the plant extracts and 0.49 for the active compounds. These findings suggest that combining oregano with H. perforatum or combining carvacrol with hypericin may provide an effective strategy for enhancing antibacterial activity against S. aureus.(Bahmani et al .,2019)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antimicrobial (antibacterial, antifungal, antibiofilm), antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, hepatoprotective, antidiabetic and anti-apoptotic activities, with antimicrobial mechanisms including enzyme inhibition, efflux pump inhibition, ATP depletion, biofilm formation inhibition and cytoplasmic membrane damage.Phytochemical profile: Essential oil rich in carvacrol and thymol (principal antimicrobial monoterpene phenols); rosmarinic acid, quercetin, apigenin (identified by HPLC as having strong antioxidant activity); terpenoids, tannins, sterols.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Essential oil rich in carvacrol and thymol (principal antimicrobial monoterpene phenols); rosmarinic acid, quercetin, apigenin (identified by HPLC as having strong antioxidant activity); terpenoids, tannins, sterols.

It grows on rocky slopes, open woodlands, scrublands, grasslands, and calcareous soils, generally between 800 and 2,000 m above sea level. distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageOriganum vulgare flowers from June to September, with peak flowering occurring during July and August.Harvesting StageThe flowering aerial parts are harvested from June to August, preferably at the beginning of full bloom, when the essential oil content and concentration of phenolic compounds are at their highest.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Aerial parts, leaves. (Lombrea et al., 2020)
traditional_medicine.uses: For respiratory disorders (cough, bronchitis), digestive issues (indigestion, diarrhea), menstrual problems, rheumatism, and as antimicrobial/tonic. (Lombrea et al., 2020)

scientific_data.experimental: A comprehensive review of O. vulgare's phytochemistry and antimicrobial properties confirmed the antimicrobial activity of the hirtum subspecies in multiple in vitro and in vivo studies, with enzyme inhibition, efflux pump inhibition, ATP depletion, biofilm inhibition and cytoplasmic membrane damage as the principal documented mechanisms. ( Soltani et al.,2021)Ethanolic oregano extract significantly suppressed Propionibacterium acnes-induced skin inflammation in a mouse ear edema model (32% reduction in ear thickness, 37% reduction in biopsy weight), with rosmarinic acid, quercetin, apigenin and carvacrol identified as the responsible antioxidant compounds by HPLC. ( Chuang et al.,2018)A novel emulgel formulated with oregano essential oil demonstrated antibacterial efficacy against Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, with in vivo testing in six patient groups (differentiated by age, sex and skin phenotype) confirming the absence of skin irritation over 20 minutes to 96 hours. ( Ganea et al.,2025)A comprehensive bio-screening of oregano and Salvia triloba extracts found significant antioxidant capacity and promising antibacterial activity against various pathogens including resistant strains, with biofilm formation inhibition also demonstrated, though the authors note clinical trials are still needed to validate efficacy. ( Antoniadou et al .,2024)

safety_profile.toxicity: Low acute toxicity (no mortality up to 5000 mg/kg in studies). Generally considered safe in traditional doses; further chronic data needed. No major adverse effects reported in preclinical work. (El Khiat et al., 2024)
safety_profile.plant_interactions: This study evaluated the phytochemical composition, antibacterial activity, and cytotoxic effects of Ononis natrix and Salvia verbenaca. Ethyl acetate extracts contained flavonoids and terpenes but no alkaloids. Both extracts exhibited antibacterial activity against the Gram-positive bacteria Bacillus subtilis and Bacillus brevis, with MIC values of 12.5–50 µg/mL. They also showed cytotoxic activity against the MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cell line, with IC₅₀ values ranging from 29 to 41 µg/mL. These findings suggest that both plants possess promising antibacterial and anticancer potential. (Al-Zereini ,2016)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial (antibacterial), anticancer/cytotoxic, antihemolytic, litholytic (kidney stone-dissolving), wound-healing, analgesic and neuroprotective activities reported across the genus and specifically for O. natrix.Phytochemical profile: Flavonoids (quercetin, amentoflavone), phenolic acids, anthranilic acid and resorcinol derivatives, aromatic lactones, coumarins, fatty acid esters (methyl stearate, hexadecanoic acid methyl ester — identified as major bioactive GC-MS constituents in one study).
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Flavonoids (quercetin, amentoflavone), phenolic acids, anthranilic acid and resorcinol derivatives, aromatic lactones, coumarins, fatty acid esters (methyl stearate, hexadecanoic acid methyl ester — identified as major bioactive GC-MS constituents in one study).

distribution.flowering_harvesting: Flowering StageOnonis natrix flowers from April to July, with peak flowering occurring during May and June.Harvesting StageThe flowering aerial parts are harvested from May to July, while the roots are generally collected in autumn (September–October) after the aerial parts have senesced, when they contain the highest concentration of bioactive constituents.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Aerial parts.(Chouman et al., 2025)
traditional_medicine.uses: traditional applications include its use for managing urinary tract infections, relieving rheumatic conditions, and promoting wound healing. It has also been used in folk medicine for skin disorders such as eczema and other dermatological diseases. (Chouman et al., 2025)

scientific_data.experimental: An in vitro study evaluated the litholytic activity of Ononis natrix extracts against calcium oxalate kidney stones, directly relevant to the traditional North African use for urinary/renal complaints and supported by prior FTIR analysis of human urinary stones from the El Bayadh district, Algeria. ( Alrifaee et al.,2024)Methanolic extract of O. natrix demonstrated significant anti-inflammatory activity (99.6% hemolysis inhibition versus 99.9% for indomethacin), strong antioxidant activity (97% DPPH scavenging versus 98% for ascorbic acid), and anticancer activity against DLD-1 (IC50 57.13 µg/mL), MCF-7 (IC50 96.69 µg/mL) and A549 (IC50 126.63 µg/mL) cell lines compared against cisplatin, with methyl stearate and hexadecanoic acid methyl ester identified as the responsible phytochemicals by GC-MS. ( Ahmed et al.,2025)A multidirectional in vitro and in silico study of O. natrix subsp. hispanica characterized total antioxidant capacity, reducing power (CUPRAC and FRAP assays) and metal-chelating activity across methanol, ethyl acetate and water extracts, supporting the genus's established antimicrobial, antioxidant, wound-healing, cytotoxic and analgesic activities documented across multiple prior studies. ( Yerlikaya et al., 2017)Ononis natrix demonstrated an ameliorative effect against chronic lead poisoning in mice, with neurobehavioral, biochemical and histological improvements documented in a dedicated experimental toxicology study.( Haj-Khlifa et al.,2025)Chemical composition analysis of O. natrix leaf methanolic extract from Tunisia identified substantial total phenol (51 mg GAE/g) and flavonoid (14.76 mg CE/g) content, with quercetin (24.5%) and amentoflavone identified as major constituents, supporting antioxidant and antimicrobial activity. ( Baya Mhamdi et al.,2015)

safety_profile.toxicity: Generally well-tolerated in food amounts (petals/leaves). Large amounts (>250g petals) may cause nausea, vomiting, seizures, or CNS effects resembling mild opioid intoxication due to alkaloids. (Günaydın et al., 2015) Acute toxicity: LD50 around 4000 mg/kg in some extracts. (Soulimani et al., 2001)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Sedative, analgesic (antinociceptive), anti-inflammatory, antidepressant, antioxidant, antimicrobial and antiulcerogenic activities reported. Additionally, anti-struvite (anti-nephrolithiasis against magnesium ammonium phosphate stones) activity has been demonstrated for stem and flower extracts.Phytochemical profile: Rhoeadine-type alkaloids (rhoeadine, rhoeagenine, isorhoeadine, isorhoeagenine, epiglaucamine, glaucamine, glaudine — characteristic to this species), proaporphine alkaloids (mecambrine), aporphine alkaloids (roemerine), protopine alkaloids (coulteropine, protopine), anthocyanins (cyanidin derivatives responsible for the red petal color), flavonoids, tannins, coumarins, saponins and terpenoids.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Primarily flowers/petals, sometimes aerial parts or whole plant. (Çoban et al., 2017)
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditionally used for cough, insomnia, pain relief, sedation, respiratory issues (e.g., asthma, bronchitis), diarrhea, and as a mild sedative or for disturbed sleep, especially in children as a cough syrup or tea from petals/flowers. (Çoban et al., 2017)

scientific_data.experimental: An alkaloid profiling study of P. rhoeas from 11 wild Turkish and Cypriot populations , isolated 12 alkaloids by column and preparative TLC and screened antimicrobial activity by microbroth dilution against 6 bacteria and 3 fungi; samples containing roemerine (an aporphine alkaloid) as the major alkaloid showed the strongest antimicrobial activity, establishing a structure-activity relationship between alkaloid profile and bioactivity for this species. ( Çoban et al .,2017)LC-QTOF-MS/MS metabolite profiling of aerial parts identified 55 alkaloids across multiple classes (protoberberine, benzylisoquinoline, aporphine, benzophenanthridine, rhoeadine-type), with rhoeadine alkaloids detected exclusively in P. rhoeas and not in P. somniferum, distinguishing the two species chemically ( Oh et al., 2018).An experimental pharmacological study of P. rhoeas stem extract (SE) and flower extract (FE) evaluated anti-struvite activity by polarizing microscopy and FT-IR, anti-inflammatory activity by the carrageenan-induced paw edema model, antinociceptive activity by the acetic acid-induced abdominal constriction test, and antidepressant activity by the forced swimming test (FST) in mice; both extracts demonstrated significant activity across all four assays ( Hmamouet al., 2023).Ethyl acetate fractions of P. rhoeas extracts inhibited LPS-induced nitric oxide production in RAW264.7 macrophages with less toxicity than the crude ethanol extract, downregulated pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) and NF-κB/STAT3 signaling, and showed significant free radical scavenging activity; the fraction additionally enhanced expression of NQO-1 (a Nrf2-target antioxidant gene), providing a mechanistic basis for the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities (Kim et al., 2021).Total phenolic content of leaf extract (24.24 mg GAE/g dry mass) and flower extract (22.10 mg GAE/g) were the highest among the four organs tested (root, stem, leaf, flower), and leaf extract showed the lowest DPPH IC50 (0.50 mg/mL), supporting the antioxidant profile; antimicrobial activity was confirmed against five pathogenic bacteria and two fungi across all organ extracts ( Hmamou et al., 2022).

safety_profile.toxicity: Acute toxicity evaluation showed no mortality or visible toxic effects in rats after oral administration of aqueous and butanolic extracts of Paronychia argentea. The LD50 was estimated to be higher than 2000 mg/kg for the aqueous extract and higher than 40 mg/kg for the butanolic extract, indicating that both extracts exhibit low acute toxicity in experimental models. (Bouanani et al., 2010)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antidiabetic (α-glucosidase inhibitory), antioxidant, anti-inflammatory (in vitro and in vivo), antiurolithiatic (anti-kidney stone), antimicrobial and nephroprotective activities. The α-amylase inhibitory effect is contradictory across studies (inhibition reported in some, no hypoglycemic effect confirmed in others), so the antidiabetic claim should be limited specifically to the well-documented α-glucosidase inhibition.Phytochemical profile: Flavonoids (isorhamnetin-3-O-dihexoside, quercetin-3-O-glucoside, quercetinmethylether-O-hexoside, quercetin, jaceosidin and isorhamnetin — six described for the first time in P. argentea by HPLC-UV/DAD-ESI-MSⁿ analysis), polyphenols, tannins, sugars, ascorbic acid.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Aerial parts, leaves, flowers.
traditional_medicine.uses: Used in Algerian/North African traditional medicine as a diuretic, for kidney stones (antiurolithiatic), diabetes, prostate issues, stomach ulcers, anorexia, flatulence, and antimicrobial effects. (Veeraraghavan et al., 2020)

scientific_data.experimental: HPLC-UV/DAD and ESI-MSⁿ analysis of the ethanolic extract, decoction and infusion of Algerian P. argentea aerial parts identified 11 flavonoid compounds, 6 for the first time in this species; the ethanol extract showed highest flavonoid content (25.4 mg/g dry mass) and best antioxidant activity, while the decoction was identified as a protective beverage against oxidative stress ( Sait et al ., 2015).An in vitro antiurolithiatic study evaluated leaf and flower extracts of Algerian P. argentea by measuring turbidity at 620 nm at six concentrations (0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 1, 2 and 5 mg/mL) in the presence and absence of extract, with total phenol and flavonoid contents also quantified; the results supported the plant's traditional Algerian use as an antiurolithiatic agent ( Mechraoui et al., 2021).A comparative study evaluated P. argentea (PA) and P. capitata (PC) aqueous and ethanolic extracts from Algerian sources for antidiabetic, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities: P. argentea aqueous and ethanolic extracts showed potent α-glucosidase inhibitory activity activity (IC50 20.62 ± 3.60 µg/mL and 26.90 ± 3.34 µg/mL respectively), all extracts demonstrated strong in vitro antioxidant activity, and in vivo anti-inflammatory activity in the xylene-induced ear edema mouse model showed 79.94 ± 4.63% inhibition for P. argentea ethanol extract versus 79.01 ± 3.52% for P. capitata, both comparable to indomethacin; LC-MS/MS confirmed quercetin and ascorbic acid among the major identified compounds. (Karbab et al.,2025)Pharmacological and toxicological study of Algerian P. argentea in an experimental calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis rat model demonstrated relevant antiurolithiatic and nephroprotective effects in vivo alongside an acute oral toxicity assessment, providing the most rigorous experimental data for this species. ( Bouanani et al., 2010)

safety_profile.toxicity: In a rat study, the leaf ethanol extract showed no mortality or obvious toxicity at low doses (10–100 mg/kg). However, at high dose (1000 mg/kg), there was an increase in liver enzyme (ALT) and blood urea nitrogen (BUN), indicating possible liver and kidney stress, with histological changes such as inflammation and tissue damage in liver and kidney. (Awe & Banjoko, 2013)
safety_profile.drug_interactions: A case report described a potential herb–drug interaction between parsley (Petroselinum crispum) and sirolimus in a renal transplant patient, where excessive parsley consumption resulted in supratherapeutic sirolimus blood levels. The findings highlight the importance of monitoring herbal product use in patients receiving drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, particularly immunosuppressants, due to the risk of clinically significant herb–drug interactions. ( Kurtaran et al.,2021)

traditional_medicine.parts_used: roots, leaves, and fruits/seeds.
traditional_medicine.uses: Petroselinum crispum (Mill.) Fuss has been traditionally used as a diuretic for urinary problems and kidney stones. It has also been used for digestive disorders (flatulence, indigestion), menstrual disorders, inflammation, and as an antimicrobial remedy. (Agyare et al., 2017)

scientific_data.experimental: A systematic review of scientific databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science) including studies under search terms Petroselinum crispum, kidney health, renal protection and clinical studies’ found animal studies demonstrated reductions in oxidative stress, improvements in metabolic biomarkers and enhanced renal function, while limited human studies revealed modest improvements in urinary composition and renal health markers; the authors concluded that robust clinical trials and long-term safety evaluations are still needed (Alobaidi,2024).Aqueous extracts of P. crispum evaluated against CCl4-induced toxicity in mammalian kidney (Vero) cells showed significant (p < 0.05) suppression of oxidative stress by scavenging reactive oxygen species and enhancing cellular antioxidant defense, alongside anti-nephrotoxic activity, with phenolic and triterpenoid compounds and vitamin C identified as responsible constituents. ( Abu-Serie et al.,2019)Parsley extract was studied in both in vitro (Ammi visnaga + P. crispum extracts showing concentration-dependent antioxidant activity and calcium oxalate kidney stone size reduction) and in vivo (oxonate-induced hyperuricemic rat model showing significant reduction in serum uric acid and improvement of kidney structure) contexts, supporting its traditional anti-nephrolithiatic use ( Malkawi et al., 2025).A dedicated nephroprotection rat model study found parsley extract was protective against prostaglandin-induced renal dysfunction in pregnant rats that had undergone clinical abortion, with antioxidant properties confirmed as the underlying mechanism ( Rezazad & Farokhi,2014).Anti-osteoporosis potential of P. crispum extract was explored in an experimentally ovariectomized rat model with network pharmacology, finding significant effects on bone mineral parameters attributable to apigenin and other flavonoids ( Saeed et al., 2024)antianemic activity, physicochemical aspects and mineral profile were also characterized in a 2024 ACS Omega study ( Nouioura et al.,2024)

scientific_data.clinical: NAFLD: A randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial using P. major seeds (2 g twice daily for 12 weeks) showed improvement in ALT and AST liver enzyme levels compared with placebo. (Jazayeri et al., 2021) Ulcerative colitis: A randomized placebo-controlled trial using roasted P. major seeds (3600 mg/day for 8 weeks) showed reduction of some gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal tenderness and discomfort. (Baghizadeh et al., 2021) Radiotherapy-induced oral mucositis: A clinical trial in cancer patients showed that P. major syrup reduced the severity of oral mucositis and pain compared with placebo. (Soltani et al., 2020)
scientific_data.experimental: An ex vivo porcine wound-healing model found both ethanol and water extracts of P. major leaves stimulated wound healing in porcine skin, with the ethanol extract showing a somewhat stronger effect; 1.0 mg/mL produced the best results for both extract types, attributed to the phenolic compound plantamajoside (Keshavarzi et al., 2022)An ex vivo porcine wound-healing model found both ethanol and water extracts of P. major leaves stimulated wound healing in porcine skin, with the ethanol extract showing a somewhat stronger effect; 1.0 mg/mL produced the best results for both extract type)s, attributed to the phenolic compound plantamajoside (Zubair et al., 2015)Endotoxin-free methanol extracts of P. major leaves (50, 100, 250 and 500 µg/mL) significantly increased nitric oxide (NO) and TNF-α production by rat peritoneal macrophages in the absence of IFN-γ or LPS, indicating direct immune-activating properties clinically relevant in chronic viral infections, tuberculosis, AIDS and cancer ( Gomez-Flores et al 2000).A P. major infusion extract encapsulated in sodium alginate at two concentrations was characterized by FTIR for interaction with the polymer matrix, and showed significant antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in dermal human fibroblast cultures in vitro, alongside wound healing stimulation; encapsulation efficiency was evaluated based on total polyphenol content retention (Bâldea et al., 2023).Acetone extract of P. major leaves showed antimicrobial activity against 9 bacterial species, and ethyl alcohol extract showed bactericidal activity against E. coli and Bacillus cereus in Turkish antibacterial screening; antiviral and antifungal activities have also been documented for P. major extracts across multiple independent studies (Keshavarzi et al., 2022).

scientific_data.experimental: A 2024 study of hydroethanolic extract of P. aviculare L. in LPS-stimulated RAW264.7 murine macrophages demonstrated anti-inflammatory activity via induction of HO-1 and inhibition of iNOS, with subsequent reduction in NO and PGE2 production; this mechanism study directly explains the anti-inflammatory activity underlying traditional use (Jang et al., 2024).UHPLC-ESI(+)-MS qualitative screening of nine independent commercial and wild-harvested Polygoni Avicularis Herba samples identified 25 major constituents, including three tentatively new natural products; quantitative UHPLC-CAD analysis using quercetin-3-O-glucuronide as a standard confirmed flavonol glucuronides as the dominant compound class across all samples, establishing a standardization method .( Benrahou et al .,2023)A study of a rabbit model with experimentally induced E. coli infection evaluated a combination of P. aviculare, Potentilla anserina and Rumex crispus extracts, finding significant reduction in E. coli-induced intestinal pathology, supporting the traditional antibacterial/astringent use ( Kupczyński et al., 2019).Antioxidant molecule isolation from P. aviculare identified potent DPPH-scavenging flavonoids, with rational derivatization producing more potent synthetic analogues; structure-activity studies confirmed quercetin and myricetin derivatives as most active ( Mahnashi et al., 2022).

scientific_data.experimental: An anti-inflammatory study of P. hydropiper stalk aqueous extract (PHL) at 125, 250 and 500 mg/kg orally for 7 days in TNBS-induced intestinal inflammation in rats found high-dose PHL significantly improved macroscopic score and histological appearance; H-PHL treatment significantly ameliorated MPO activity and GSH content; downregulation of iNOS, Cox-2, TNF-α and IL-1β was confirmed with significantly reduced NF-κB protein expression, establishing the NF-κB pathway as the principal anti-inflammatory mechanism. ( Zhang et al .,2018)A gastroprotective study of P. hydropiper ethanol extract in an ethanol-induced gastric mucosal damage model found the extract attenuated gastric damage through combined antioxidant (increased SOD, decreased MDA) and anti-inflammatory (reduced TNF-α and IL-1β, inhibited neutrophil infiltration) pathways, confirming the ethanol extract superior to the water extract in gastroprotective efficacy.(Ren et al., 2021)Anti-angiogenic, anti-tumor and cytotoxic activities of P. hydropiper solvent extracts and isolated saponins were evaluated using the chick embryo chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) anti-angiogenesis assay, brine shrimp lethality assay and NIH/3T3 fibroblast cytotoxicity assay; methanolic extract and saponin fraction showed significant anti-angiogenic potential alongside notable cytotoxicity ( Ayaz et al., 2016).A comprehensive phytochemical review compiled 324 compounds isolated from P. hydropiper across major compound classes; the majority of pharmacological studies confirmed diverse bioactivities of extracts, flavonoids and volatile oil elements including antibacterial, antifungal, insecticidal, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities ( Kong et al., 2023).P. hydropiper compound extract (PHCE) administered to broiler chickens with Clostridium perfringens-induced necrotic enteritis significantly inhibited NLRP3 inflammasome signaling, reduced intestinal damage scores in jejunum and ileum, significantly increased SOD while decreasing MDA, H2O2, TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6 (all p < 0.01 or p < 0.05); MIC of PHCE against C. perfringens was 3.13 mg/mL and MBC was 12.5 mg/mL. ( Zhang et al.,2024)

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Immunomodulatory, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, hepatoprotective, expectorant, mild laxative, wound-healing, antibacterial and potentially cognitive-protective (via ecdysteroid-mediated mechanisms) activities reported. Related species Polypodium leucotomos (PLE) has well-documented clinical photoprotective and dermatological activity (psoriasis, vitiligo, atopic dermatitis) relevant for contextualizing P. vulgare's ecdysteroid pharmacology.Phytochemical profile: Phytoecdysteroids (ecdysterone/polypodin A, 5β-hydroxyecdysterone/polypodin B; 11 ecdysteroids total including 3 novel compounds isolated in 2001 — the most comprehensively characterized ecdysteroid profile of any Polypodium species), steroidal saponins (osladin, polypodosapogenin-based glycosides), caffeoylquinic acids (chlorogenic acid), flavonoids (rutin), phloroglucinol derivatives, cycloartane triterpenoid (cyclopodmenyl acetate), essential oil (lauric acid, butyric acid, methyl salicylate, isovaleric esters), minerals (potassium, calcium, magnesium, iron).

distribution.habitat_description: Distributionfound in northern Algeria, mainly in the Tell Atlas, where it occurs in the humid mountain regions of Kabylie, the Babors, Edough Massif, Jijel, Skikda, and Tlemcen. It grows in shaded forests, moist rocky slopes, moss-covered rocks, tree trunks, and ravines, particularly in areas with high humidity, from approximately 500 to 2,000 m above sea level.Flowering StageAs a fern, Polypodium vulgare does not produce flowers. Instead, it reproduces by spores, which are produced in sori on the underside of the fronds. Spore production generally occurs from June to September under Algerian climatic conditions.Harvesting StageThe rhizomes, which constitute the medicinally used part, are generally harvested in autumn (September–November) or early spring (March–April), when they contain the highest concentration of bioactive constituents. The fronds may also be collected during the growing season if required for traditional medicinal use.
distribution.flowering_harvesting:
Flowering Stage
As a fern, Polypodium vulgare does not produce flowers. Instead, it reproduces by spores, which are produced in sori on the underside of the fronds. Spore production generally occurs from June to September under Algerian climatic conditions.
Harvesting Stage
The rhizomes, which constitute the medicinally used part, are generally harvested in autumn (September–November) or early spring (March–April), when they contain the highest concentration of bioactive constituents. The fronds may also be collected during the growing season if required for traditional medicinal use.

traditional_medicine.uses: Expectorant for cough/cold, respiratory issues, laxative, digestive aid, rheumatism
traditional_medicine.dosage: 2–3 g dried rhizome in 150 mL boiling water, 3–4 times daily (short-term use). Posology: Oral use as infusion (herbal tea) in adults and adolescents over 12 years, mainly for cough/cold or mild constipation, for short duration only (about 1 week). European Medicines Agency (EMA). (2008). Assessment report on Polypodium vulgare L., rhizoma. Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC). EMEA/HMPC/600669/2007.

scientific_data.experimental: The most comprehensive ecdysteroid characterization study of P. vulgare isolated and structurally elucidated 11 ecdysteroids from rhizomes by 1D and 2D NMR and MS analysis; 3 were entirely new natural compounds and 6 known ecdysteroids were reported from P. vulgare for the first time, expanding the known ecdysteroid profile from 8 to 11 compounds; this study established the complete.( Simon et al., 2001 )Five phytoecdysteroids not previously reported in P. vulgare — including inokosterone — were isolated from methanol extracts of in vitro tissue cultures of prothalli, demonstrating that ecdysteroid production is maintained in cell culture and enabling biotechnological production of these bioactive compounds. ( Messeguer et al.,1998)A comprehensive bioactive compound review confirmed that chlorogenic acid and rutin are the major quantified polyphenols in P. vulgare fronds by HPLC, and reviewed traditional hepatoprotective, wound-healing, expectorant and laxative uses supported by available phytochemical and pharmacological evidence. (Farràs et al., 2023) In vitro studies of P. vulgare extracts EquisteA critical ethnopharmacological review of P. vulgare (Bisfaij) compiled evidence for immunomodulatory properties — including early studies on macrophage stimulation — and antibacterial activity against S. aureus by Iranian fern extract studies (MIC 2–8 µg/mL), supporting its traditional use in chronic and infectious conditions (Nikhat et al., 2023).

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:No formal LD50 or subchronic toxicity data specific to P. nigra identified; salicin-containing preparations should be used cautiously in individuals with salicylate/aspirin hypersensitivity, and in children (Reye's-syndrome-type caution by analogy with salicylates).Drug-plant interaction:Potential additive effect with anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs (salicylate content); theoretical interaction with NSAIDs.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Ethanolic bud extract showed moderate antioxidant activity (~40%, ABTS) and potent anti-inflammatory activity (49.9% inhibition of carrageenan-induced paw oedema in mice); complete histological protection against AlCl3-induced hepatotoxicity (Boudjelal et al., 2013).Endothelium-independent vasorelaxant effect on porcine coronary artery rings, correlated with antioxidant flavonoid content, likely via inhibition of Ca2+ influx.

traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Carminative, digestive, expectorant, mild galactagogue, infant colic remedy; EMA traditional-use indications: dyspepsia and catarrh of the upper respiratory tract.Parts Used:Dried ripe fruit (aniseed), essential oil.Dosage:Crushed fruit: 3 g as infusion, up to 3 times daily; essential oil: 0.05–0.2 g/day (EMA monograph).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Crushed fruit: 3 g as infusion, up to 3 times daily; essential oil: 0.05–0.2 g/day (EMA monograph).

scientific_data.clinical: Clinical trials support use for functional dyspepsia (symptom relief) and reduction of menopausal hot-flash frequency, attributed to the mild estrogenic activity of anethole (EMA, 2014).
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Anethole exhibited dose-dependent antispasmodic activity on isolated intestinal and tracheal smooth muscle.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Essential oil can irritate mucous membranes and kidneys at high doses; prolonged high-dose use is discouraged given limited modern safety data.Drug-plant interaction:None well documented; theoretical additive irritant effect with other diuretic/urinary agents.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

distribution.habitat_description: Native to Indonesia (Java, Sumatra); cultivated in SE Asia and traded as a dried spice/medicinal fruit used in North African and Middle Eastern traditional medicine.Flowering:Year-round in native tropical climate.Harvesting:Unripe fruit picked and sun-dried, retaining the stalk (‘tailed pepper’).

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Dried unripe fruit, essential oil.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Dried unripe fruit used for urogenital infections, bronchitis and digestive complaints; chewed traditionally for halitosis and throat irritation.Parts Used:Dried unripe fruit, essential oil.Dosage:Powdered fruit: 1–4 g/day (traditional use; not formally standardized in modern pharmacopoeias).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Powdered fruit: 1–4 g/day (traditional use; not formally standardized in modern pharmacopoeias).

scientific_data.clinical: No modern controlled clinical trials identified; historical clinical use for gonorrhoea/urethritis predates antibiotics and is no longer standard practice.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Cubebin and related lignans demonstrated anti-inflammatory and hepatoprotective activity in rodent models; essential oil showed antimicrobial activity against urinary and respiratory pathogens in vitro.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Piperine oral LD50 in rodents is approximately 200–400 mg/kg; high doses of pepper/piperine can irritate the gastrointestinal mucosa.Drug-plant interaction:Significant — piperine inhibits CYP3A4/P-gp and can increase plasma levels (and toxicity risk) of many co-administered drugs (e.g., phenytoin, propranolol, some chemotherapeutics).Plant-plant interaction:Enhances absorption/bioavailability of curcumin (Curcuma longa) and other co-administered phytochemicals.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Carminative and digestive stimulant; used for fever, cough and arthritic pain (rubefacient); Ayurvedic use as a bioavailability enhancer (in ‘Trikatu’ formulations).Parts Used:Dried fruit (peppercorns).Dosage:Culinary/traditional use: <1 g/day; piperine extract in clinical bioavailability studies typically 5–20 mg co-administered with the target drug.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: Classic clinical trial (Shoba et al., 1998) showed piperine (20 mg) increased curcumin bioavailability in humans by 2000%; similar enhancement demonstrated for coenzyme Q10 and other nutrients/drugs.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Piperine inhibited hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein in vitro/in vivo, increasing bioavailability of co-administered compounds; anti-inflammatory effects shown in rodent paw-oedema models.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.

safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Rose hips used traditionally for colds, vitamin-C deficiency, and joint pain/osteoarthritis; EMA-recognized traditional use for minor joint pain and to increase urine volume.Parts Used:Fruit (hips), with seed hairs removed.Dosage:Powdered hip: ~5 g/day (standardized rosehip powder used in clinical trials).

scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:GOPO galactolipid shows chemotactic-inhibitory and anti-inflammatory activity relevant to joint inflammation in preclinical models.

scientific_data.clinical: RCTs (e.g., Pengelly et al., 2012) show rosemary extract improves cognitive performance and mood in healthy adults; topical preparations reported to improve local circulation.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Carnosic acid and carnosol show neuroprotective activity against oxidative stress in cell/animal models; rosmarinic acid shows anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity in vitro.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Infusion of leaves/bark used as a gastric tonic, hypotensive, purgative/laxative, diuretic, antihypertensive, hepatoprotective agent, and for dermatological complications.Parts Used:Roots, bark, berries, leaves.Dosage:Leaf/bark infusion, traditional use; not formally standardized — narrow margin of safety noted (see Toxicity).

scientific_data.clinical: No controlled human trials; a documented case report describes acute toxicity (including nephropathy) following excessive ingestion (Ben Ghezala et al., 2015).
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Methanolic bark extract was cytotoxic to human monocytic leukaemia cells (U937, IC50 6.39 µg/mL, trypan blue assay); isolated flavonoid glycosides protected human lymphoblastoid (TK6) cells against DNA damage and enhanced antioxidant activity (Bhouri et al., 2012).Leaf extract also showed antistaphylococcal activity (MIC 0.25–2.00 mg/mL), among the most active of Mediterranean species screened, alongside Punica granatum.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Due to the genotoxic and oncogenic potential of several anthraquinone constituents (notably lucidin), the European Commission (CPMP, 2004) classified R. tinctorum as a plant with serious health risks; oral/internal use of root preparations is prohibited/not advised in the EU, and products have been withdrawn from European markets.Drug-plant interaction:None formally documented; theoretical additive nephrotoxic/genotoxic risk with other anthraquinone-containing plants.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Root traditionally used for urinary stones, jaundice, anaemia, constipation, liver disorders and diarrhoea, and as a diuretic (recorded in the Russian Pharmacopoeia); historically also a major source of red dye (alizarin).Parts Used:Root and rhizome.Dosage:Historically 1.5–3 g dried root/day as decoction — no longer recommended for internal use (see Toxicity).

scientific_data.clinical: Clinical trials of combination formulations (e.g., Cyclo 3 Fort, containing R. aculeatus extract with hesperidin methylchalcone and ascorbic acid) show improvement in venous-insufficiency symptoms and plethysmographic parameters; effects attributable to R. aculeatus alone are less well isolated due to the combination formulations used.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Ruscogenin/neoruscogenin show venotonic and anti-oedema activity in vascular smooth-muscle and animal oedema models.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Narrow margin of safety: furanocoumarin content causes phototoxic dermatitis on skin contact plus sun exposure; oral ingestion, especially in higher doses or during pregnancy, has been associated with severe hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, GI haemorrhage, and abortion/teratogenic effects — contraindicated in pregnancy.Drug-plant interaction:Furanocoumarins inhibit CYP3A4/CYP1A2 (grapefruit-juice-like effect), potentially increasing plasma levels of co-administered drugs metabolized by these enzymes; additive photosensitizing risk with other photosensitizing drugs.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

distribution.habitat_description: Native to eastern North America, widely naturalized/planted in Algeria and the Mediterranean as an ornamental/soil-stabilizing tree (‘black locust’).Flowering:April–June (fragrant white racemes).Harvesting:Flowers collected at bloom for infusion/syrup; bark and seeds not used medicinally due to toxicity.

traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Flowers traditionally used as a mild antispasmodic, diuretic, and for headache/dizziness in European folk medicine; flowers also used to flavour syrups and liqueurs.Parts Used:Flowers only (bark, leaves, seeds, and roots are toxic and not used medicinally).Dosage:Flower infusion: 1–2 g dried flowers per cup, occasional traditional use.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: No controlled clinical trials; case reports document livestock and human poisoning after ingestion of bark, leaves, or seeds (nausea, vomiting, weakness, mydriasis).
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Flower flavonoid extracts show antioxidant activity in vitro; bark/seed lectin (robin) shown to cause haemagglutination and cytotoxicity in cell studies, underpinning historical reports of poisoning.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:High oxalate content in leaves warrants caution in individuals prone to kidney stones or with renal impairment; anthraquinone-containing root preparations should not be used long-term (laxative-dependence/electrolyte-disturbance risk, by analogy with related Rumex species).Drug-plant interaction:Anthraquinone component may have additive effect with other laxatives/diuretics.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Mild laxative (anthraquinone glycosides), astringent (tannins), antioxidant, antimicrobial — activities inferred from genus-level Rumex phytochemistry.Phytochemical profile:Anthraquinones (chrysophanol, emodin-type, as in related Rumex spp.), tannins, oxalates, flavonoids, vitamin C.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Anthraquinones (chrysophanol, emodin-type, as in related Rumex spp.), tannins, oxalates, flavonoids, vitamin C.

distribution.habitat_description: Mediterranean basin incl. Algeria; grows in disturbed/cultivated ground and coastal areas, as with other Rumex spp.Flowering:April–June.Harvesting:Roots collected in autumn; leaves collected young in spring.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:As with related Rumex species (dock, sorrel), roots traditionally used as a mild laxative and for skin conditions (eczema, itching); leaves used as a spring green/vegetable and mild diuretic.Parts Used:Root, leaves.Dosage:Root decoction, traditional use only; not formally standardized.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: No species-specific controlled clinical trials identified for R. gallicus.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Genus-level (Rumex spp.) studies show anthraquinone-driven laxative activity and antioxidant/antimicrobial activity of leaf and root extracts in vitro.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Narrow margin of safety, essentially as for R. graveolens: furanocoumarin-mediated phototoxicity on skin contact, and hepatotoxic/nephrotoxic and abortifacient effects on ingestion; contraindicated in pregnancy; documented cases of severe poisoning from traditional abortifacient use in North Africa.Drug-plant interaction:Furanocoumarins inhibit CYP3A4/CYP1A2, potentially raising plasma levels of co-administered drugs; additive photosensitizing risk with other photosensitizers.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antispasmodic, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, uterotonic/abortifacient, insecticidal.Phytochemical profile:Furanocoumarins (bergapten, psoralen, chalepensin, rutamarin), alkaloids (arborinine, graveoline, kokusaginine), essential oil rich in 2-undecanone.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Furanocoumarins (bergapten, psoralen, chalepensin, rutamarin), alkaloids (arborinine, graveoline, kokusaginine), essential oil rich in 2-undecanone.

distribution.habitat_description: Mediterranean basin incl. Algeria (‘fringed rue’), often more common than R. graveolens in North Africa.Flowering:March–June.Harvesting:Aerial parts (leaves) collected before/at flowering.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Used in North African traditional medicine as an emmenagogue/abortifacient, antispasmodic, anthelmintic, and for rheumatic and neurological complaints; also used as an insect repellent.Parts Used:Leaves, aerial parts, essential oil.Dosage:Traditional use only, at very low doses; internal use strongly discouraged due to toxicity (see below).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: Case reports document hepatotoxicity, phytophotodermatitis and abortifacient poisoning after ingestion, particularly when used (unsafely) for attempted pregnancy termination; no controlled clinical trials support therapeutic use.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Extracts show uterotonic/abortifacient activity and antispasmodic effects on smooth muscle in animal models, similar to R. graveolens; furanocoumarins show phototoxic and antimicrobial activity in vitro.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally well tolerated; contraindicated in salicylate hypersensitivity/aspirin allergy, in children under 12 (Reye's syndrome risk, by analogy with aspirin), and in peptic ulcer disease.Drug-plant interaction:May potentiate anticoagulants/antiplatelet drugs and other NSAIDs; may reduce efficacy of uricosuric agents (as with salicylates generally).Plant-plant interaction:Additive salicylate effect with Populus and other salicin-containing plants.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory, antiplatelet (mild), antioxidant.Phytochemical profile:Salicin and related phenolic glycosides (salicortin, tremulacin), flavonoids, tannins.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Salicin and related phenolic glycosides (salicortin, tremulacin), flavonoids, tannins.

distribution.habitat_description: Europe, western/central Asia, North Africa incl. Algeria; grows along riverbanks and wetlands (‘white willow’).Flowering:March–April (catkins).Harvesting:Bark stripped from 2–3-year-old branches in spring.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Bark used traditionally and per EMA/ESCOP for fever, mild rheumatic/muscular pain, headache, and as an antipyretic — historical precursor to aspirin (salicin).Parts Used:Bark.Dosage:Equivalent to 60–120 mg total salicin/day, as decoction or standardized extract (EMA monograph).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: RCTs (e.g., Chrubasik et al.) show standardized willow bark extract reduces pain in osteoarthritis and low back pain, with efficacy comparable to low-dose NSAIDs in some trials.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Salicin is metabolized in vivo to salicylic acid, providing COX-inhibitory anti-inflammatory/analgesic activity, generally with a milder and slower onset than synthetic aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid).

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Standard leaf/infusion preparations are safe; the essential oil is rich in thujone, a neurotoxic/convulsant compound at high doses — prolonged high-dose or essential-oil use should be avoided, particularly in pregnancy, epilepsy, and in children.Drug-plant interaction:May potentiate sedatives/anticonvulsants (thujone-CNS interaction, theoretical) and antidiabetic drugs (hypoglycaemic effect reported).Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antihidrotic, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, cognitive-enhancing/anticholinesterase, oestrogen-modulating (menopausal symptom relief).Phytochemical profile:Essential oil (α/β-thujone, camphor, 1,8-cineole), diterpenes (carnosic acid, carnosol), rosmarinic acid, flavonoids.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Essential oil (α/β-thujone, camphor, 1,8-cineole), diterpenes (carnosic acid, carnosol), rosmarinic acid, flavonoids.

distribution.habitat_description: Native to the Mediterranean, widely cultivated incl. Algeria (‘common/garden sage’).Flowering:May–July.Harvesting:Leaves harvested just before/at flowering for maximal essential-oil content.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:EMA-approved traditional use for dyspepsia, excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis), and topically/as a gargle for mild inflammation of the mouth and throat.Parts Used:Leaves.Dosage:Infusion: 1–2 g dried leaf per cup, up to 3 times daily; gargle: 2.5 g per 100 mL (EMA monograph).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: RCTs show sage extract improves cognitive performance/memory in healthy adults and Alzheimer's patients (Akhondzadeh et al., 2003), and significantly reduces hot-flash frequency/severity in menopausal women; fresh sage-leaf tablets reduce hyperhidrosis-related sweating in clinical trials.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Sage extracts show acetylcholinesterase-inhibitory activity relevant to cognitive function in vitro/animal models; rosmarinic acid and carnosic acid show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally well tolerated by inhalation/topical dilution; the essential oil is not intended for internal use and may cause skin sensitization; caution advised in pregnancy given uterotonic/hormonal activity reported in traditional use.Drug-plant interaction:Theoretical additive sedative effect with CNS depressants; theoretical interaction with hormone-sensitive conditions/therapies (sclareol oestrogenic activity).Plant-plant interaction:Commonly blended with other essential oils in aromatherapy (no adverse interaction documented).
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antispasmodic, anxiolytic/mood-modulating, antimicrobial, antioxidant, mild oestrogenic (phytoestrogen-like) activity.Phytochemical profile:Essential oil dominated by linalyl acetate and linalool, with sclareol (a diterpene with oestrogenic activity).
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Essential oil dominated by linalyl acetate and linalool, with sclareol (a diterpene with oestrogenic activity).

distribution.habitat_description: Native to the northern Mediterranean and Central Asia, cultivated in Algeria and elsewhere for essential oil (‘clary sage’).Flowering:June–August.Harvesting:Flowering tops harvested at full bloom for essential-oil distillation.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Used traditionally as an antispasmodic, for menstrual/menopausal complaints, and as an aromatic/carminative digestive aid; essential oil used in aromatherapy for stress and mood.Parts Used:Flowering aerial parts, essential oil.Dosage:Essential oil used mainly by inhalation/topical dilution (aromatherapy); internal use not standardized.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: Small clinical trials suggest clary sage aromatherapy reduces labour pain/anxiety and menopausal symptoms; evidence base remains limited in size and rigor.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Inhalation of clary sage essential oil reduced cortisol levels and improved mood parameters in small human studies; sclareol shows oestrogen-receptor-modulating and antiproliferative activity in vitro.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Raw/unripe berries, leaves, bark, and seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides (sambunigrin) and can cause nausea, vomiting and cyanide-related toxicity if consumed raw in quantity; berries must be cooked (heat-processed commercial preparations are safe).Drug-plant interaction:May have additive effect with immunosuppressant drugs (theoretical, due to immunomodulatory activity) and with diuretics/laxatives.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Diaphoretic, antiviral, immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant.Phytochemical profile:Anthocyanins (cyanidin-3-glucoside), flavonoids (quercetin, rutin), triterpenes, cyanogenic glycosides (in unripe/raw parts).
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Anthocyanins (cyanidin-3-glucoside), flavonoids (quercetin, rutin), triterpenes, cyanogenic glycosides (in unripe/raw parts).
