distribution.habitat_description: Europe, North Africa incl. Algeria, western Asia; grows in hedgerows, woodland edges, disturbed ground (‘elder’).Flowering:May–June.Harvesting:Flowers collected at full bloom; ripe berries harvested August–September (must be cooked before consumption).

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Flowers, ripe berries (cooked).
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Flowers used for common cold/influenza symptoms, fever, and as a diaphoretic (EMA-approved); berries used as an immune-supportive and antiviral remedy.Parts Used:Flowers, ripe berries (cooked).Dosage:Flower infusion: 2–4 g dried flowers per cup, 3 times daily; standardized berry extract: 300–1200 mg/day in clinical studies for cold/flu.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Flower infusion: 2–4 g dried flowers per cup, 3 times daily; standardized berry extract: 300–1200 mg/day in clinical studies for cold/flu.

scientific_data.clinical: Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses show standardized elderberry extract reduces the duration and severity of cold/influenza symptoms when taken early in illness.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Elderberry extracts inhibit influenza virus haemagglutination and replication in vitro, and modulate cytokine production in immune cell assays.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Acute toxicity studies indicate a moderate-to-low toxicity profile for the essential oil; nonetheless, comprehensive dose-dependent and long-term toxicity data remain limited, and unsupervised high-dose or prolonged use is not recommended.Drug-plant interaction:None specifically documented.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Essential oil rich in hydrocarbon and oxygenated sesquiterpenes, plus monoterpenes (camphor, 1,8-cineole, borneol, β-pinene); high total phenolic content.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Used in European/North African folk medicine for wound healing, digestive disorders and skin infections; also traditionally used as an anthelmintic and insect repellent.Parts Used:Aerial flowering parts, essential oil.Dosage:Traditional infusion, not formally standardized.

scientific_data.clinical: No controlled human clinical trials identified; evidence remains preclinical.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Essential oil demonstrated antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticandidal and moderate cytotoxic activity in vitro, with a favourable (low-to-moderate) predicted toxicity class in in silico screening.A pharmacological study (acute toxicity, anti-inflammatory and antiulcer activity) established a reasonable margin of safety in animal models along with confirmed anti-inflammatory/antiulcer effects.

traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Primarily an industrial/fibre plant (cordage, mats, esparto paper); in local folk practice the leaves/roots have occasionally been used as a mild diuretic and for digestive complaints, though this is a minor and poorly documented use compared to its economic role.Parts Used:Leaves (fibre), occasionally roots.Dosage:Not established for medicinal use; traditional/occasional folk infusion only.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Not established for medicinal use; traditional/occasional folk infusion only.

scientific_data.clinical: No clinical trial data identified; this species is not established as a medicinal plant in modern pharmacognosy.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Most research on S. tenacissima addresses its fibre/biomass and papermaking properties rather than pharmacology; a small number of screening studies report modest antioxidant activity of leaf extracts.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally considered safe at traditional doses; high-tannin preparations (especially galls) may cause GI upset or reduce iron/protein absorption with prolonged use.Drug-plant interaction:Tannins may reduce absorption of co-administered alkaloid drugs/iron.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Tannins (particularly high in galls), flavonoids (quercetin derivatives), phenolic acids, triterpenes.

distribution.habitat_description: Mediterranean coasts and North Africa incl. Algeria; salt-tolerant shrub/small tree of coastal and saline habitats (‘French tamarisk’).Flowering:April–September.Harvesting:Bark, leaves and galls collected year-round; galls (rich in tannin) especially valued.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Bark/leaves used traditionally as an astringent for diarrhoea, and for liver and spleen disorders, skin diseases and wound healing; galls used as a potent astringent for haemorrhage and diarrhoea.Parts Used:Bark, leaves, galls.Dosage:Decoction of bark/leaves, traditional use; not formally standardized.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: No controlled human clinical trials identified; evidence remains preclinical and ethnobotanical.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Bark/leaf extracts show significant hepatoprotective activity against chemically induced liver injury and strong antioxidant activity correlating with high tannin/phenolic content in rodent studies.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally well tolerated; may cause mild GI upset or allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to Asteraceae; contraindicated in bile-duct obstruction given cholagogue activity.Drug-plant interaction:May have additive effect with diuretics and potentiate lithium retention (via diuretic-related electrolyte shifts, as documented for the genus); theoretical interaction with anticoagulants (vitamin K content of leaves).Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

distribution.habitat_description: Europe, North Africa incl. Algeria, temperate regions; grows in dry, sandy or rocky ground, distinguished from the common dandelion (T. officinale) by more deeply lobed leaves.Flowering:March–June.Harvesting:Roots lifted in autumn; leaves collected young in spring.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:As with T. officinale, root and leaf used traditionally as a mild diuretic (‘pissenlit’), digestive bitter/cholagogue, and mild laxative; leaves consumed as a spring green vegetable.Parts Used:Root, leaves.Dosage:Root decoction: 3–4 g dried root per cup, 3 times daily; leaf infusion similarly dosed (traditional use, extrapolated from T. officinale monographs).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: Small clinical studies of T. officinale-type dandelion extracts show a modest diuretic effect in humans; no species-specific trials for T. laevigatum identified.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Genus-level studies (largely on T. officinale, extrapolated to T. laevigatum) show diuretic activity attributed to high potassium content, and choleretic/hepatoprotective activity of root extracts in animal models.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Significant hepatotoxicity risk: France withdrew germander products from the market in 1992, and Italy subsequently banned sale of germander-containing herbal preparations; contraindicated in pregnancy, lactation, children under 12, and in anyone with liver disease; toxic effects typically appear within about 9 weeks of regular use and are manifested as jaundice and elevated liver enzymes.Drug-plant interaction:May potentiate other hepatotoxic drugs (e.g., paracetamol, methotrexate); possible interaction with anticoagulants via flavonoid content.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antispasmodic, cholagogic, anti-inflammatory (phenylethanoid glycoside fraction); the neo-clerodane diterpenoid fraction is hepatotoxic rather than therapeutically useful.Phytochemical profile:Phenylethanoid glycosides (teucrioside — beneficial fraction), neo-clerodane diterpenoids (teucrin A and related furano-diterpenes — hepatotoxic fraction), flavonoids.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Phenylethanoid glycosides (teucrioside — beneficial fraction), neo-clerodane diterpenoids (teucrin A and related furano-diterpenes — hepatotoxic fraction), flavonoids.

distribution.habitat_description: Mediterranean basin incl. Algeria, central/southern Europe; grows on rocky, calcareous hillsides (‘wall germander’).Flowering:June–September.Harvesting:Aerial parts (flowering tops) collected at early bloom, when diterpene content peaks.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Aerial parts (flowering tops).
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Historically used for over 2000 years as a diuretic, diaphoretic, tonic, antispasmodic and cholagogic remedy, and for diabetes, dyspepsia, gout, and as a weight-loss/anorectic slimming decoction.Parts Used:Aerial parts (flowering tops).Dosage:Historical traditional dose ~1–3 g dried herb/day as infusion — modern use is strongly discouraged (see Toxicity); limit any use, if undertaken, to 2–3 weeks with a month's rest between courses.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Historical traditional dose ~1–3 g dried herb/day as infusion — modern use is strongly discouraged (see Toxicity); limit any use, if undertaken, to 2–3 weeks with a month's rest between courses.

scientific_data.clinical: Multiple documented clinical case series of acute hepatitis/severe liver injury (elevated ALT/AST, jaundice, in some cases cholestatic hepatitis) following use of wild-harvested germander decoctions/slimming preparations, with recovery over weeks to months after cessation.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Teucrin A is metabolized via CYP3A4 to reactive epoxide intermediates that cause midzonal hepatocyte necrosis in animal and human liver-cell models; teucrioside (the phenylethanoid glycoside fraction) shows anti-inflammatory/antioxidant activity without the hepatotoxic diterpenoid liability.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:No significant toxicity reported in the preclinical literature reviewed to date; nonetheless, essential-oil preparations should be used with the general caution applied to Lamiaceae essential oils (potential mucosal irritation at high concentration).Drug-plant interaction:None specifically documented; theoretical additive hypoglycaemic effect with antidiabetic drugs.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antimicrobial, antioxidant, anticancer (preclinical), anti-ulcer, antidiabetic, insecticidal, anti-inflammatory.Phytochemical profile:Essential oil (composition variable by region — e.g., α-pinene and acorenone reported in Algerian populations), high content of polyphenols, flavonoids and terpenoids.
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Essential oil (composition variable by region — e.g., α-pinene and acorenone reported in Algerian populations), high content of polyphenols, flavonoids and terpenoids.

distribution.habitat_description: Endemic/native to the Mediterranean, mainly distributed in Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia; grows in dry, rocky steppe and mountain habitats.Flowering:April–June.Harvesting:Aerial flowering parts collected at bloom for infusion/essential-oil distillation.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Aerial flowering parts, essential oil.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Used for centuries in North African traditional medicine for inflammation, diabetes, rheumatism, digestive and respiratory complaints, as a flu remedy, antirheumatic and diuretic agent.Parts Used:Aerial flowering parts, essential oil.Dosage:Infusion: 1–2 g dried herb per cup, 2–3 times daily (traditional use; not formally standardized).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion: 1–2 g dried herb per cup, 2–3 times daily (traditional use; not formally standardized).

scientific_data.clinical: No controlled human clinical trials identified; comprehensive review (Mahdi et al., 2022) notes no toxicity observed in the in vivo/preclinical studies reviewed.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Extracts show a positive effect on leukocyte migration/inflammation mediation in immune-response models, and antioxidant activity correlated with phenolic content, generally moderate relative to other Mediterranean aromatic plants (e.g., Rosmarinus officinalis) in comparative DPPH assays.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally well tolerated as tea/culinary herb; the concentrated essential oil can cause GI irritation, and in high doses CNS depression; contact dermatitis reported with topical essential-oil use; caution advised in pregnancy with high-dose essential oil.Drug-plant interaction:May potentiate sedative drugs (theoretical); may have additive effect with other antitussive/expectorant agents.Plant-plant interaction:Commonly and safely combined with primula root (Primula veris) in standardized cough-syrup products.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

distribution.habitat_description: Native to the western Mediterranean, widely cultivated worldwide incl. Algeria (‘common/garden thyme’).Flowering:May–July.Harvesting:Aerial parts harvested at flowering, when essential-oil content is highest.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:EMA-approved traditional use for cough associated with colds, and as a symptomatic remedy for catarrh of the upper respiratory tract; also traditionally used as a carminative digestive aid.Parts Used:Aerial parts (leaves and flowers).Dosage:Infusion: 1–2 g dried herb per cup, up to 3 times daily; standardized liquid extract (with primula root) used in cough-syrup clinical trials.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: RCTs of a standardized thyme/primula root combination liquid extract show significant reduction in cough frequency and bronchitis symptoms compared with placebo, with efficacy comparable to some conventional expectorants.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Thymol/carvacrol show broncholytic (smooth-muscle relaxant) and expectorant activity in isolated tracheal preparations, plus broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity in vitro.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally well tolerated; common side effects include GI upset (bloating, diarrhoea) and a maple-syrup-like body/urine odour; contraindicated in pregnancy at medicinal doses due to uterotonic activity reported in animal studies.Drug-plant interaction:May potentiate antidiabetic drugs and anticoagulants (coumarin-like constituents); may affect absorption of concurrently administered oral drugs due to high mucilage/fibre content.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

distribution.habitat_description: Native to the eastern Mediterranean/western Asia, cultivated worldwide incl. Algeria (‘fenugreek’).Flowering:April–June.Harvesting:Seeds harvested when pods mature, late spring/early summer.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Seeds used traditionally for loss of appetite (EMA-approved), as a galactagogue for breastfeeding mothers, and in Ayurvedic/North African folk medicine for diabetes and digestive complaints.Parts Used:Seeds.Dosage:Powdered seed: 5–30 g/day (traditional/clinical dosing range) in divided doses, with meals.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses show fenugreek seed supplementation modestly improves fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipid profile in type 2 diabetes, and increases breast-milk volume in lactating mothers.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:4-Hydroxyisoleucine stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion in isolated pancreatic islet studies; galactomannan fibre slows gastric emptying and carbohydrate absorption in animal models.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally well tolerated; not recommended in patients with oedema due to reduced cardiac or renal function requiring restricted fluid intake, consistent with other aquaretic herbs.Drug-plant interaction:May have additive effect with other diuretics.Plant-plant interaction:Often combined with other urinary-tract herbs (e.g., Solidago virgaurea) in traditional formulations.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

distribution.habitat_description: Europe, North Africa incl. Algeria, temperate Asia; a common rhizomatous grass weed of cultivated and waste ground (‘couch grass’, ‘dog grass’).Flowering:June–August.Harvesting:Rhizomes lifted in spring or autumn, washed and dried.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Rhizome used traditionally and per ESCOP as an aquaretic for mild lower urinary tract complaints and to increase urine volume in cases of renal gravel; also a mild traditional laxative.Parts Used:Rhizome.Dosage:Decoction: 6–9 g dried rhizome per day, with adequate fluid intake (ESCOP/traditional dosing).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: Long traditional/ESCOP-recognized use for urinary tract irrigation therapy; no large modern controlled clinical trials identified.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Rhizome extracts show mild diuretic activity in animal models, attributed to fructan/mannitol content and osmotic effects; mucilage provides a demulcent, soothing effect on urinary tract mucosa in traditional preparations.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally safe as a food/traditional remedy in typical quantities; isothiocyanate content can be irritant to the GI mucosa in excess; contraindicated in gastric/duodenal ulcers and kidney inflammation (renal irritant potential at high doses).Drug-plant interaction:None significant documented.Plant-plant interaction:Traditionally and clinically combined with horseradish (Armoracia rusticana) for synergistic antimicrobial effect.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

distribution.habitat_description: Native to South America (Andes); widely cultivated as an ornamental/edible plant in Algeria and worldwide (‘garden nasturtium’).Flowering:Summer–autumn.Harvesting:Leaves and flowers collected fresh as needed; seeds collected when mature.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Leaves/flowers used traditionally (often combined with horseradish) for urinary tract infections and respiratory infections (EMA-approved traditional use); also used as an edible, peppery salad plant.Parts Used:Fresh aerial parts (leaves, flowers).Dosage:Fresh herb: ~5 g/day (or standardized combination product with horseradish root, per EMA monograph).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: A standardized combination of nasturtium herb and horseradish root has been studied in clinical trials for acute sinusitis, bronchitis and urinary tract infection, showing efficacy comparable to standard antibiotics in some studies.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Benzyl isothiocyanate shows potent broad-spectrum antibacterial activity in vitro against common urinary and respiratory pathogens, supporting traditional use.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Contains hepatotoxic, genotoxic and carcinogenic pyrrolizidine alkaloids; regulatory agencies in several countries (e.g., Germany) restrict internal use to short durations (a few weeks per year) and to preparations with pyrrolizidine-alkaloid content below strict limits; contraindicated in pregnancy, lactation and in children; several case reports of hepatic veno-occlusive disease linked to coltsfoot use.Drug-plant interaction:May have additive hepatotoxic effect with other hepatotoxic drugs/herbs.Plant-plant interaction:Additive pyrrolizidine-alkaloid hepatotoxic risk if combined with other PA-containing plants (e.g., comfrey, Senecio spp.).
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

distribution.habitat_description: Europe, North Africa incl. Algeria, temperate Asia; grows on disturbed, clay-rich ground (‘coltsfoot’).Flowering:February–April (flowers appear before leaves).Harvesting:Flowers collected in early spring; leaves collected in summer.

scientific_data.clinical: No modern controlled clinical trials support internal use given the hepatotoxicity/carcinogenicity concerns associated with pyrrolizidine alkaloid content; traditional use is now largely discouraged or restricted to pyrrolizidine-alkaloid-free certified preparations.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Mucilage and flavonoid fractions provide demulcent and mild anti-inflammatory activity in respiratory-tract models.

traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Root resin used for centuries (since Hippocrates/Theophrastus, ~300–400 BC) in Mediterranean folk medicine for pulmonary disease, female infertility, catarrh, fever, and as a rubefacient/counter-irritant plaster for rheumatic pain; still used in present-day Moroccan/North African traditional medicine.Parts Used:Root and fruit resin (external/topical use only in traditional practice, due to severe skin-irritant properties).Dosage:Historical topical plaster preparations only; no safe oral traditional dosage established — modern use is restricted to pharmaceutical derivatives (see below).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: A thapsigargin-derived prodrug (mipsagargin/G-202), designed to selectively target tumour vasculature, entered clinical trials in 2008 for solid tumours — representing a modern pharmaceutical derivative rather than use of the raw plant.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Thapsigargin potently and irreversibly inhibits the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA) pump, inducing apoptosis in nearly all cell types studied; identified as a histamine liberator from rat mast cells, explaining its intense skin-irritant/counter-irritant action.

scientific_data.clinical: No controlled human clinical trials identified for U. minor/campestris specifically (contrasts with the more extensively studied North American Ulmus rubra, 'slippery elm', which has similar traditional uses).
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Mucilage-rich bark extracts show soothing/demulcent activity on irritated mucous membranes and mild antimicrobial activity in vitro, consistent with traditional wound-care and GI-soothing use.

Algeria; grows in nitrogen-rich disturbed ground, hedgerows and woodland edges ('stinging nettle').Flowering:June–September.Harvesting:Aerial parts (leaves) collected before/at flowering (gloves required due to stinging hairs); roots lifted in autumn.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Leaves used traditionally and per EMA/ESCOP for rheumatic complaints, as an adjuvant diuretic for urinary-tract irrigation, and to increase urine volume; root used traditionally for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) symptoms; leaves also consumed as a nutritive spring vegetable.Parts Used:Aerial parts (leaves), root.Dosage:Leaf infusion: 8–12 g dried leaf/day; root extract (BPH): 300–1200 mg/day standardized extract (EMA/clinical dosing).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: Multiple RCTs (including combination with Serenoa repens/saw palmetto) show nettle root extract improves urinary flow and reduces symptoms in mild-to-moderate BPH; leaf preparations show modest benefit as adjunct therapy in osteoarthritis/rheumatic pain in smaller trials.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Nettle root extract inhibits binding of sex-hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) to its prostate membrane receptor and shows mild 5-alpha-reductase inhibitory activity in vitro, relevant to BPH pathophysiology; leaf extracts show anti-inflammatory activity in models of rheumatoid arthritis-related cytokine release.

traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Root used traditionally and per EMA/ESCOP for mild nervous tension and to aid sleep (mild sedative/hypnotic) — one of the most widely used and best-studied traditional sedative herbs.Parts Used:Root and rhizome.Dosage:Dried root extract: 400–900 mg, 30–60 minutes before bedtime for sleep; 120–200 mg up to 3 times daily for nervous tension (EMA monograph).

scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Valerenic acid shows positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors in vitro, providing a mechanistic basis for the sedative/anxiolytic effect; extracts reduce locomotor activity and increase sleep duration in animal models.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally well tolerated; mild GI upset, headache, acneiform skin reactions, and menstrual cycle changes occasionally reported; not recommended during pregnancy/lactation or with hormone-sensitive conditions given hormone-modulating activity.Drug-plant interaction:May reduce efficacy of dopamine antagonists (e.g., antipsychotics, metoclopramide) and may interact with hormonal contraceptives/hormone replacement therapy (theoretical, due to hormone-modulating activity).Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Fruit used traditionally and per EMA/ESCOP for premenstrual syndrome (PMS), cyclical mastalgia (breast pain), and menstrual cycle irregularities; historically also used to reduce libido ('monk's pepper').Parts Used:Ripe fruit (berries).Dosage:Standardized extract (e.g., Ze 440 or similar): 20–40 mg dried fruit extract/day (EMA/clinical dosing).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses show Vitex agnus-castus extract significantly reduces PMS symptoms (irritability, mood alteration, breast tenderness, bloating) and cyclical mastalgia compared with placebo, with efficacy in some trials comparable to low-dose fluoxetine or pyridoxine for PMS.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Clerodadienol diterpenes bind to and activate dopamine D2 receptors in vitro, reducing prolactin release from pituitary lactotroph cells — the key mechanism underlying efficacy in cyclical mastalgia and PMS.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally very well tolerated; mild GI upset or headache occasionally reported with standardized extracts; grape/wine consumption in excess carries the general risks associated with alcohol (not attributable to the plant itself).Drug-plant interaction:May potentiate anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs (theoretical, given flavonoid/proanthocyanidin antiplatelet activity); resveratrol may inhibit certain CYP450 enzymes at high supplemental doses.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

distribution.habitat_description: Native to the Mediterranean/western Asia, extensively cultivated in Algeria and worldwide ('grapevine').Flowering:May–June.Harvesting:Leaves collected in early summer (for medicinal use); fruit (grapes) harvested August–October; seeds obtained from wine-making by-products.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Red vine leaf used traditionally and per EMA/ESCOP for chronic venous insufficiency (leg heaviness, varicose vein discomfort, oedema); seed extract used for antioxidant/vascular support; fruit consumed as food and processed into wine.Parts Used:Leaves (red vine leaf), seeds, fruit.Dosage:Standardized red vine leaf extract: 360–720 mg/day (EMA monograph); grape seed extract: 150–300 mg/day in clinical studies.
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: Multiple RCTs show standardized red vine leaf extract significantly reduces leg volume, oedema, and subjective symptoms (heaviness, pain) in chronic venous insufficiency compared with placebo; grape-seed extract shows modest benefit on vascular endothelial function and antioxidant status in clinical trials.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Red vine leaf extract reduces capillary permeability and leukocyte adhesion in models of venous insufficiency; grape-seed proanthocyanidins show potent free-radical-scavenging activity, exceeding that of vitamins C and E in some in vitro comparative assays.

safety_profile.contraindications: Déconseillé chez la femme enceinte ou allaitante par principe de précaution.
safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally very well tolerated; not recommended in patients with oedema due to reduced cardiac or renal function requiring restricted fluid intake, as with other aquaretic herbs; rare allergic reactions reported.Drug-plant interaction:May have additive effect with other diuretics and antidiabetic drugs (theoretical, given hypoglycaemic activity reported preclinically).Plant-plant interaction:Commonly combined with other urinary-tract herbs (e.g., Solidago virgaurea, Elymus repens) in traditional formulations.
safety_profile.drug_interactions: Surveiller en cas de traitement chronique concomitant.
safety_profile.plant_interactions: Synergies possibles avec les Lamiacées et Astéracées locales.

pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Flavonoids (maysin), saponins, mucilage, potassium salts, allantoin, sterols.

distribution.habitat_description: Domesticated in Mesoamerica; cultivated worldwide as a staple crop incl. Algeria ('maize', 'corn').Flowering:Summer, variety-dependent.Harvesting:Styles/stigmas ('corn silk') collected when the female flower is fresh, before pollination completes; grain harvested at maturity.

traditional_medicine.parts_used: Parties aériennes, sommités fleuries ou feuilles
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Corn silk (stigmas/styles) used traditionally and per EMA/ESCOP as a mild diuretic/aquaretic for lower urinary tract complaints; grain used as a major dietary staple.Parts Used:Styles and stigmas (corn silk); grain (food).Dosage:Infusion: 4–8 g dried corn silk per day, with adequate fluid intake (traditional/ESCOP dosing).
traditional_medicine.dosage: Infusion standard à 5% (1 cuillère à café par tasse d'eau bouillante)

scientific_data.clinical: Traditional/ESCOP-recognized use for urinary-tract irrigation therapy; limited modern controlled human clinical trial data, though corn silk has a long history of safe traditional use across multiple cultures (European, Chinese, Native American).
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Corn silk extracts show diuretic activity in animal models attributed to potassium salt content, and antioxidant/hypoglycaemic activity in preclinical studies of metabolic disease models.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:No formal LD50 or subchronic toxicity data specific to P. nigra identified; salicin-containing preparations should be used cautiously in individuals with salicylate/aspirin hypersensitivity, and in children (Reye's-syndrome-type caution by analogy with salicylates).Drug-plant interaction:Potential additive effect with anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs (salicylate content); theoretical interaction with NSAIDs.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, hepatoprotective, antimicrobial (antibacterial/antifungal), vasorelaxant, antitumor, hypouricemic.Phytochemical profile:Phenolic glycosides (salicin, populin), flavones/flavanones (chrysin, pinocembrin, pinostrobin, apigenin), phenolic acids (caffeic, ferulic), essential oil terpenoids (~48 compounds, e.g., cadinene, bisabolene, farnesol).

distribution.habitat_description: Native to Europe, western Asia and North Africa; widely present across Algeria, along riverbanks and cultivated as ornamental/windbreak tree.Flowering:February–April (catkins, before leaf-out).Harvesting:Resinous buds collected in late winter/early spring, before opening.
distribution.flowering_harvesting:
Flowering Stage: Late winter through spring.
Harvesting: Gathered from late autumn through spring while vegetative growth is dense.

traditional_medicine.parts_used:
Leaves, flowers, stems, and underground tubers.
Dosage & Preparation: Eaten raw in salads or boiled to mitigate the sharp acid taste.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Rheumatism, arthritis, lower-back pain, urinary complaints, liver disorders, fever, wound healing (bud infusion/tincture, bark decoction).Parts Used:Buds, bark, leaves.Dosage:Bud tincture (1:5, 45% ethanol): 1–2 mL, 2–3 times daily; infusion of bark: 2–4 g dried bark per cup, 2–3 times daily (traditional, not formally standardized).

scientific_data.clinical: No controlled human clinical trials identified; use remains based on traditional/pharmacognostic evidence.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Ethanolic bud extract showed moderate antioxidant activity (~40%, ABTS) and potent anti-inflammatory activity (49.9% inhibition of carrageenan-induced paw oedema in mice); complete histological protection against AlCl3-induced hepatotoxicity (Boudjelal et al., 2013).Endothelium-independent vasorelaxant effect on porcine coronary artery rings, correlated with antioxidant flavonoid content, likely via inhibition of Ca2+ influx.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Considered safe as a food and traditional remedy; high oxalate content warrants caution in individuals prone to oxalate kidney stones or on oxalate-restricted diets.Drug-plant interaction:Potential additive hypoglycaemic effect with antidiabetic drugs (theoretical, monitor blood glucose).Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Anti-hyperglycaemic, anti-hyperlipidaemic, hepatoprotective, renoprotective, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, neuroprotective, antimicrobial, skeletal-muscle relaxant.Phytochemical profile:Omega-3 fatty acids (α-linolenic, γ-linolenic acid), flavonoids, alkaloids (oleracein A–E), betalains (β-cyanin), polysaccharides, vitamins A/C/E, minerals (K, P, Ca, Mg).
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Omega-3 fatty acids (α-linolenic, γ-linolenic acid), flavonoids, alkaloids (oleracein A–E), betalains (β-cyanin), polysaccharides, vitamins A/C/E, minerals (K, P, Ca, Mg).

distribution.habitat_description: Cosmopolitan succulent weed of warm climates; common in cultivated fields, gardens and waste ground throughout Algeria.Flowering:May–September.Harvesting:Whole aerial parts collected at flowering stage, used fresh or dried.
distribution.flowering_harvesting:
Flowering Stage: Spring to early summer.
Harvesting: Leafy greens harvested 20–30 days post-germination; seeds gathered when seed pods dry.

traditional_medicine.parts_used:
Leaves, seeds, juice, and extracted seed oil.
Dosage & Preparation: Fresh leaves consumed in salads. Seeds are pressed for oil or taken as decoctions.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Dysentery, diarrhoea, fever, inflammation, urinary complaints, skin eruptions; also eaten as a nutritious vegetable (‘global panacea’, WHO-listed). Recorded by Dioscorides (as ‘andrachne’) and in TCM.Parts Used:Aerial parts (stems, leaves), seeds.Dosage:Dried aerial parts: 9–15 g/day as decoction (TCM standard); fresh leaves consumed as food.

scientific_data.clinical: Clinical trials demonstrated anti-hyperglycaemic and anti-hyperlipidaemic effects; renoprotective and hepatoprotective benefits reported; most frequent adverse effect was constipation, with no serious adverse events (Iranshahy et al., 2017).
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Extracts reduced LPS-induced NO, iNOS and COX-2 expression in RAW264.7 macrophages (Kim et al., 2018); β-cyanin upregulated antioxidant enzymes (SOD, catalase, GSH-Px) and reduced malondialdehyde in a D-galactose neurotoxicity mouse model, outperforming vitamin C.Alkaloidal extract inhibited acetylcholinesterase (IC50 29.4 µg/mL).

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Experimental and traditional evidence indicates a favourable safety profile; Potentilla species generally show no toxic effects in acute or chronic use in available studies; in silico toxicity screening supports low risk.Drug-plant interaction:Tannin content may reduce absorption of co-administered alkaloid drugs and iron/protein if taken concurrently.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antinociceptive/analgesic, anti-ulcerogenic, antimicrobial, antioxidant, antiproliferative.Phytochemical profile:Tannins (6–12%), flavonoids and glycosides (quercetin, kaempferol, rutin, quercetin-3-O-glucoside, apigenin-7-O-glucoside, luteolin-7-O-glucoside), phenolic acids (gallic, caffeic).
pharmacology.phytochemical_profile: Tannins (6–12%), flavonoids and glycosides (quercetin, kaempferol, rutin, quercetin-3-O-glucoside, apigenin-7-O-glucoside, luteolin-7-O-glucoside), phenolic acids (gallic, caffeic).

distribution.habitat_description: Europe, North Africa (incl. Algeria) and temperate Asia; grows in damp grassy areas, roadsides and field margins.Flowering:May–September.Harvesting:Roots/rhizomes collected in autumn; aerial parts collected during flowering.
distribution.flowering_harvesting:
Flowering Stage: Early spring, with catkins appearing alongside new leaves.
Harvesting: Bark is peeled away during early spring when sap flow is high; leaves picked in summer.

traditional_medicine.parts_used:
Bark, twigs, and leaves.
Dosage & Preparation: Decoctions of dried bark (typically 1–3g powder) taken up to three times daily.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Known as ‘Banṭāfulun’ in Arabic medicine; astringent, anti-inflammatory and analgesic remedy for diarrhoea, mouth/throat ulcers, toothache, and wound healing.Parts Used:Roots, leaves, whole herb.Dosage:Root decoction: 2–4 g dried root per cup, 2–3 times daily (traditional use; not formally standardized).

scientific_data.clinical: No controlled human trials identified.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Hydroalcoholic root/aerial extract (100–500 mg/kg, oral) dose-dependently reduced acetic-acid-induced writhing and increased hot-plate latency in mice; effect was significantly antagonized by naloxone, indicating opioid-receptor mediation; no rotarod-detected motor impairment.Leaf extract showed significant gastroprotective activity against ethanol-induced gastric ulcers in rats, confirmed histopathologically (Gurbuz, 2005).

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Flowers and fruit pulp are considered safe at traditional doses; however, the seeds (kernels) contain cyanogenic glycosides (amygdalin) and should not be ingested.Drug-plant interaction:None specifically documented; theoretical additive effect with diuretics given traditional diuretic use.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory (pro-inflammatory enzyme inhibition), antitumor/cytotoxic in vitro.Phytochemical profile:Flavonoids, A-type proanthocyanidins, anthocyanins, phenolic acids — 57 marker constituents identified in flowers (up to 584 mg/g dw total phenolics).

distribution.habitat_description: Europe, North Africa and western Asia; thorny hedgerow shrub, present in northern Algeria.Flowering:February–April, before leaf emergence.Harvesting:Flowers collected at full bloom; fruits (sloes) harvested September–November, after first frost.
distribution.flowering_harvesting:
Flowering Stage: Mid-spring to early summer.
Harvesting: Bark collected in early autumn; mature drupes harvested in late summer.

traditional_medicine.parts_used:
Bark, leaves, and fruits.
Dosage & Preparation: Bark boiled down as a strong purgative decoction; used sparingly due to immediate drastic effects.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Central/Eastern European folk remedy for urinary-tract disorders, gastrointestinal inflammation, diarrhoea, and as adjunct cardiovascular/anti-hypertensive support; fruit also processed into jams, liqueurs.Parts Used:Flowers, fruit (pulp), bark.Dosage:Flower infusion: 1–2 g dried flowers per cup, 2–3 times daily (traditional use).

scientific_data.clinical: No controlled human clinical trials identified.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Flower extract fractions inhibited pro-inflammatory enzymes and protected against oxidative stress in vitro while showing good cellular safety (Frontiers in Pharmacology, 2017).Fruit (flower) extract exhibited concentration-dependent cytotoxicity in HepG2 hepatocarcinoma cells at concentrations above 50 µg/mL (neutral red/kenacid blue assays).

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Fruit, juice and peel extracts are generally safe at dietary/supplemental doses; root/stem bark contains piperidine alkaloids (pelletierine) which are more toxic and have a narrow safety margin — high doses can cause dizziness, vomiting, and CNS effects, so bark preparations are no longer recommended.Drug-plant interaction:Pomegranate juice can inhibit CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, potentially increasing plasma levels of statins, some antihypertensives and warfarin.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

distribution.habitat_description: Native to Iran/Himalayan region; extensively cultivated across the Mediterranean, incl. Algeria.Flowering:April–June.Harvesting:Fruit harvested September–November; peel/bark collected after fruit processing.
distribution.flowering_harvesting:
Flowering Stage: Spring to summer.
Harvesting: Seeds collected in late summer when capsules ripen and turn brown.

traditional_medicine.parts_used:
Primarily seeds; occasionally roots.
Dosage & Preparation: Ground seeds taken in micro-doses (under 1–2g) or burned as incense for therapeutic inhalation.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Fruit/peel used for diarrhoea, dysentery, sore throat and wound healing; bark historically used as an anthelmintic (tapeworm); juice for general cardiovascular tonic.Parts Used:Fruit, peel (pericarp), seed oil, bark/root (anthelmintic use, less common today).Dosage:Peel decoction: 1–2 g dried peel per cup, 2–3 times daily; juice: 200–250 mL/day in clinical studies.

scientific_data.clinical: Multiple RCTs show pomegranate juice/extract reduces blood pressure, LDL oxidation and carotid intima-media thickness, and improves markers of atherosclerosis; generally well tolerated.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Peel extract showed strong antistaphylococcal activity (MIC 0.25–2.00 mg/mL), among the most active of 17 Mediterranean species screened, alongside Rhamnus alaternus.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Generally recognized as safe; mastic is an approved food additive/chewing gum base; allergic contact reactions are rare.Drug-plant interaction:No significant interactions established; theoretical additive effect with other antimicrobial H. pylori regimens.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antimicrobial (notably anti-Helicobacter pylori), anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, gastroprotective, hepatoprotective.Phytochemical profile:Triterpenes (masticadienonic acid, oleanolic/moronic acid), essential oil (α-pinene, myrcene, β-caryophyllene), tannins, flavonoids.

distribution.habitat_description: Evergreen Mediterranean maquis shrub; widespread in coastal and mountainous northern Algeria.Flowering:March–May.Harvesting:Resin (mastic gum) tapped from bark incisions in summer; leaves collected year-round.
distribution.flowering_harvesting:
Flowering Stage: Late spring to early summer.
Harvesting: Aerial parts harvested at the peak of full flowering.

traditional_medicine.parts_used:
Dried aerial parts.
Dosage & Preparation: Strict, small-scale infusions. Extreme caution required due to high potency.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Resin (mastic) chewed/used for dyspepsia, gastric ulcer, halitosis; leaves and oil applied for wound healing and GI complaints; antiseptic.Parts Used:Resin (mastic gum), leaves, fruit oil.Dosage:Mastic gum: 1–3 g/day in clinical studies (chewed or as capsules).

scientific_data.clinical: Randomized clinical trials (e.g., Huwez et al., 1998) reported mastic gum reduced H. pylori load and improved dyspeptic symptoms in a subset of patients; subsequent trials show more modest/mixed eradication results, generally as adjunct rather than monotherapy.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Mastic gum showed in vitro bactericidal activity against H. pylori and gastroprotective effects in ulcer models.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:At normal culinary/medicinal doses the fruit is safe; the essential oil, at high doses, can be hepatotoxic and neurotoxic. Estragole is classified by EFSA as a genotoxic/carcinogenic component of concern at high, chronic exposure, so essential-oil use is limited in duration and dose; contact dermatitis has been reported.Drug-plant interaction:May potentiate estrogen-dependent conditions; theoretical interaction with hormone therapy.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

Flowering Stage: Blooms from late winter through spring.
Harvesting: Leafy matter gathered in late winter for local food preparations.

traditional_medicine.parts_used:
Leaves, stems, and flowers.
Dosage & Preparation: Steamed or boiled as a wild vegetable dish; occasionally crushed as fresh juice for topical applications.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Carminative, digestive, expectorant, mild galactagogue, infant colic remedy; EMA traditional-use indications: dyspepsia and catarrh of the upper respiratory tract.Parts Used:Dried ripe fruit (aniseed), essential oil.Dosage:Crushed fruit: 3 g as infusion, up to 3 times daily; essential oil: 0.05–0.2 g/day (EMA monograph).

scientific_data.clinical: Clinical trials support use for functional dyspepsia (symptom relief) and reduction of menopausal hot-flash frequency, attributed to the mild estrogenic activity of anethole (EMA, 2014).
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Anethole exhibited dose-dependent antispasmodic activity on isolated intestinal and tracheal smooth muscle.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Essential oil can irritate mucous membranes and kidneys at high doses; prolonged high-dose use is discouraged given limited modern safety data.Drug-plant interaction:None well documented; theoretical additive irritant effect with other diuretic/urinary agents.Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

distribution.habitat_description: Native to Indonesia (Java, Sumatra); cultivated in SE Asia and traded as a dried spice/medicinal fruit used in North African and Middle Eastern traditional medicine.Flowering:Year-round in native tropical climate.Harvesting:Unripe fruit picked and sun-dried, retaining the stalk (‘tailed pepper’).
distribution.flowering_harvesting:
Flowering Stage: Mid-spring to late summer.
Harvesting: Roots dug out in late autumn; leafy stems collected mid-summer.

traditional_medicine.parts_used:
Roots and aerial parts.
Dosage & Preparation: Decoctions of dried roots used as a wash for skin irritations or taken in moderation for respiratory relief.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Dried unripe fruit used for urogenital infections, bronchitis and digestive complaints; chewed traditionally for halitosis and throat irritation.Parts Used:Dried unripe fruit, essential oil.Dosage:Powdered fruit: 1–4 g/day (traditional use; not formally standardized in modern pharmacopoeias).

scientific_data.clinical: No modern controlled clinical trials identified; historical clinical use for gonorrhoea/urethritis predates antibiotics and is no longer standard practice.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Cubebin and related lignans demonstrated anti-inflammatory and hepatoprotective activity in rodent models; essential oil showed antimicrobial activity against urinary and respiratory pathogens in vitro.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Piperine oral LD50 in rodents is approximately 200–400 mg/kg; high doses of pepper/piperine can irritate the gastrointestinal mucosa.Drug-plant interaction:Significant — piperine inhibits CYP3A4/P-gp and can increase plasma levels (and toxicity risk) of many co-administered drugs (e.g., phenytoin, propranolol, some chemotherapeutics).Plant-plant interaction:Enhances absorption/bioavailability of curcumin (Curcuma longa) and other co-administered phytochemicals.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, bioavailability enhancer (CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein inhibition), antidepressant-like, anticancer (preclinical).Phytochemical profile:Piperine (main alkaloid, 5–9%), piperlongumine, essential oil (β-caryophyllene, limonene, sabinene).

Flowering Stage: Late spring through summer.
Harvesting: Seeds collected when the capsule structures turn brittle and tan.

traditional_medicine.parts_used:
Seeds.
Dosage & Preparation: Decocted seeds (typically 4–9g) combined with water; or applied topically as a poultice over skin swellings.
traditional_medicine.uses: Traditional Uses:Carminative and digestive stimulant; used for fever, cough and arthritic pain (rubefacient); Ayurvedic use as a bioavailability enhancer (in ‘Trikatu’ formulations).Parts Used:Dried fruit (peppercorns).Dosage:Culinary/traditional use: <1 g/day; piperine extract in clinical bioavailability studies typically 5–20 mg co-administered with the target drug.

scientific_data.clinical: Classic clinical trial (Shoba et al., 1998) showed piperine (20 mg) increased curcumin bioavailability in humans by 2000%; similar enhancement demonstrated for coenzyme Q10 and other nutrients/drugs.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Piperine inhibited hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein in vitro/in vivo, increasing bioavailability of co-administered compounds; anti-inflammatory effects shown in rodent paw-oedema models.

safety_profile.toxicity: Toxicity / Safety:Relatively low acute toxicity based on the murine LD50 (1.66 g/kg); doses approaching or exceeding this threshold should be avoided.Drug-plant interaction:Potential additive hypoglycaemic/hypolipidaemic effect with antidiabetic or lipid-lowering drugs (theoretical).Plant-plant interaction:None specifically documented.

pharmacology.activities: Pharmacological activities: Antioxidant, antidiabetic, antihyperlipidaemic, antimicrobial, antitumor, antinociceptive.Phytochemical profile:Hispolone derivatives, terpenoids, phenolic compounds, essential oil (α-pinene, terpinolene, β-myrcene).

Inner bark.

Seeds.

scientific_data.clinical: Randomized controlled trials show prunes are more effective than psyllium for improving stool frequency and consistency in chronic constipation (Attaluri et al., 2011); other RCTs show a favourable effect on bone mineral density in postmenopausal women.
scientific_data.experimental: Experimental essays:Prone polyphenols show antioxidant activity and modulate gut microbiota in vitro.
